## Commentary on the Mahāvagga
## Saṃyutta Nikāya
## Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One
## 1. Maggasaṃyutta
## 1. Avijjāvagga
## 1-2. Commentary on the Avijjā Sutta, etc.

1-2. In the first sutta of the Mahāvagga, 'precursor' (pubbaṅgama) means being a precursor in two ways: by way of conascence (sahajāta) and by way of decisive support (upanissaya).

'Samāpattiyā' means for the sake of fulfillment, for the sake of obtaining its own nature, or for the sake of arising.

'Anvadeva ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ' means that ignorance (avijjā), which is the precursor and head of unwholesome states in the manner mentioned above, arises only together with lack of moral shame (ahirika), which is established by the mode of not being disgusted by evil, and lack of moral dread (anottappa), which is established by the mode of not fearing evil. It means it does not arise without these two factors.

'Avijjāgatassa' means for one who has approached ignorance, or one who is possessed of ignorance.

'Micchādiṭṭhi' (Wrong view) is a view that sees incorrectly or falsely, a view that does not lead to liberation (aniyyānika).

'Pahoti' means it occurs or it arises.

In the case of wrong intention (micchāsaṅkappa) and so forth, their state of being 'wrong' should also be understood by way of being incorrect and not leading to liberation.

Thus, these eight factors are called the factors of wrongness (micchatta-aṅga) for the attainment of unwholesome states.

However, all eight of these factors of wrongness are not obtained in a single moment; they are obtained only in different moments.

How? When a mind associated with wrong view arises, producing bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), then there are six factors: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, and wrong action...
154:
...wrong concentration, and wrong action, making six factors. When a mind dissociated from wrong view arises, there are five factors, excluding wrong view. When those two types of mind [associated or dissociated from view] produce vocal intimation (vacīviññatti), then in the place of wrong action, there is wrong speech (micchāvācā), and those same factors become either six or five. This thing called livelihood (ājīva), when it is corrupted, is corrupted only in either the bodily door or the vocal door; it is not corrupted in the mind door. Therefore, when those same minds produce bodily intimation or vocal intimation based on livelihood, the bodily action is called wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva), and similarly, the vocal action is called wrong livelihood. Thus, by way of wrong livelihood, those same factors become either six or five. However, when those minds arise without producing intimation (viññatti), then by way of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration, there are five factors; or by way of wrong intention and so forth, there are four factors. Thus, all are not obtained in a single moment, but only at different times.

In the wholesome side (sukkapakkha), 'knowledge' (vijjā) refers to the knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa). Here too, the state of being a precursor should be understood in two ways: by way of conascence and by way of decisive support. 'Hirottappa' refers to shame (hiri) and dread (ottappa). Between those two, the state established by the mode of disgust is called shame (hiri), and the state established by the mode of fear is called dread (ottappa). This is just a summary here; the detailed explanation has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. 'Vijjāgatassa' means the state of one who has approached or is possessed of knowledge. 'Viddasuno' means the state of the wise one who knows. 'Sammādiṭṭhi' (Right view) is the view that sees correctly as it is, the view that leads to liberation (niyyānika). The same method applies to right action (sammākammanta) and so forth. Thus, due to the fulfillment of wholesome states, these eight factors arise. These factors are not all obtained together in a mundane path moment (lokiya-magga-kkhaṇa), but they are obtained in a supramundane path moment (lokuttara-magga-kkhaṇa). Furthermore, those factors occur in the path associated with the first jhāna; however, in the second jhāna and so forth, there are only seven factors, excluding right intention (sammāsaṅkappa).

In that regard, if someone should say: "Because it is stated in the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya: 'Whatever view such a person has, that is his right view. Whatever intention such a person has, that is his right intention. Whatever effort such a person has, that is his right effort. Whatever mindfulness such a person has, that is his right mindfulness. Whatever concentration such a person has, that is his right concentration. Even beforehand, his bodily action, vocal action, and livelihood are well-purified.' Therefore, the supramundane path also has five factors." That person should be told: "In that very sutta, why is this statement: 'Thus, this Noble Eightfold Path of his goes to the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā)' not..."
155:
Do you not see? Furthermore, the phrase "Pubbeva kho panassa" is spoken to show the state of purity starting from the day of ordination. Indeed, for one who has ordained, the bodily actions and so forth, which are pure from that day onwards, become exceedingly pure at the moment of the supramundane path (lokuttara magga); this is the meaning intended.

In the Abhidhamma, the statement "At that time, there is a five-factored path" (Vibha. 212) is also spoken to show a specific function. At the time when one abandons wrong action and fulfills right action, at that time wrong speech or wrong livelihood does not occur. Right Action (sammākammanta) is fulfilled only within these five performing factors (kārakaṅga): Right View, Right Intention, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. Indeed, Right Action is said to be fulfilled by the power of abstinence (virati). The same method applies to Right Speech and Right Livelihood. Thus, this was taught in this way to show this specific function. At the moment of the mundane path (lokiya magga) also, only five factors occur, for abstinence is not constant. Therefore, instead of saying "a six-factored path," it is stated only as "a five-factored path." "Monks, for the person with a mind remote from defilements, with a mind free from taints, who is possessed of the noble path, and who is developing the noble path, whatever avoidance, abstinence, refraining, abstaining, non-performance, and non-commitment there is from the three types of bodily misconduct (M. Ni. 3.139)—monks, this is called Right Action which is noble, taintless, and supramundane." Thus it is taught. In this way, because the status of Right Action and so forth as factors of the supramundane path is established in many suttas such as the Mahācattārīsaka Sutta, it should be understood that the supramundane path is indeed eight-fold. In this sutta, this eight-fold path is taught as a mixture of the mundane and supramundane.

The second sutta has already been taught (explained) in the Kosala Saṃyutta.

## ၃။ သာရိပုတ္တသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

3. In the third sutta, regarding the words "Sakalamidaṃ bhante," the Elder Ānanda did not know that the entire holy life of the path is obtained by relying on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), because he had not yet reached the summit of a disciple's perfection of knowledge (sāvakapāramīñāṇa). However, the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, knew this because he stood at the summit of a disciple's perfection of knowledge; therefore, he spoke in this way. Precisely because he spoke thus, the Blessed One gave the Venerable Sāriputta the approval, saying, "Sādhu, sādhu."

## ၄။ ဇာဏုဿောဏိဗြာဟ္မဏသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the fourth sutta, "sabbasetena vaḷavābhirathena" means by a chariot drawn by four mares, which is entirely brilliant white. That chariot was reportedly fully adorned and plated with silver on its wheels, frame, and pole. Chariots are of two types: the war chariot (yodharatha) and the ornamental chariot (alaṅkāraratha). Among them, the war chariot is square-shaped, not very large, and capable of carrying only two or three people. The ornamental chariot, however, is large, long in length, and wide in breadth. In that chariot, eight or ten people, such as the umbrella-bearer, the yak-tail fan-bearer, and the palm-leaf fan-bearer, can easily stand, sit, or lie down. This chariot of the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was also an ornamental chariot.

"Setā sudaṃ assā" means those mares were naturally white in color. "Setālaṅkārā" means their ornaments were made of pure silver. "Seto ratho" means the chariot was also white, as mentioned, because it was plated with silver and inlaid with ivory work in various places. "Setaparivāro" means that unlike other chariots which might be covered with lion skins, tiger skins, or red blankets, this chariot was covered with thick white dukūla cloth. "Setā rasmiyo" means the reins were also beautifully wound with silver threads through silver tubes. "Setā patodalatṭhī" means the goad was also plated with silver.

"Setaṃ chattaṃ" means the umbrella raised in the middle of the chariot was also white. "Setaṃ uṇhīsaṃ" means the silver headband (diadem), eight finger-breadths wide, was white. "Setāni vatthāni" means his clothes were also as white as a mass of foam. Among those clothes, the lower garment was worth five hundred pieces of currency, and the upper robe was worth a thousand. "Setā upāhanā" means although footwear is usually for those traveling on a path or entering a forest, since this Brahmin was a chariot rider, it should be understood that the silver-adorned foot-ornaments suitable for a chariot rider are what is meant by "white footwear." "Setāya sudaṃ vālabījaniyā" refers to a white yak-tail fan with a crystal handle. Not only was this much of him white, but that Brahmin also smeared himself with white ointment, wore white flowers, and all his ornaments, such as rings on all ten fingers and earrings in both ears, were made of pure silver.
157:
...was. The ten thousand attendant Brahmins of that Jāṇussoṇi the Brahmin also had white garments, white unguents, white garlands, and white ornaments, just like him.

Regarding the statement 'He departs from Sāvatthī,' this is a clear explanation of his departure from the city in a grand and magnificent manner. It is heard that Jāṇussoṇi the Brahmin used to circumambulate the city once every six months. An announcement would be made well in advance: 'From this day, in so many days, he will circumambulate the city.' Hearing this announcement, those who had not yet left the city would stay. Even those who were outside the city would return, thinking, 'We shall behold the glorious prosperity of the meritorious one.' On the day the Brahmin toured the city, early in the morning, they would sweep the city streets, spread white sand, scatter flowers including parched rice as the fifth, place full water pots, set up banana trees and banners, and fill the entire city with the fragrance of incense and perfumes.

Early in the morning, the Brahmin would wash his head, eat his morning meal, and, according to the aforementioned method, adorn himself with white garments and so on, descend from his palace, and mount his chariot. Then, those Brahmins, adorned with all-white garments, unguents, garlands, and ornaments, would surround Jāṇussoṇi the Brahmin, holding white parasols. After that, to gather the crowd, they would first scatter various fruits for the youths. Next, they would scatter māsaka coins and the like. Then, they would scatter kahāpaṇas. Once the crowd had gathered, there would be shouting and the waving and tossing of garments. Then, while auspicious and prosperous people uttered blessings and words of 'May you be happy,' the Brahmin would tour the city with great prosperity. Meritorious people would ascend to one-story palaces and the like, opening window shutters that resembled the wings of a parrot to look out. The Brahmin, as if overwhelming the city with his glorious prosperity, would head toward the southern gate. It was with reference to this procession that this was said.

'Having seen him, the people' means the multitude of people, having seen that chariot. The name 'Brahma' is a designation for the 'excellent.' 'Truly, sirs, a divine vehicle!' means 'Truly, sirs, it is like an excellent vehicle'; this is the meaning here. Ānanda, it is the nature of people to give wealth to those who compose praises, and have them sing songs of praise for their young daughters, saying, 'She is beautiful, lovely to behold, possessing great wealth and great possessions.' However, they do not become beautiful or wealthy merely by such words of praise. In the same way...
158:
Even though the multitude of people, having seen the Brahmin's chariot, speak words of praise such as 'Truly, sirs, a divine vehicle!', this vehicle does not become a 'Divine Vehicle' merely by such words of praise. For this vehicle is inferior and like a rotting corpse. Ānanda, in the ultimate sense, this name 'Divine Vehicle' (Brahmayāna) is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path. This Path is excellent because it is free from all faults. Because the Noble Ones go to Nibbāna by this Path, it is called the 'Divine Vehicle' (Brahmayāna). Because it is the supreme Dhamma and is a vehicle, it is called the 'Dhamma Vehicle' (Dhammayāna). Because it is unsurpassed and because the battle of defilements has been won, it is also fit to be called the 'Unsurpassed Victory in Battle.' Now, wishing to show the faultlessness and the battle-winning nature of this Path-vehicle, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'rāgavinayapariyosānā.' In that phrase, it is called 'rāgavinayapariyosānā' because it ends by dispelling lust, or because it reaches completion. This method should be understood in all instances.

'He who has faith and wisdom' (yassa saddhā ca paññā ca) means that in this chariot of the Noble Path, faith (saddhā) by way of the faith-follower and wisdom (paññā) by way of the Dhamma-follower—these two qualities are always yoked to the pole; they are yoked to the pole of equanimity (tatramajjhattatā). 'Shame is the pole' (hirī īsā) means that moral shame (hiri) which has an internal origin, together with moral dread (ottappa) which has an external origin and resides with it, is the pole of that Path-chariot. 'The mind is the tether' (mano yottaṃ) means that insight-consciousness and path-consciousness are the tether. Just as a rope made of fiber or the like firmly binds oxen to a single yoke, so the mundane insight-consciousness of the Path-chariot firmly binds more than fifty wholesome states, and the supramundane insight-consciousness binds more than sixty wholesome states to a single object. Therefore, it is said, 'The mind is the tether.'

'Mindfulness is the watchful charioteer' (sati ārakkhasārathi) means that mindfulness associated with the Path is like a watchful charioteer. Just as a charioteer who guards the chariot performs tasks such as bearing the yoke, yoking, greasing the axle, sending the chariot forth, and making the oxen yoked to the chariot free from conflict, so the mindfulness of the Path-chariot has the nature of guarding and is said to be like a charioteer because it investigates the destinations of wholesome and unwholesome states. 'The chariot' (ratho) refers to the chariot of the Noble Eightfold Path. 'Equipped with virtue' (sīlaparikkhāro) means it has the ornaments of the fourfold purification of virtue. 'The axle of jhāna' (jhānakkho) means it has an axle made of jhāna by way of the five jhāna factors associated with insight. 'The wheels of energy' (cakkavīriyo) means it has wheels of energy; it means that the two types of energy known as bodily energy and mental energy are the wheels of that Path-chariot. Equanimity...
159:
Dhura-samādhi means the stability of the yoke. It signifies the equality of both ends of the yoke because there is no aspect of rising or falling. This tatramajjhattūpekkhā (equanimity) removes the states of sluggishness and restlessness of the mind's arising and establishes the mind in a balanced state during effort. Therefore, this chariot of the path is called "Dhura-samādhi." Anicchā parivāraṇa means that just as an external chariot is covered with lion skins and so forth, in this chariot of the Noble Path, the lack of desire known as non-greed (alobha) is the covering.

Abyāpāda refers to loving-kindness (mettā) and the states preceding loving-kindness. Avihiṃsā refers to compassion (karuṇā) and the states preceding compassion. Viveka refers to the three kinds of seclusion, such as physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). "Yassa āvudhaṃ" refers to these five weapons of the clansman who stands in the chariot of the Noble Path. Just as a person standing in a chariot shoots enemies with five weapons, so too, the practitioner (yogāvacara) standing in this mundane and supramundane chariot of the path destroys anger (dosa) with loving-kindness, cruelty (vihiṃsā) with compassion, socializing with a group (gaṇasaṅgaṇikā) with physical seclusion, socializing with defilements (kilesasaṅgaṇikā) with mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and all unwholesome states with seclusion from substrates (upadhi-viveka). Therefore, these five states are called his "weapons." Titikkhā is the virtue of patience (khanti) which endures the pathways of speech that are ill-spoken and ill-received. Cammasannāho is the leather armor that is worn. Just as a charioteer standing in a chariot, wearing leather armor, endures all incoming arrows and those arrows cannot pierce him, so too, a monk endowed with the virtue of patience endures all incoming pathways of speech and those words cannot strike him. Therefore, it is said, "Patience is the leather armor." "Yogakkhemāya vattati" means it leads to Nibbāna, which is the security from the four yokes; it means one surely goes towards Nibbāna, and does not stop or perish.

"Etadattani sambhūtaṃ" means this vehicle of the path is said to have arisen within oneself because it is obtained by relying on one's own human effort. "Brahmayānaṃ anuttaraṃ" means the incomparable, supreme vehicle. "Niyyanti dhīrā lokamhā" means those wise persons who possess this vehicle depart from the world. "Aññadatthu" means certainly. "Jayaṃ jayanti" means they celebrate victory while repeatedly conquering enemies such as greed (rāga).

## 5-6. Commentary on Kimatthiya Sutta, etc.

5-6. In the fifth sutta, in the word "ayameva," the word "eva" has the sense of restriction. By that word, other paths are excluded. In this sutta, the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) and the mixed path (missakamagga) are taught. The sixth sutta is clear in its meaning.
160:
## 7. Commentary on the Second Aññatarabhikkhu Sutta
In the seventh sutta, "Monk, this is a name for the Nibbāna element" means it is a name for the Nibbāna element which is unconditioned (asaṅkhata) and deathless (amata). "By that (removal of lust, etc.), it is called the destruction of taints" means that by the removal of lust and so forth, it is also called the destruction of taints (āsavas). Āsavakkhaya refers to the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala); it is shown that for that Arahatship, "removal of lust" (rāga-vinaya) and so forth are indeed names. "He spoke these words" means "The Teacher, by speaking of the Nibbāna element, has spoken of the deathless Nibbāna, but the path to it has not yet been spoken. I will cause that path to be spoken," thus, being skilled in sequence (anusandhi), he spoke these words desiring to ask.

## 8. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta
In the eighth sutta, "Bhikkhus, what is right view?"—having analyzed the Eightfold Path by one method, desiring to analyze it again by another method, He began this teaching. Therein, "knowledge of suffering" is the knowledge that has arisen through four aspects: hearing (savana), examining (sammasana), penetration (paṭivedha), and reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa). The same method applies to the Truth of Origin (samudaya). However, in the remaining two truths (Cessation and Path), since there is no examining (sammasana), only three aspects are appropriate. In this way, by "knowledge of suffering" and so forth, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the Four Truths is shown.

Among those four truths, the first two truths (Suffering and Origin) are the round (vaṭṭa), and the last two truths (Cessation and Path) are the end of the round (vivaṭṭa). Among those truths, for a monk, there is the application of the meditation subject to the truths of the round; however, there is no application to the truths of the end of the round. Indeed, having learned the first two truths from a teacher in brief as "the five aggregates of clinging are suffering, craving is the origin," and in detail by the method "which are the five aggregates? the aggregate of form," etc., and reciting them repeatedly with the voice, the practitioner performs the work of meditation. But in the other two truths, he performs the work of meditation only by hearing: "The Truth of Cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the Truth of the Path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing." One who acts thus penetrates the four truths with a single penetration and realizes them with a single realization. He penetrates suffering by the penetration of full understanding (pariññā), the origin by the penetration of abandoning (pahāna), cessation by the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā), and the path by the penetration of development (bhāvanā). He realizes suffering by the realization of full understanding... pe ... the path by the realization of development.

Thus, for that practitioner, in the preliminary stage, there is the penetration of learning, questioning, hearing, memorizing, examining, and penetrating in the two truths (Suffering and Origin); in the [other] two truths, there is only the penetration of hearing. In the later stage...
161:
Penetration occurs by way of function in the three truths; penetration occurs by way of object in the Truth of Cessation. Reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), however, occurs only for the Noble One (ariya) who has attained the truths. For this monk, from the time of comprehension (pariggaha) in the preliminary stage, there is no reviewing through attention, application, and reflection such as "I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, I develop the path"; it occurs only from the time of comprehension onwards. In the later stage, however, suffering is indeed fully understood... the path is indeed developed.

Among those four truths, two truths are deep because they are difficult to see, and two are difficult to see because they are deep. The Truth of Suffering is manifest by its occurrence in one's own continuity; when struck by a stump or a thorn, one even comes to say, "Oh, what suffering!" The Truth of Origin is also manifest by its occurrence by way of the desire to chew, the desire to eat, and so forth. However, by way of penetration of characteristics, both are deep. Thus, they are deep because they are difficult to see. The exertion to see the other two truths is like stretching out a hand to grasp the peak of existence (bhavagga), or stretching out a foot to touch the Avīci hell, or hitting the tip of a hair split a hundred times with another hair-tip. Thus, they are difficult to see because they are deep. In these four truths, which are deep because they are difficult to see and difficult to see because they are deep, it is taught by way of learning and so forth as "knowledge of suffering," and so on. At the moment of penetration (the Path), however, that knowledge is only one.

In renunciation-intention (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) and so forth, it is called renunciation-intention because of its opposition to sense-desires (kāma), or because of its state of departure from sense-desires, or because it arises in one who is contemplating sense-desires, or because it arises while destroying the foundation of sense-desires and effecting the subsiding of sense-desires, or because it arises in seclusion from sense-desires. In the remaining two terms (non-ill will and non-harming), the method is the same. All these, such as renunciation-intention, are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions associated with abstinence from sense-desire, ill will, and cruelty. At the moment of the Path, however, by way of cutting off the cause of unwholesome intention that arises in these three instances and thus effecting its non-arising, a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the path-factor. This is called Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa).

Right Speech (sammā-vācā), such as abstinence from false speech, is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions associated with abstinence from false speech and so forth. At the moment of the Path, however, in these four instances...
162:
By cutting off the cause of the arisen unwholesome volition of misconduct and thus effecting its non-arising, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path-factor. This is called Right Speech (sammā-vācā).

Right Action (sammā-kammanta), such as abstinence from taking life, is also diverse in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) due to the diversity of perceptions associated with abstinence from taking life and so forth. However, at the moment of the Path, by way of non-doing and by cutting off the cause of the unwholesome volition of misconduct that arises in these three instances, and thus effecting its non-arising, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path-factor. This is called Right Action (sammā-kammanta).

'Wrong livelihood' (micchā-ājīva) refers to bodily and verbal misconduct performed for the sake of food, snacks, and so forth. 'Pahāya' means having avoided those misconducts. 'Sammā-ājīvena' means by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. 'Jīvikaṃ kappeti' means one carries on the activity of livelihood. Right Livelihood is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions associated with abstinence from scheming (kuhana) and so forth. However, at the moment of the Path, by cutting off the cause of the base volition of wrong livelihood that would arise in these seven instances, and thus effecting its non-arising, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path-factor. This is called Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva).

'Anuppannānaṃ' refers to unwholesome states that have not arisen in oneself in a particular life or toward such an object. Seeing unwholesome states arising in others, one thinks, "May such evil states not arise in me," and thus exerts for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. 'Chanda' means generating the desire associated with energy (vīriya) that effects the practice for the non-arising of those unwholesome states. 'Vāyamati' means making an effort. 'Vīriyaṃ ārabhati' means initiating energy. 'Cittaṃ paggaṇhāti' means uplifting the mind with energy. 'Padahati' means initiating supreme effort (sammappadhāna) thinking, "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain." 'Uppannānaṃ' refers to unwholesome states that have previously arisen in oneself by way of habitual practice. One generates the desire to abandon those unwholesome states, thinking, "Now I will not let such states arise again."

'Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ' refers to wholesome states such as the first jhana that have not yet been attained. 'Uppannānaṃ' refers to those same wholesome states that have been attained. 'Ṭhitiyā' means for the sake of stability by way of repeated and continuous occurrence. 'Asammosāya' means for the sake of non-disappearance. 'Bhiyyobhāvāya' means for the sake of further development. 'Vepullāya' means for the sake of abundance. 'Pāripūriyā' means for the sake of fulfilling the development (bhāvanā). This Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma) is also diverse in the preliminary stage because the mind that effects functions such as non-arising occurs at different moments. At the moment of the Path, however, by way of effecting the function in these four instances mentioned, a single wholesome energy arises, fulfilling the path-factor. This is called Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma).

Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati) is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of minds that comprehend the body, feelings, mind, and dhammas. At the moment of the Path, however, by way of effecting the function of removing the adherence to beauty, happiness, permanence, and self in those four instances, a single wholesome mindfulness arises, fulfilling the path-factor. This is called Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati).

The jhana factors occur respectively in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path. In the preliminary stage, they occur respectively by way of attainment (samāpatti). At the moment of the Path, however, they occur in respective moments by way of the respective paths. In brief, for some, the first path is associated with the first jhana. The second path and so forth are also associated with the first jhana, or with any one of the other jhanas such as the second jhana.
163:
Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma) is diverse in the preliminary stage because of the various thoughts aimed at preventing unarisen unwholesome states and so forth. At the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), however, a single wholesome energy (vīriya) arises, fulfilling the Path factor by way of accomplishing the task in these four instances mentioned above. This is called Right Effort.

Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati) is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of thoughts that grasp the body and so forth. But at the moment of the Path, a single mindfulness arises, fulfilling the Path factor by way of accomplishing the task in these four instances. This is called Right Mindfulness.

Jhānas and so forth differ both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path. In the preliminary stage, they differ by way of attainment (samāpatti), while at the moment of the Path, they differ by way of the respective Paths. For some, the first Path is associated with the first jhāna, and the second Path and so forth are also associated with the first jhāna or any other jhāna such as the second. For another, the first Path is associated with any other jhāna such as the second, and the second Path and so forth are also associated with any other jhāna such as the second or with the first jhāna. Thus, the four Paths may be similar, dissimilar, or partially similar by way of jhāna.

This distinction occurs by the determination of the foundation jhāna (pādaka-jhāna). By the determination of the foundation jhāna, for one who has attained the first jhāna, when they practice insight (vipassanā) after emerging from the first jhāna, the Path that arises is associated with the first jhāna; in this Path, the Path factors and the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are complete. For one who practices insight after emerging from the second jhāna, the Path that arises is associated with the second jhāna; in this Path, there are seven Path factors. For one who practices insight after emerging from the third jhāna, the Path that arises is associated with the third jhāna; in this Path, there are seven Path factors and six factors of enlightenment. This method should be understood from the fourth jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).

In the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi), the fourth and fifth jhānas arise; it is said that these jhānas are only supramundane (lokuttara) and not mundane (lokiya). How is this so? In this formless realm, for one who has attained the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) after emerging from one of the jhānas such as the first, and then develops the formless attainments and is reborn in that formless realm, the three higher Paths associated with that jhāna arise in that formless realm. Thus, only the foundation jhāna provides the determination. However, some elders say, "The aggregates which are the objects of insight provide the determination."
164:
...so they say. Some teachers say, "The individual's inclination (puggala-ajjhāsaya) determines it." Others say, "Insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) determines it." The decision on these teachers' views should be understood according to the method stated in the section on insight leading to emergence in the Visuddhimagga.

In the statement, "Bhikkhus, this is called Right Concentration," this Right Concentration is said to be mundane in the preliminary stage and supramundane in the later stage.

## 9. Sūkasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "micchā-paṇihitaṃ" means: what is called a sūka (awn of grain), if placed with the tip pointing upwards, can pierce and break the hand or the foot. If not placed that way, it is called wrongly directed (micchā-paṇihita). "Micchā-paṇihitāya diṭṭhiyā" means by the knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-paññā) that is wrongly established. "Avijjaṃ bhindissati" means he will break and abandon ignorance (avijjā) which covers the Four Noble Truths. "Vijjaṃ uppādessati" means he will bring about the knowledge (vijjā) of the Path of Arahantship. "Micchā-paṇihitattā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiyā" means because of the wrong establishment or non-arising of the knowledge of the ownership of deeds and the development of the Path. In this sutta, the Path mixed with mundane and supramundane is taught by making the knowledge of the ownership of deeds a prerequisite for the Path.

## 10. Nandiyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "paribbājako" refers to Channa the Wanderer. The remaining words in this sutta are clear and easy to understand.

## 2. Chapter on Dwellings (Vihāravagga)

## 1. Paṭhamavihārasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the second chapter, "Bhikkhus, I wish to dwell in seclusion for half a month (fifteen days)" means "Bhikkhus, I wish to dwell alone, in seclusion, hiding away for one half-month." "No one should approach me except for the one who brings alms-food" means that monk who, without making a verbal intimation (viññatti) himself...
165:
“For my sake, alms-food prepared in faithful families should be brought and offered to me; except for that one monk who brings the alms-food, no other monk or layman should approach me,” he said.

Why did he say this? It was because during that fortnight, there were no beings to be disciplined. Then the Teacher thought: “I will spend this entire fortnight in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti-sukha). By doing so, there will be a pleasant dwelling for me, and future generations will follow the example, thinking, ‘Even the Teacher lived alone, leaving the group; why should we not?’ This will be for their long-term welfare and happiness.” For this reason, he spoke thus. The Saṅgha, accepting the Teacher's word, assigned one monk. That monk, early in the morning, performed all duties such as sweeping the precinct of the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), offering water for washing the face and tooth-sticks, and then departed.

“Yena svāhaṃ” should be resolved as “Yena so ahaṃ.” “Paṭhamābhisambuddho” refers to the period within the first forty-nine days after attaining Buddhahood. The word “viharāmi” uses the present tense in a past sense. “Tassa padesena vihāsiṃ” means he dwelt by way of a portion of that dwelling of the first enlightenment. Here, “portion” (padesa) is of various kinds: portions of aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), truths (sacca), faculties (indriya), modes of conditions (paccayākāra), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), jhanas, and name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Referring to all of these, he said, “Tassa padesena vihāsiṃ.” Just as a king who has attained kingship might have various chambers opened to inspect his essential treasures—gold, silver, pearls, and gems—to see his own wealth, so too the Buddha, during the first forty-nine days of his enlightenment, dwelt contemplating the five aggregates without remainder (nippadesa). However, during this fortnight, he dwelt contemplating only the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha), which is a portion of those aggregates. As the Buddha contemplated, “These beings experience such pleasant feeling, and such painful feeling,” all pleasant feelings occurring up to the highest plane of existence (bhavagga) and all painful feelings occurring down to the Avīci hell appeared to him in every aspect. Then he dwelt comprehending those feelings in such ways as “experienced due to wrong view,” and so forth.

Similarly, while in the first enlightenment he dwelt contemplating the twelve bases without remainder, in this fortnight he dwelt contemplating a portion of those bases—a part of the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) by way of feeling; a portion of the elements—a part of the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu) by way of feeling; a portion of the truths—a part of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) by way of the aggregate of feeling; a portion of the conditions...
166:
...a portion of the conditions by way of feeling due to contact (phassa-paccaya); a portion of the jhanas; a part of the jhana factors by way of feeling; a portion of name-and-form; and a part of name by way of feeling. During the first forty-nine days of his enlightenment, he dwelt contemplating the seven books (of the Abhidhamma) with their infinite methods, having made the wholesome and other states without remainder (nippadesa). But in this fortnight, he dwelt contemplating only the Triad of Feeling (vedanā-ttika), which is a portion of all states. In each respective place, those various meditative attainments (vihara-samāpatti) arose through the power of feeling.

Now, wishing to show the manner in which he dwelt, he spoke the words beginning with “micchādiṭṭhi-paccayāpi.” In the phrase “micchādiṭṭhi-paccayā,” feelings associated with wrong view, wholesome and unwholesome feelings arising in dependence (upanissaya) on wrong view, and resultant (vipāka) feelings are all included. Among those, feelings associated with wrong view are only unwholesome. However, depending on wrong view, both wholesome and unwholesome feelings arise. Those with wrong view, depending on their wrong view, give gruel, rice, and so on on the uposatha days of the fortnight; they perform duties for travelers; they build rest-houses at crossroads; they have ponds dug; they plant flowering trees at shrines and the like; they lay bridges over rivers and ravines; they make uneven roads even. Thus, wholesome feelings arise in them. Yet, depending on that same wrong view, they abuse and threaten those with right view; they commit acts of killing and binding; they kill living beings to make offerings to deities. Thus, unwholesome feelings arise in them. Resultant feelings, however, occur only for those who have gone to another existence.

In the phrase “sammādiṭṭhi-paccayā,” feelings associated with right view, wholesome and unwholesome feelings arising in dependence on right view, and resultant feelings are also included. Among those, feelings associated with right view are only wholesome. However, depending on right view, they perform meritorious deeds such as worshipping the Buddha, offering lamps, listening to the sublime Dhamma, and establishing stupas in regions where none existed before. Thus, wholesome feelings arise in them. Depending on that same right view, they abuse and threaten those with wrong view; they exalt themselves and disparage others. Thus, unwholesome feelings arise in them. Resultant feelings, however, occur only for those who have gone to another existence. The same method applies to the phrases beginning with “micchā-saṅkappa-paccaya.” In the phrases beginning with “chanda-paccayā,” the feelings associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed due to the condition of desire (chanda) should be understood.
167:
Due to the condition of initial thought (vitakka), only the feeling of the first jhāna arises. Due to the condition of perception (saññā), excluding the first jhāna, the remaining six feelings of the meditative attainments of perception arise.

In the passages beginning with "chando ca avūpasanto" (and desire is not calmed), as long as the three—desire, initial thought, and perception—are not yet calmed, the feeling associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed arises. When desire alone is calmed, only the feeling of the first jhāna arises. When desire and initial thought are calmed, the feelings of the second jhāna and so forth are intended. When all three are calmed, the feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises.

"Appattassa pattiyā" means for the sake of attaining the fruit of Arahantship. "Atthi āyāmaṃ" means there is energy (vīriya). When one reaches the path which is the cause of the fruit of Arahantship through the power of that exertion of energy, the feeling caused by the ground of Arahantship, referred to as "tappaccayāpi vedayitaṃ," arises. By this, only the supramundane feeling that arises together with the four paths is taken.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Vihāra Sutta

In the second sutta, the reason for seclusion should be understood as previously stated. "Micchādiṭṭhivūpasamapaccayā" refers to right view, which is the calming of wrong view. Therefore, the feeling caused by right view should be understood as the feeling caused by the calming of wrong view. In this sutta, it is said that they do not take the resultant feeling (vipāka-vedanā), considering it too remote. In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere. For whenever it is said "due to the condition of the calming of such and such," the feeling caused by the condition of the opposite state (paṭipakkha-dhamma) is intended. In the passages beginning with "chandavūpasamapaccayā," the feeling of the first jhāna should be understood as being due to the calming of desire. The feeling of the second jhāna is due to the calming of initial thought. The feelings of the six attainments are due to perception. The feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is due to the calming of perception. The passages beginning with "chando ca vūpasanto" have the same meaning as already stated.

"Sekhāya" refers to being endowed with the right view that arises together with the three fruits and the four paths. That right view is also called "sekha" because its task is not yet finished and it is still practicing its own path-task. The fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh suttas have clear meanings.

## 3. Commentary on the Micchatta Vagga

21-30. In the first sutta of the third chapter, "micchattaṃ" means the nature of wrongness. "Sammattaṃ" means the nature of rightness. "Micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetu" means because of the cause of practicing wrong conduct. It means "because one practices wrong conduct, therefore..." "Nārādhako" means one who does not accomplish or fulfill. "Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ" refers to the Dhamma of the Noble Path. "Micchāñāṇī" means having wrong knowledge or wrong reflection. "Micchāvimuttī" means false liberation, a liberation that does not lead out of saṃsāra. In these four suttas starting from the third, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are discussed. Among these, in the last two suttas, the person is asked about and the Dhamma is analyzed; thus, the person is shown by way of the Dhamma. "Suppavattiyo" means well-conducted, meaning it can be conducted just as one runs towards whatever direction one desires. "Saupanisaṃ saparikkhāraṃ" means with its cause and with its requisites. The rest of the terms everywhere have clear meanings.

## 4. Commentary on the Paṭipatti Vagga

31-40. In the fourth chapter, "micchāpaṭipattiṃ" means wrong conduct. "Micchāpaṭipannံ" means one who practices wrongly. Thus, one sutta is taught by way of the Dhamma, and one sutta is taught by way of the person. "Apārā pāraṃ" means from the round of rebirth to Nibbāna. In the term "pāragāmino," all those who have reached the further shore of Nibbāna, those who are going, and those who will go, should be understood as "pāragāmino" (those going to the further shore).

"Tīramevānudhāvatī" means running repeatedly only within the round of rebirth, wandering in the round of rebirth. "Kaṇhaṃ" refers to unwholesome states (akusala-dhamma). "Sukkaṃ" refers to wholesome states (kusala-dhamma). "Okā anokaṃ" means from the round of rebirth to Nibbāna.
169:
*Āgamma* means having resorted to, having intended, or having relied upon. *Pariyodapeyya* means one should make pure. *Cittaklesehi* refers to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) that defile the mind. *Sambodhiyaṅgesu* refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).

*Sāmaññattha* refers to Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is called *sāmaññattha* because it is to be attained through the Noble Path (*sāmañña*). *Brahmanya* is the state of being noble. *Brahmanyattha* refers to Nibbāna, as it is to be attained through the Noble Path (*brahmanya*). Teachers say that wherever the term "destruction of lust" (*rāgakkhaya*) appears below and in these three suttas, it also refers to the fruition of Arahantship (*arahattaphala*).

## 5. Commentary on the Chapter of the Repetition Series of Other Sectarians (Aññatitthiyapeyyālavagga)

41–48. In the *Aññatitthiyapeyyāla*, *addhānapariññattha* means that by reaching Nibbāna, the journey of Saṃsāra is fully understood. Therefore, Nibbāna is called "full understanding of the journey" (*addhānapariññā*); it means for the sake of that Nibbāna. *Anupādāparinibbānattha* means for the sake of absolute extinguishment which is not a cause for further rebirth. Thus, in this repetition series, the fruition of Arahantship is taught by the term "the fruit of knowledge and liberation" (*vijjāvimuttiphala*). By the term "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*), reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is taught; by the remaining terms, Nibbāna is taught.

## 6. Commentary on the Chapter of the Repetition Series of the Sun (Suriyapeyyālavagga)

49–62. In the *Suriyapeyyāla*, the rising of the dawn is like good friendship (*kalyāṇamittatā*). The Noble Path together with insight (*vipassanā*), which arises by standing in that good friendship, is like the appearance of the sun; in this way, the meaning should be understood in all suttas. *Sīlasampadā* is the virtue of fourfold purification (*catupārisuddhisīla*). *Chandasampadā* is the desire to act (*kattukamyatāchanda*) which is wholesome. *Attasampadā* is the state of having a perfected mind. *Diṭṭhisampadā* is the perfection of knowledge. *Appamādasampadā* is the perfection of heedfulness that prompts the practice of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). *Yonisomanasikārasampadā* is the perfection of wise attention. Again, the words starting with good friendship are taught for the sake of bringing about Right View and so forth in another way. All these suttas are taught respectively according to the dispositions (*āsaya*) of individuals.
170:
They are taught for the sake of showing the arising (of Right View, etc.) in another way. All these suttas are also taught respectively according to the inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*) of individuals.

63–138. Both the *Ekadhammapeyyāla* and the *Gaṅgāpeyyāla* were taught respectively according to the inclinations of individuals; when taught in such and such a way, they were spoken according to the inclinations of those who understand easily.

## 8. The Chapter of the Repetition Series of Heedfulness (Appamādapeyyālavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Tathāgata Sutta

In the *Appamādapeyyāla*, regarding the text "*evameva kho*" (even so), just as the Fully Enlightened Buddha is supreme among all beings, so too, heedfulness (*appamāda*) which prompts (right effort) is to be understood as supreme among all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). Is it not that this heedfulness is only mundane (*lokiya*), while wholesome states are also supramundane (*lokuttara*)? And this heedfulness belongs only to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while wholesome states belong to the four planes. How then is heedfulness supreme among those wholesome states? It is supreme in the sense of being the means of attainment (*paṭilābhakaṭṭhena*). For those wholesome states are attained through heedfulness; therefore, that heedfulness is supreme among those wholesome states. Because of this, it is said: "All those are rooted in heedfulness" (*sabbe te appamādamūlakā*), and so forth.

## 2. Commentary on the Footprint Sutta (Padasutta)

"*Jaṅgalānaṃ*" means of those beings who usually live on the surface of the earth. "*Pāṇānaṃ*" means of beings with feet. "*Padajātāni*" means footprints. "*Samodhānaṃ gacchanti*" means they come to be included or contained within. "*Aggamakkhāyati*" means it is declared supreme. "*Yadidaṃ mahantattena*" means it is declared supreme because of its greatness (size), not because of its quality (*guṇa*).

141–148. "*Vassikaṃ*" refers to the jasmine flower. It is said that after hearing this sutta, King Bhātiya, wishing to test it, had a chamber smeared with four kinds of perfumes, had fragrant flowers brought, placed a handful of jasmine in the center of a basket, and placed the remaining flowers in handfuls around that jasmine. Then he closed the door and went outside. Then, after a moment had passed, he opened the door...
171:
King Bhātiya, wishing to test it, had a chamber smeared with four kinds of perfumes, had fragrant flowers brought, placed a handful of jasmine in the center of a basket, and placed the remaining flowers in handfuls around that jasmine. Then he closed the door and went outside. Then, after a moment had passed, when the king opened the door and entered, the scent of the jasmine flower struck his nose before all other flowers. That king prostrated himself on the very floor of the great hall facing the Great Stupa (*Mahācetiya*) and worshipped the stupa, saying, "The Fully Enlightened Buddha spoke well when he said, 'Jasmine is the best of them.'"

*Kuṭṭarājāno* means minor kings. There is also a variant reading "*khuddarājāno*." *Tantāvutānaṃ* means those woven on a loom, or those made by being placed on a loom and woven. This word is in the genitive case used with the meaning of the nominative case. The meaning here is: "There are any cloths woven on a loom." Or, the meaning in this sutta should be understood by the method of the remaining text as: "Among cloths woven on a loom, there are any cloths." The rest of the words are clear in meaning in all the suttas.

## 9. The Chapter on Deeds to be Done with Strength (Balakaraṇီyavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Strength Sutta (Balasutta)

In the *Balakaraṇīyavagga*, *balakaraṇīya* refers to tasks to be done by the strength of the thighs and the strength of the arms, such as running, jumping, exerting heat, and carrying. *Sīle patiṭṭhāya* means standing in the virtue of fourfold purification (*catupārisuddhisīla*). *Aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ* refers to the Noble Path along with insight (*vipassanā*).

## 2. Commentary on the Seed Sutta (Bījasutta)

In the text *bījagāmabhūtagāma*, the five kinds of seeds are called *bījagāma*. That same collection of seeds, from the time it is endowed with leaves and is green, should be known as *bhūtagāma*.

## 3. Commentary on the Serpent Sutta (Nāgasutta)

*Balaṃ gāhenti* means they take strength; having gained strength, they become firm in body. In the passages beginning with *kusobbhe otaranti*, the successive explanation is as follows: It is said that female nagas...
172:
Female nāgas, when they have a pregnancy established during the season, think: "If we give birth in this place, our young will not be able to withstand the force of the waves or the force of the Garuḍa swooping down in flight." They dive into the great ocean, reach the river mouths, enter the five great rivers, and go to the Himalayas. There, living in golden, silver, and ruby caves where Garuḍas cannot oppress them, they give birth and lead the young nāgas into waters the depth of a heel and so on to teach them how to swim.

Then, when those young nāgas are gradually able to swim and cross back and forth from this bank to that bank and from that bank to this bank of rivers such as the Ganges, the mothers know, "Now our children will be able to withstand the force of the waves and the force of the Garuḍa." By their own power, they cause a great rain to fall, making the entire Himalayas like a single sheet of water. They create boats made of gold, silver, and so on. Above, they fix cloth canopies adorned with golden stars and hanging garlands of fragrant flowers. Taking fragrant sandalwood, flowers, and such, they descend into the five great rivers with those boats and gradually reach the great ocean. Living in that great ocean, they reach sizes of ten, a hundred, a thousand, and a hundred thousand fathoms, attaining greatness and vastness.

In the same way, the fourfold purification of virtue (caturpārisuddhisīla) should be seen as the king of mountains, the Himalayas; the practitioners (yogāvacara) as the young nāgas; the Noble Path (ariyamagga) as the small streams and channels; and Nibbāna as the great ocean. Just as the young nāgas, staying in the Himalayas, reach the great ocean through the small streams and channels and attain greatness of body, so too, practitioners, depending on virtue and established in virtue, reach Nibbāna through the Noble Path and attain greatness of the body of qualities in the six higher powers (abhiññā) obtained through the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga) alone.
