## 3-4. Upādānasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
174-175. "Kāmupādāna" means clinging to sense-pleasure. The same method applies to "diṭṭhupādāna" and so on. "Gantha" refers to the dhammas that are sticky like resin. "Kāyagantha" is the defilement that constantly sticks to the mental body (nāmakāya). "Idaṃsaccābhinivesa" is the wrong conviction arising through the power of the view of holding to extremes (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi) in the form "only this view is true."
175:
## 5-10. Anusayasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
176-181. "Kāmarāgānusaya": because it reaches a state of being firmly established in the continuum of beings, and because sensual lust itself repeatedly lies latent, it is called the underlying tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya). The same method applies to the remaining underlying tendencies. "Orambhāgiya" refers to the dhammas belonging to the lower part. "Saṃyojana" refers to the dhammas that bind. "Uddhambhāgiya" refers to the dhammas belonging to the upper part. In all the remaining suttas, the meaning is clear.

## Eleventh: Ogha Vagga.

## The Commentary on the Magga Saṃyutta is finished.
176:
## 2. Bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttaṃ
## 1. Pabbata-vagga
## 1. Himavanta-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta, the term 'nāgā' refers to those nāgas living between the waves on the surface of the great ocean, not to those residing in celestial mansions. Everything regarding their bodily growth depending on the Himalayas should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In the word 'bojjhaṅga', they are called factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas) because they are either the factors of enlightenment (bodhi) or the factors of the enlightened person (bodhi-puggala).

What is meant is this: The noble disciple awakens (bujjhati) through the harmony of states (dhamma-sāmaggī) known as mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. This harmony of states, which arises at the moment of the mundane and supramundane paths, is the opposite of many dangers such as sluggishness, restlessness, stagnation, over-exertion, devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, annihilationism, and eternalism. Therefore, this collection of states is called 'bodhi' (enlightenment). 'Awakens' means rising from the sleep of the continuum of defilements, or penetrating the Four Noble Truths, or realizing Nibbāna itself. As it is said: "Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he attained the unsurpassed supreme enlightenment." Because they are components of that enlightenment known as the harmony of states, they are called 'bojjhaṅgas' (factors of enlightenment), just like the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅga) or the factors of the path (maggaṅga). Furthermore, since the noble disciple awakens through this harmony of states in the manner described, the noble disciple is also called 'bodhi'; because they are the factors (causes) of that enlightened person, they are called 'bojjhaṅgas', just like the factors of an army (senaṅga) or the factors of a chariot (rathaṅga). Therefore, the commentators said: "They are bojjhaṅgas because they are the factors of the person who awakens."

Furthermore, the meaning of bojjhaṅga should also be understood according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "In what sense are they bojjhaṅgas? They are bojjhaṅgas because they lead to awakening, they are bojjhaṅgas because they awaken, they are bojjhaṅgas because they awaken sequentially, they are bojjhaṅgas because they awaken through penetration, they are bojjhaṅgas because they awaken fully," and so on.

In terms such as 'satisambojjhaṅga', 'sambojjhaṅga' refers to a factor of enlightenment that is praised and excellent. 'Satisambojjhaṅga' means mindfulness itself is the factor of enlightenment. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances. 'Bhāveti' means he develops (increases).
177:
To cause to arise repeatedly in one's own mental continuum, to bring into existence as a noble state, means "he develops" (bhāveti). The terms such as "dependent on seclusion" (vivekanissita) should be understood in the same way as stated in the Kosala Saṃyutta: "He develops right view dependent on seclusion."

Specifically, although only the three kinds of seclusion—seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgaviveka), seclusion by eradication (samucchedaviveka), and seclusion by deliverance (nissaraṇaviveka)—are mentioned in that Kosala Saṃyutta, some teachers also explain the fivefold "dependent on seclusion" when it comes to the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). These teachers do not point out the factors of enlightenment only at the moments of strong insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruition (phala), but they also point them out in the kasiṇa absorptions (jhāna), mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), foulness (asubha), and the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), which are the bases for insight. Such an explanation is not prohibited by the commentators (aṭṭhakathācariya). Therefore, according to their view, at the moment when those absorptions occur, it should be said that one develops the factors of enlightenment dependent on seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhanaviveka) by way of function. Just as it is said that at the moment of insight, one develops the factors of enlightenment dependent on seclusion by deliverance (nissaraṇaviveka) by way of inclination, it is also appropriate to say that one develops the factors of enlightenment dependent on seclusion by tranquilization (paṭipassaddhiviveka). The remaining points in this discourse are just as explained below.

## 2. Kāyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second discourse, "subsisting on nutriment" (āhāraṭṭhitika) means having the four causes—kamma-born, mind-born, temperature-born, and nutriment-born—as the basis for subsistence. "Depending on nutriment" (āhāraṃ paṭicca) means depending on a cause (condition). "The sign of the beautiful" (subhanimitta) refers to either a beautiful thing or a beautiful object. "Unwise attention" (ayoniso manasikāra) means improper attention or attention on the wrong path. It is the attention that takes the impermanent as permanent, the suffering as pleasant, the non-self as self, and the foul as beautiful. For one who frequently applies such attention to that beautiful object, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises. Therefore, it was said: "Monks, there is the sign of the beautiful," and so on. In this same way, the application should be understood for all the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).

Regarding the terms such as "the sign of repulsion" (paṭighanimitta), both repulsion (paṭigha) itself and the object of repulsion are called the sign of repulsion. "Aversion" (arati) means lack of delight (boredom). Referring to that aversion, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Therein, what is aversion? In secluded lodgings or in any of the higher wholesome states, there is lack of delight, the state of not delighting, non-delight, non-enjoyment, boredom, and anxiety; this is called aversion."

"Sloth" (tandī) means the adventitious physical laziness arising due to causes such as extreme cold. When that sloth arises, one is prone to say, "It is too cold, it is too hot, I am too hungry, I am too full, I have traveled too far." Referring to that sloth, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Therein, what is sloth? That which is laziness, the state of being lazy, the condition of laziness..." and so on.
178:
Tandī refers to the adventitious laziness of the body caused by reasons such as extreme cold. When that laziness occurs, one is prone to say, 'It is too cold, it is too hot, I am too hungry, I am too full, I have traveled a very long distance.' Regarding this tandī, it is said (in Vibhaṅga, 857): 'Among those states, what is tandī? That which is laziness, the manner of being lazy, the state of being lazy, sloth, the manner of being slothful, the state of being a slothful person; this state is called tandī.'

Vijambhitā refers to the bending and twisting of the body through the power of defilements. Regarding this vijambhitā, it is said (in Vibhaṅga, 858): 'Among those states, what is vijambhitā? The stretching of the body, the movement, the constant restless writhing, the shaking, the bending downwards or forwards, the curving upwards or backwards, the excessive drooping and inclining downwards, the moving and stretching while lifting the body upwards, the state of being a lazy person; this state is called vijambhitā.'

Bhattasammado refers to the distress and exhaustion caused by food. Regarding this bhattasammado, it is said (in Vibhaṅga, 859): 'Among those states, what is bhattasammado? The drowsiness and stupor of one who has eaten, the exhaustion due to food, the distress due to food, the bodily discomfort caused by excessive food; this state is called bhattasammado.'

Cetaso līnattaṃ refers to the manner of the mind shrinking away from its object. Regarding this meaning, it is said (in Vibhaṅga, 860): 'Among those states, what is cetaso līnattaṃ? The lack of health of the mind, the lack of fitness for work, the manner of shrinking downwards, the manner of shrinking all around, shrinking, the manner of shrinking, the state of being shrunk, the lack of vigor without effort, the manner of lacking vigor, the state of the mind being unable to compose itself and lacking vigor; this state is called cetaso līnattaṃ.'

Cetaso avūpasamo refers to the unsettled state of the mind, just as a glowing coal without flame continues to produce heat as long as it is not extinguished, or as a kiln continues to produce heat as long as it is not cooled. In terms of its ultimate reality (atthato), this state is indeed restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca).

Vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā dhammā refers to the objects of doubt (vicikicchā). Inappropriate attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is to be understood in the same manner as already explained in all places. Thus, in this sutta, these two states—sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and doubt (vicikicchā)—are taught by way of their objects. Ill-will (byāpāda) is taught by way of its object and its decisive support (upanissaya). The remaining states, sloth and torpor (thina-middha) and restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), are taught by way of conascence (sahajāta) and decisive support.

Satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā refers to the objects of mindfulness, which are the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) and the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). Among those, the development of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra-bahulīkāra) refers to the repeated practice of wise attention (upāya-manasikāra) regarding those states.

In the phrases beginning with kusala-akusalā dhammā, wholesome (kusala) refers to states that arise from wisdom, are faultless, and yield happy results. Unwholesome (akusala) refers to states that arise from lack of skill, are faulty, and yield painful results. Faulty states are unwholesome; faultless states are wholesome. The same method applies to the terms low (hīna), excellent (paṇīta), dark (kaṇha), and bright (sukka). Sappaṭibhāgā refers to the dark and bright states themselves. This is because the dark unwholesome states...
179:
...because dark unwholesome states give dark results, and bright wholesome states give bright results, they are called sappaṭibhāgā in the sense of having portions of results similar to themselves. Alternatively, they are called sappaṭibhāgā because they have an opposing part. Since the opposite of the dark is the bright, and the opposite of the bright is the dark, they are thus called sappaṭibhāgā. Or, they are called sappaṭibhāgā in the sense of obstructing. Unwholesome states obstruct wholesome states and give their own results; wholesome states also obstruct unwholesome states (and give their own results). Thus, the dark and bright states are called sappaṭibhāgā.

Ārambhadhātu refers to the initial effort put forth. Nikkamadhātu refers to the effort that is stronger than the initial effort because it has emerged from laziness. Parakkamadhātu refers to the effort that is even stronger than that because of its ability to reach higher and higher stages. By these three terms, only energy (vīriya) is spoken of.

Pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā refers to the states that are objects of joy (pīti). Kāyapassaddhi refers to the tranquility of the distress of the three aggregates: feeling, perception, and mental formations. Cittapassaddhi refers to the tranquility of the distress of the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). Samathanimitta refers to both serenity (samatha) and its object as the cause of serenity. Abyagganimitta is a synonym for that same samathanimitta.

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā refers to the states that are objects of equanimity (upekkhā). In terms of meaning, it should be understood as the causal states for the arising of equanimity, which has the characteristic of neutrality. Thus, in this context, the mindfulness (sati), investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), and equanimity (upekkhā) factors of enlightenment are taught by way of their objects, while the remaining factors of enlightenment are taught by way of both their objects and decisive support.

## 3. Sīlasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, in the term 'sīlasampannā', the mundane and supramundane virtue of an Arahant is taught; it means being endowed with that virtue. The same method applies to concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā). Liberation (vimutti), however, is only the liberation of fruition (phala-vimutti). Knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). Thus, in this context, the three beginning with virtue are both mundane and supramundane, liberation is exclusively supramundane, and knowledge and vision of liberation is exclusively mundane.

'Dassanampāhaṃ' means 'I (the Buddha) also [speak of] seeing.' That seeing is of two kinds: visual seeing (cakkhu-dassana) and knowledge seeing (ñāṇa-dassana). Among them, seeing the Noble Ones with eyes clarified by faith is called visual seeing. Seeing the characteristics seen by the Noble Ones, and penetratingly knowing the truth that has been penetrated, whether through jhāna, insight (vipassanā), or the Paths and Fruits (magga-phala), is called knowledge seeing. In this context, however, visual seeing is intended. This is because [seeing] the Noble Ones with clarified eyes...
180:
Beholding the Noble Ones (Ariyas) is also of great benefit. Hearing (savana) means hearing with the ear when people say, 'Such and such an Arahant (Khīṇāsava) is residing in such and such a country, district, village, market town, monastery, or cave'; this hearing is also of great benefit. Approaching (upasaṅkamana) means drawing near to the Noble Ones with a mind of such nature as: 'I will give a gift, I will ask a question, I will listen to the Dhamma, or I will perform a service.' Attending (payirupāsana) means attending by way of asking questions. It means that having heard of the virtues of the Noble Ones, one approaches them, invites them, gives a gift, and then asks questions in such a manner as: 'Venerable Sir, what is wholesome?' and so forth. Recollection (anussati) means recollecting while sitting in one's night quarters or day quarters: 'Now the Noble Ones are spending their time with the bliss of jhāna, vipassanā, the Path, and the Fruit in caves, grottos, pavilions, and so forth.' Or, it is the recollection of the advice received from them, reflecting: 'In this place, he taught virtue (sīla); in this place, concentration (samādhi); in this place, insight (vipassanā); in this place, the Path (magga); in this place, the Fruit (phala).'

Following into monkhood (anupabbajjā) means having gained faith in the Noble Ones, leaving the household life and ordaining in their presence. Indeed, the ordination of one who, having gained faith in the presence of the Noble Ones, ordains in their very presence and lives expecting their advice and instruction, is called 'anupabbajjā'. Even if one ordains elsewhere out of faith in the Noble Ones but lives expecting advice and instruction in the presence of the Noble Ones, that ordination is also called 'anupabbajjā'. However, the ordination of one who, out of faith in others, ordains in their presence and lives expecting only their advice and instruction, is not called 'anupabbajjā'.

Among those who ordained in this way, there were about one hundred thousand who followed Mahākassapa Thera into monkhood. Likewise, there were one hundred thousand each who followed the Elder’s pupil Candagutta Thera, his pupil Suriyagutta Thera, his pupil Assagutta Thera, and his pupil Yonakadhammarakkhita Thera. The followers of Yonakadhammarakkhita Thera’s pupil, Tissa Thera, who was the younger brother of King Asoka, numbered twenty-five million (two and a half crores). There is no limit to the number of those who followed Mahinda Thera into monkhood. To this day, those in the island of Laṅkā who ordain out of faith in the Teacher (the Buddha) are said to follow the ordination of Mahinda Thera.
181:
"Taṃ dhammaṃ" means the Dhamma of their advice and instruction. "Anussarati" means he recollects. "Anuvitakketi" means he applies thought to it. "Āraddho hoti" means it becomes fulfilled. The words beginning with "pavicinati" are all spoken here solely by way of the movement of knowledge (ñāṇa). Alternatively, "pavicinati" means he investigates the characteristics of various phenomena (dhammas). "Pavicarati" means he makes his knowledge circulate therein. "Parivīmaṃsamāpajjati" means he arrives at investigation, scrutiny, and searching.

"Seven fruits, seven benefits" (satta phala sattāniśaṃsa)—both these terms are identical in meaning. "In this very life, he attains the other (Arahantship) beforehand" (diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacca aññaṃ ārādheti) means that if he is to complete the Fruit of Arahantship, he completes it in this very existence, even before reaching the time of death. "Or at the time of death" (atha maraṇakāle) means (completing it) at the time near death.

"Antarāparinibbāyī" (one who attains Nibbāna in the interval) refers to a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) who attains Nibbāna without exceeding the middle of the lifespan, and such a person is of three types. For instance, in the Aviha realm where the lifespan is a thousand aeons, one person attains Arahantship on the very day of rebirth. If he does not attain it on the day of rebirth, he attains it within the first hundred aeons. This is the first Antarāparinibbāyī. Another, being unable to do so, attains it within two hundred aeons; this is the second Antarāparinibbāyī. Another, being unable to do even that, attains it within four hundred aeons; this is the third Antarāparinibbāyī.

One who attains Arahantship after passing the fifth hundredth aeon is called an "Upahaccaparinibbāyī" (one who attains Nibbāna after more than half the lifespan). The same method applies to the Atappa realm and others. One who attains Arahantship with exertion and effort in any realm is called a "Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī". One who attains it without exertion and effort is called an "Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī". One who is reborn in realms like Aviha, stays there for the full lifespan, and then is reborn in higher and higher realms until reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm is called an "Uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī" (one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm).

In this context, forty-eight types of Non-returners (Anāgāmīs) should be mentioned. In the Aviha realm, there are 5 types: 3 Antarāparinibbāyī, 1 Upahaccaparinibbāyī, and 1 Uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī. These 5 types become 10 by being either Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī or Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. The same applies to Atappa and the other (Suddhāvāsa) realms. However, in the Akaniṭṭha realm, there is no "Uddhaṃsoto" (upstream-goer), therefore there are 8 types: 4 Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī and 4 Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Thus, there are forty-eight types in total. Among them, the Uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī is the eldest of all and...
182:
That Uddhaṃsoto Akaniṭṭhagāmī Anāgāmī is the eldest among all and also the youngest among all. How so? Because that Anāgāmī has a lifespan of sixteen thousand aeons, he is the eldest among all in terms of age. Because he reaches the fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala) later than all others, he is the youngest among all. In this sutta, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) which are the preliminary stage of insight (vipassanā) for the path of Arahatship, occurring in a single thought-moment with various characteristics, neither before nor after, are taught.

## 4. Vattha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "If such a reflection as 'the enlightenment factor of mindfulness' (satisambojjhaṅga) should occur to me." "It occurs to me as 'measureless'." Susumāraddho means well-perfected. In the word "tiṭṭhati" (stands), the enlightenment factor of mindfulness stands by way of eight modes. The enlightenment factor of mindfulness stands because of not reflecting on the arising (uppāda) of formations (saṅkhāra) and because of reflecting on Nibbāna, which is free from arising. It stands because of not reflecting on the occurrence (pavatta) of formations, and because of reflecting on Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence; because of not reflecting on the sign (nimitta) of formations, and because of reflecting on Nibbāna, which is signless; because of not reflecting on formations, and because of reflecting on Nibbāna, which is unconditioned (visaṅkhāra). The Elder knows that it stands by these eight modes. He clearly knows that it falls away from its standing position by way of fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) through the eight modes that are the opposite of the aforementioned modes. The same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment.

Thus, in this fourth sutta, the factors of enlightenment included in the Elder's fruition attainment are taught. When the Elder enters fruition attainment making the enlightenment factor of mindfulness the leader, the other six factors follow that mindfulness factor. When he enters fruition attainment making any one of the factors such as investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya) the leader, the remaining factors follow that leading factor. Thus, the Elder taught this sutta showing his mastery (vasībhāva) practiced in fruition attainment.

## 5. Bhikkhu Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "bodhāya saṃvattanti" means they lead to the benefit of knowing. For the benefit of knowing what? They lead to the benefit of knowing the unconditioned (asankhata) Nibbāna through the Noble Path. They lead to the benefit of knowing the state of having completed the task of the path through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā). Alternatively, they lead to awakening from the slumber of defilements through the Path. It is also said to be for the benefit of the state of awakening through the Fruit. Therefore, in this sutta, everything—the realization of Nibbāna, the abandonment of defilements, and the reviewing—is shown.
183:
## 6-7. Kuṇḍaliya Sutta and Others Vaṇṇanā
187-188. In the sixth sutta, ārāmanissayī means one who is a park-dweller because of living depending on a park (ārāma). Parisāvacara means one who frequents assemblies (parisā). As for an assembly, both fools and wise people enter it. Specifically, one who is able to crush the doctrines of others and demonstrate his own doctrine is called a parisāvacara. Ārāmena ārāmaṃ means wandering from one park to another, not outside; this is the meaning. In the phrase uyyānena uyyānaṃ, the same method applies. Or, entering through one park to another park, through one garden to another garden; this is the meaning here. Itivādappamokkhānisaṃsaṃ means there is the benefit of establishing a doctrine and being released from a doctrine in this manner: "Such is the questioning, such is the answering, such is the grasping, such is the explanation." Upārambhānisaṃsaṃ means there is the benefit of finding faults in a doctrine, such as "This is a fault in the questioning, this is a fault in the answering."

"Kuṇḍaliya, how is the restraint of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara) developed?" The Teacher, knowing that "The wanderer (paribbājaka) has asked this much, and now he is unable to ask further," and thinking, "This teaching has not yet reached its proper conclusion (yathānusandhi). Now I will bring that teaching to its proper conclusion," started this teaching by asking himself. In that teaching, manāpaṃ nābhijjhāti means not being greedy for a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa). Nābhihasanti means not delighting with a delight accompanied by the bait of defilements (sāmisa). The mental body (nāmakāya) and mind of that monk stand fixed on the meditation object. Susaṇṭhitaṃ means well-established by the power of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Suvimuttaṃ means well-freed by the meditation subject. Amanāpaṃ means an unpleasant object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa). Na maṅku hoti means not being crestfallen by that object. Appatiṭṭhitacitto means having a mind that does not stand by the power of defilements. Adīnamānaso means having a mind that is not miserable by the power of grief (domanassa). Abyāpannacetaso means having a mind that is not putrid (apūti) by the power of anger (dosa).

"Kuṇḍaliya, the restraint of the faculties thus developed, thus frequently practiced, fulfills the three kinds of good conduct (sucarita)." In this context, the fulfillment of good conduct should be understood thus: First, in these six doors, eighteen kinds of misconduct (ducarita) occur. How? In the eye-door...
184:
Firstly, when a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) appears at the eye-door, for one who gives rise to greed for that object without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, mental misconduct (manoduccarita) occurs. For one who says with a mind accompanied by greed, "Indeed, this is desirable, pleasant, and delightful," verbal misconduct (vacīduccarita) occurs. For one who touches that very object with the hand, bodily misconduct (kāyaduccarita) occurs. The same method applies to the remaining doors.

The distinction here is: bodily misconduct should be understood for one who touches musical instruments such as conch shells, pipes, and drums which are the basis of the sound-object at the ear-door; flowers, perfumes, etc., which are the basis of the odor-object at the nose-door; fish, meat, etc., which are the basis of the taste-object at the tongue-door; robes, bedding, etc., which are the basis of the tangible-object at the body-door; and ghee, oil, honey, molasses, etc., which are the mental-objects by way of concepts at the mind-door. In brief, in these six doors, transgression by body is bodily misconduct, transgression by speech is verbal misconduct, and transgression by mind is mental misconduct—thus there are only three types of misconduct.

This meditating monk, established in his reflection on meditation, transforms these types of misconduct into good conduct (sucarita). How? Firstly, when a desirable object appears at the eye-door, for one who initiates insight (vipassanā) regarding the visible object without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, mental good conduct (manosucarita) occurs. For one who says with a mind accompanied by insight, "It is of the nature to be exhausted, it is of the nature to perish," verbal good conduct (vacīsucarita) occurs. For one who does not touch it, reflecting "This is an object not to be touched," bodily good conduct (kāyasucarita) occurs. The same method applies to the remaining doors. Thus, in detail, there are eighteen types of good conduct. In brief, in these six doors, restraint of the body is bodily good conduct, restraint of speech is verbal good conduct, and restraint of the mind is mental good conduct—thus there are only three types of good conduct. In this way, it should be understood that the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) fulfills the three types of good conduct. By this much, the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara-sīla) protected by virtue is explained.

In the Pali passages beginning with "kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāya," there are three types of bodily misconduct, four types of verbal misconduct, and three types of mental misconduct. By way of their opposites, bodily good conduct and so forth should be understood. By this much, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is explained through bodily and verbal restraint, and the remaining three virtues through mental restraint—thus the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) is explained. In this entire sutta, the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) based on good conduct are mixed with the supramundane. The seventh sutta is clear in its meaning. In the eighth sutta, "paccattaṃ" means by oneself. "Yonisomanasikārā" means by way of wise attention. "Ārabbhamāno vā" means only by bringing it about. "Suvimuttaṃ" means well-liberated through reflection on the meditation subject. "Aṭṭhiṃ katvā" means having made it a matter of interest (having paid attention). In the ninth sutta, "nāññatra tathāgatassa pātubhāvā" means that they do not arise at any other time except for the appearance of the Tathāgata.
185:
The foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) occurring in the preliminary stage, which are the basis of the seven factors of enlightenment, are mixed with the supramundane. Those factors of enlightenment in the preliminary stage, which have the foundations of mindfulness as their basis, are also only preliminary (mundane). However, those factors of enlightenment based on knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti) should be understood as being taught as purely supramundane. The seventh sutta is clear in its meaning.

In the eighth sutta, "paccattaṃ" means by oneself. "Yonisomanasikārā" means by way of wise attention. "Ārabbhamāno vā" means only by bringing it about. "Suvimuttaṃ" means well-liberated through reflection on the meditation subject. "Aṭṭhiṃ katvā" means having made it a matter of interest or being one who desires it.

In the ninth sutta, "nāññatra tathāgatassa pātubhāvā" means that they do not arise at any other time except for the appearance of the Tathāgata.

All terms such as "vipula" (expansive) and so on are spoken with reference to the state of being well-developed. Indeed, a well-developed factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (sati-sambojjhaṅga) is called expansive, exalted, immeasurable, and free from ill-will. "Through the abandoning of craving, kamma is abandoned" means that whatever kamma rooted in craving would arise, that kamma is abandoned by the abandoning of craving so that it does not arise again. Although terms like "the destruction of craving" refer only to the destruction of craving and so on, it should be understood that by these words, Nibbāna is preached in terms of ultimate meaning. The mind that is developed by those factors, or stands having developed those factors, is indeed only the supramundane fruition mind (lokuttara-phala-citta) that has arisen. ## 8. Commentary on Āvaraṇanīvaraṇa Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā" means those things that make wisdom weak. Indeed, when the hindrances frequently arise, the wisdom that arises in the intervals becomes weak, dull, and unclear.

The five hindrances do not exist at that time. The seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) reach fulfillment in development at that time. For, when a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) is listening to the suitable Dhamma...
189:
For one who is listening to the Dhamma, the five hindrances are far away. If that person is able to produce distinction (special attainment) in that very place, then the seven factors of enlightenment reach fulfillment in development for him. If he is not able to do so, then having risen from that place of listening to the Dhamma and gone to a place for the night or a place for the day, not abandoning that very rapture (pīti), he will produce distinction by suppressing the five hindrances. Even if he is not yet able in that place, he will produce distinction by suppressing the hindrances without abandoning that very rapture within seven days; this was said with reference to this point. The factors of enlightenment obtained once, which are on the side of rapture and gladness (pīti-pāmojja) by virtue of listening to the Dhamma, may disappear due to delighting in activities and so forth; however, when they arise again after obtaining a suitable climate (utusappāya) and so forth of such a nature, it is said that they reach fulfillment in development at that time.

190:
## 2. Cakkavattisuttavaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, regarding the phrase "rañño bhikkhave cakkavattissa": He is called "rājā" (king) because he shines with his own splendor and prosperity, or because he pleases the people with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu); thus, "of that king" (is the meaning). He is called "cakkavatti" (Wheel-turning Monarch) because he causes the Wheel-treasure to turn, urging it with the words, "May the noble Wheel-treasure turn," which arise through the power of his merit; thus, "of that Wheel-turning Monarch" (is the meaning). "Pātubhāvā" means by way of manifestation. "Sattannaṃ" is the delimitation of the number. "Ratanānaṃ" is the demonstration of the defined meaning. In this context, the word-definition of "ratana" (treasure) is that it is called a treasure because it generates delight (ratijanana).

Furthermore:
"It is called a treasure because it is honored, highly valuable, 
incomparable, rare to see, 
and used only by noble beings."

From the time the Wheel-treasure arises, there is no other place considered a shrine; everyone performs offerings with scents, flowers, etc., and pays homage to that Wheel-treasure alone. Thus, it is called a treasure in the sense of being honored. Because no price can be set for the Wheel-treasure, such as "it is worth this much wealth," it is also called a treasure in the sense of being highly valuable. Because the Wheel-treasure is unlike any other treasures existing in the world, it is a treasure in the sense of being incomparable. Since Wheel-turning Monarchs appear only in the aeons (kappa) where Buddhas arise, and Buddhas arise only once in a long while, it is a treasure in the sense of being rare to see. That Wheel-treasure arises only for a noble and magnificent being who is distinguished by birth, appearance, family, and power, and not for anyone else; thus, it is also called a treasure in the sense of being used only by noble beings. As it is with the Wheel-treasure, so it is with the remaining treasures. Therefore, it is said:

"It is called a treasure because it is honored, highly valuable, 
incomparable, rare to see, 
and used only by noble beings."

"Pātubhāvo hoti" means the arising occurs. In this statement, the connection (yojanā) is as follows: While some might say it is improper to state, "Due to the appearance of the Wheel-turning Monarch, the appearance of the seven treasures occurs," it is not improper to connect it as: the king is called a Wheel-turner only after he has caused the arisen Wheel to turn. Why? Because it regards the certainty of the turning of the wheel. For a king who will certainly turn the wheel is entitled to be called "The Wheel-turning Monarch has appeared" from the moment of his conception (paṭisandhi). This is also appropriate because it speaks of the initial arising of a man who has already acquired the name. This...
191:
The appearance, which is called the conception (paṭisandhi) of the special being named the Wheel-turner, is the meaning in this context. Indeed, due to the appearance of that future Wheel-turning Monarch, the treasures appear. In another way, the accumulation of merit (puññasambhāra) of that king matures along with those treasures that have appeared; at that time, the Wheel-turning Monarch is united with them. Then, the perception that "these treasures have appeared" arises among the people. This statement is also appropriate because it uses the plural (bahulavacana) based on the appearance of many treasures. When the perception that "these treasures have appeared" arises among the people, at that time, the Wheel-treasure alone appears first, and later the other six treasures appear; thus, this is also appropriate according to the plural usage. 

This statement is also appropriate due to the specific nuance of the word "pātubhāva." Indeed, not only is the mere manifestation called "pātubhāva," but that which causes manifestation is also called "pātubhāva." This is the specific nuance of the word "pātubhāva." Because that accumulation of merit causes the king to appear as a Wheel-turner by the power of conception, it is "due to the pātubhāva (merit that causes appearance) of the king, the Wheel-turner." Indeed, it is not only the Wheel-turning Monarch who appears, but these seven treasures also appear. This is the meaning here. Just as that accumulation of merit is the productive cause (janaka-hetu) for the king, so too is it the decisive support cause (upanissaya-hetu) for the treasures by way of method. Therefore, the statement, "Monks, due to the appearance of the Wheel-turning Monarch, the appearance of the seven treasures occurs," is entirely appropriate.

Now, to show those treasures by their specific nature, the Buddha said, "Which seven? The Wheel-treasure," and so forth. Among those terms, "cakkaratanassa" etc., the summary of the meaning is as follows: The appearance of the Wheel-treasure occurs, which is capable of taking and giving the glory and wealth of the four great islands together with their retinue of two thousand small islands. Furthermore, the appearance of the Elephant-treasure occurs, which is capable of traveling the entire earth bounded by the ocean and can travel through the sky even before the morning meal; and of the Horse-treasure, which has similar qualities; and of the Gem-treasure, which is capable of dispelling darkness and providing light for the distance of one league (yojana) even in fourfold darkness; and of the Woman-treasure, whose conduct is pleasing to her husband and who avoids the six faults; and of the Householder-treasure, who is capable of seeing treasures buried underground within a distance of one league; and of the Advisor-treasure, who is the eldest son born from the womb of the chief queen and is capable of advising the entire kingdom. This is the summary of the meaning here. In detail, however, the manner of the appearance of the Wheel-treasure and others has already appeared in suttas such as the Mahāsudassana Sutta. The meaning of that manner has also been explained in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) of those suttas.
192:
In the passages beginning with "Sati-sambojjhaṅga-ratanassa" (the jewel of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness), the similarity should be understood as follows: Just as the Wheel-treasure of a Universal Monarch is the precursor to all other treasures, so too the jewel of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is the precursor to all states belonging to the four planes. Because of its nature as a precursor, it is like the Wheel-treasure of a Universal Monarch. Among the treasures of a Universal Monarch, the Elephant-treasure is endowed with a large body, is lofty, vast, and great; similarly, this jewel of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) is endowed with a great body of Dhamma, is a mansion of Dhamma that is lofty, vast, and powerful, and thus it is like the Elephant-treasure. The Horse-treasure of a Universal Monarch has a swift and light speed; similarly, this jewel of the enlightenment factor of energy (viriya-sambojjhaṅga) has a swift and light speed. Because of this swift and light speed, it is like the Horse-treasure. The Gem-treasure of a Universal Monarch dispels darkness and reveals light; similarly, this jewel of the enlightenment factor of rapture (pīti-sambojjhaṅga), being purely wholesome, dispels the darkness of defilements and reveals the light of knowledge through the power of conascence-condition and so on. Because of this dispelling of darkness and revealing of light, it is like the Gem-treasure.

The Queen-treasure of a Universal Monarch calms the distress of body and mind and especially allays feverish heat. This jewel of the enlightenment factor of tranquillity (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga) also calms the distress of body and mind and especially allays feverish heat, and thus it is like the Queen-treasure. The Householder-treasure of a Universal Monarch, by giving wealth at any desired moment, cuts off distraction and makes the mind one-pointed; similarly, this jewel of the enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) fulfills absorption (appanā) according to one's wish, cuts off distraction, and makes the mind one-pointed, and thus it is like the Householder-treasure. The Counselor-treasure (parināyaka-ratana) of a Universal Monarch, by accomplishing all necessary tasks, makes the monarch free from concern; similarly, this jewel of the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga) frees the arising of consciousness from sluggishness (līna) and restlessness (uddhacca), and by maintaining it in a balanced effort (payoga-majjhatta), makes one free from concern, and thus it is like the Counselor-treasure. Thus, it should be understood that in this sutta, the classification of all states included in the four planes is taught.

## 6. Sākaccha-vagga (The Chapter on Discussion)
## 1. Commentary on the Āhāra Sutta

In the first sutta of the sixth chapter, regarding the words "This nutriment is for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness..." and so on, the distinction from the previous method is as follows: It is not only the previously mentioned causes that serve as conditions for the arising of mindfulness and the other enlightenment factors, or for the fulfillment through development of those already arisen; other causes should also be understood as follows.

Four other things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), avoiding muddle-minded persons, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and inclination towards that mindfulness. Mindfulness arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances such as moving forward and so on; by avoiding muddle-minded persons who are like a crow perched on a bowl of rice; by associating with persons of established mindfulness like the Elder Tissadatta and the Elder Abhaya; and by having a mind inclined, leaning, and sloping towards the establishment of mindfulness while standing, sitting, and so on. The fulfillment through development of that mindfulness which has arisen through these four causes occurs by means of the Path of Arahantship.

Seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga): inquisitiveness, cleansing the physical basis, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reviewing the conduct of deep knowledge, and inclination towards that investigation. Therein, "inquisitiveness" (paripucchakatā) means being frequent in questioning concerning the meaning of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), powers (bala), enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), path factors (maggaṅga), jhāna factors, serenity (samatha), and insight (vipassanā).

"Cleansing the physical basis" (vatthu-visadakiriya) means making the internal and external objects clean and bright. When a monk's hair, fingernails, toenails, and body hair are long, or when the body is impure due to the provocation of humors like wind, bile, and phlegm, or smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclean and impure. When the robes are worn out, dirty, and foul-smelling, or when the dwelling and bedding are cluttered with refuse, then the external basis is unclean and impure. Therefore, the internal basis should be made clean by cutting the hair and so on, by making the body light through purgatives and emetics, and by anointing and bathing. The external basis should be made clean by sewing, washing, dyeing, and repairing the robes and so on. If these internal and external bases are unclean, the knowledge (ñāṇa) in the arising consciousness and mental factors will also be unclean and impure. Just as the flame of a lamp that arises depending on an impure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil...
194:
It is like a light. When consciousness and mental factors arise in a clear internal or external physical basis (vatthu), knowledge also becomes clear. This is like the light of a lamp flame that arises depending on a clean lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. Therefore, it is said: "Cleansing the physical basis leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga)."

Balancing the faculties (indriya-samatta-paṭipādanā) means bringing the faculties such as faith and others into a state of mutual balance. If a meditator's faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is excessively strong while the other faculties are weak, then the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) cannot perform the function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) cannot perform the function of establishing awareness, the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) cannot perform the function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) cannot perform the function of seeing the nature of phenomena. Therefore, that faculty of faith should be weakened either by reflecting on the nature of phenomena or by not attending to it in the manner that caused it to become strong. The story of the Elder Vakkali (Vakkali Thera) is an example here. If the faculty of energy is excessively strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform the function of resolution (adhimokkha), nor can the other faculties perform their respective functions. Therefore, that energy should be weakened by developing tranquility (passaddhi) and so on. In this case, the story of the Elder Soṇa (Soṇa Thera) should be shown. In the same way, it should be understood that if any one of the remaining faculties is excessively strong, the others will be unable to perform their own functions.

Particularly, in this context, the balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, is praised. One with strong faith but weak wisdom has blind devotion and gains confidence in what is not a proper ground. One with strong wisdom but weak faith tends towards the side of cunning; like a disease caused by medicine, such a person is difficult to cure. Thinking excessively that "merit occurs merely by the arising of a thought," they fail to perform acts of generosity (dāna) and so on, and may be reborn in hell. Only when the two are balanced does one have confidence in what is truly a proper ground for confidence. If concentration is strong and energy is weak, because concentration tends towards the side of sloth (kosañña), sloth overcomes the mind. If energy is strong and concentration is weak, because energy tends towards the side of restlessness (uddhacca), restlessness overcomes the mind. However, when concentration is joined with energy, it does not fall into sloth; when energy is joined with concentration, it does not fall into restlessness. Therefore, both should be made balanced. For only when both are balanced does absorption (appanā) occur.

Furthermore, for one who works on concentration, even strong faith is suitable. Only by thus believing and being convinced will one reach absorption. Between concentration and wisdom, for one who works on concentration, strong one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is suitable. Only in this way can he reach absorption. For one who works on insight (vipassanā), strong wisdom is suitable. Only in this way can he reach the penetration of the three characteristics (lakkhaṇa).
195:
Absorption (appanā) also occurs through the balance of both concentration and wisdom. However, mindfulness (sati) should be strong in all circumstances. Indeed, mindfulness protects the mind from falling into restlessness through the power of faith, energy, and wisdom, which belong to the side of restlessness; and from falling into sloth through concentration, which belongs to the side of sloth. Therefore, mindfulness is desired in all instances, like salt in all dishes, or like a prime minister who is in charge of all royal affairs. Thus it was said: "Mindfulness, however, has been declared by the Blessed One to be useful everywhere. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection; without mindfulness, there is no exerting or restraining of the mind."

Avoiding unwise persons (duppañña-puggala-parivajjanā) means avoiding from afar those persons of poor wisdom who do not penetrate the divisions of the aggregates (khandha) and so on through the power of learning and knowledge. Associating with wise persons (paññavanta-puggala-sevanā) means associating with persons endowed with the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), which grasps the fifty characteristics. Reflecting on the field of deep knowledge (gambhīra-ñāṇa-cariya-paccavekkhaṇā) means reflecting on the distinctions of deep wisdom occurring in deep subjects such as the aggregates. Being inclined towards that (tadadhimuttatā) means having a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined towards the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) while standing, sitting, and so on. For one in whom it has thus arisen, the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā) occurs through the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga).

Eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of energy (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga): reflecting on the fear of woeful states (apāya-bhaya-paccavekkhaṇatā), seeing the benefits of energy, reflecting on the path to be traveled, honoring the almsfood (reflecting on the gratitude for almsfood), reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher (the Buddha), reflecting on the greatness of the lineage, reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners, avoiding lazy persons, associating with energetic persons, and being inclined towards that energy.

Among those eleven, the enlightenment factor of energy arises in one who reflects on the fear of woeful states thus: "In the hells, when suffering great pain starting from the fivefold binding; in the animal realm, when being caught by nets, baskets, and so on; when being beaten with spiked whips and forced to pull carts; in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), when being afflicted by hunger and thirst for many thousands of years or even for the interval between two Buddhas; among the Kalakañjika Asuras, when experiencing the suffering of wind and heat with a body sixty or eighty cubits high consisting only of skin and bones—at such times it is not possible to arouse the enlightenment factor of energy. Now is the only time for you, O bhikkhu!"

It also arises in one who sees the benefits of energy thus: "A lazy person cannot attain the nine supramundane states (nava-lokuttara-dhamma); only one with aroused energy can attain them. This is the benefit of energy."
196:
This path is the one traveled only by all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples; I too must travel this path. This path cannot be traveled by one who is lazy. Thus, the factor of enlightenment of energy (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga) arises in one who reflects on the way of travel in this manner.

These people who support you with alms-food and so forth are not your relatives, nor are they your slaves or servants. They do not give you choice alms-food with the thought, 'We shall live depending on you.' Rather, they give, longing for the great fruit of their own meritorious deeds. Even the Teacher did not allow these requisites for you, seeing that 'This monk, by using these four requisites, will live happily with a firm and strong body.' Rather, he allowed them, seeing that 'This monk, while using these four requisites, will perform the duties of a recluse and be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirth.' Now, if you live lazily, you will not be reciprocating the honor of that alms-food. Indeed, the reciprocation of alms-food belongs only to one who has aroused energy. Thus, the factor of enlightenment of energy arises in one who reflects on the reciprocation of alms-food in this manner, as in the case of Elder Mahāmitta.

It is said that the Elder resided in a cave called Kassakalena. In the village where he went for alms, a great female lay follower looked after the Elder, treating him like a son. One day, as she was about to go to the forest, she said to her daughter: "Dear daughter, in such a place there is old rice, in such a place milk, in such a place ghee, and in such a place molasses. When your brother, the Venerable Mitta, comes, cook the rice and offer it to him along with the milk, ghee, and molasses. You should eat as well. As for me, I have eaten yesterday's leftover rice with fermented rice-water." The daughter asked, "Mother, what will you eat for lunch?" She replied, "Put in some leaves and cook a sour gruel with broken rice, dear daughter."

While the Elder was putting on his robe and taking out his bowl, he heard those words and admonished himself: "The great lay follower has eaten leftover rice with fermented rice-water and will eat sour gruel of broken rice and leaves for lunch. For your sake, however, she pointed out old rice and so forth. Indeed, this lay follower does not long for fields, property, food, or clothing depending on you, but gives, aspiring only for the three types of attainments (sampatti). Will you be able to give those attainments to this lay follower, or will you not?" He asked himself. "You are not able to take this alms-food with greed, hatred, and delusion," he admonished. He put the bowl back in its bag, unfastened the robe-knot, turned back, and went to Kassakalena. He placed the bowl under the bed and the robe on the robe-rack.
197:
"I shall not leave without reaching Arahantship," he resolved, arousing energy, and sat down. That monk, who had lived heedfully for a long time, developed insight and attained Arahantship even before the mealtime. Like a blooming lotus, the great Arahant (khīṇāsava), whose taints were exhausted, came out with a smile. A deity dwelling in a tree at the cave entrance uttered this inspired utterance:

"Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man!
Whose taints are exhausted; you, sir, are worthy of offerings."

Having uttered this, the deity said, "Venerable sir, by giving alms to Arahants like you who enter for alms, old women will be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirth." The Elder rose, opened the door, and looking at the time, realized, "It is still early morning." He took his bowl and robe and entered the village.

The young woman, having prepared the meal, sat looking toward the door, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now he will come." When the Elder reached the door of the house, she took the bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and placed it in his hands. The Elder said, "May you be happy," gave the blessing, and departed. The young woman remained standing, just looking at the Elder. Indeed, at that time, the Elder's complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were serene, and his face was radiant like a ripe palmyra fruit fallen from its stalk.

The great female lay follower returned from the forest and asked, "Dear daughter, did your brother come?" The young woman reported everything that had happened. The lay follower, realizing, "Today my son's task of monkhood has reached its summit," said, "Dear daughter, your brother delights in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not dissatisfied."

"Indeed, this is the great heritage of the Teacher, namely the seven noble wealths (ariya-dhana); they cannot be obtained by one who is lazy. Just as parents might cast out a misbehaving son, saying, 'This is not our son,' and he does not receive the inheritance after their passing, so too a lazy person does not receive this heritage of noble wealth. Only one who has aroused energy receives it." Thus, the factor of enlightenment of energy arises in one who reflects on the greatness of the heritage.
198:
Parents may cast out a son, saying, 'This is not our son.' Such a son cannot receive the inheritance when the parents pass away. Similarly, a lazy person, because of their laziness, becomes one of improper conduct and does not deserve the inheritance of the noble wealth (ariya-dhana) that should be received from the Blessed One. Only one with aroused energy deserves it. Thus, for one who reflects on the greatness of the inheritance, the enlightenment factor of energy (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga) arises.

Furthermore, 'Your Teacher, the Blessed One, is truly great. At the time of your Teacher’s conception in his mother’s womb, at his great renunciation, at his supreme enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the performance of the twin miracle, at the descent from the celestial realm, at the relinquishing of the life-force, and at the time of his final passing (parinibbāna), the ten-thousandfold world system shook. Is it fitting for you, having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Teacher, to be lazy?' Thus, for one who reflects on the greatness of the Teacher, the enlightenment factor of energy arises.

'By birth, you are no longer of low status. You are born into the Okkāka royal dynasty, descended from the unbroken lineage of Mahāsammata. You are the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of the Venerable Rāhula. Being such a son of the Conqueror (Jinaputta), it is not fitting for you to live lazily.' Thus, for one who reflects on the greatness of birth, the enlightenment factor of energy arises.

'Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Moggallāna, and the eighty great disciples realized the supramundane Dhamma only through energy. Will you follow the path of these fellow practitioners, or will you not?' Thus, for one who reflects on the greatness of fellow practitioners, the enlightenment factor of energy arises.

The enlightenment factor of energy also arises for one who avoids lazy persons who, like pythons that have filled their bellies and lie still, have abandoned both bodily and mental energy; for one who associates with persons of aroused energy whose minds are directed towards Nibbāna; and for one who has a mind inclined, leaning, and sloping towards arousing energy in postures such as standing and sitting. This enlightenment factor of energy, once arisen, reaches the fulfillment of development through the path of Arahantship.

Eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy (pĩti-sambojjhaṅga). They are: the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dhamma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of virtue (sĩla), the recollection of generosity (cāga), the recollection of deities (devatā), the recollection of peace (upasama), avoiding coarse persons, associating with refined persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses (suttantas), and being inclined towards that enlightenment factor of joy.

For one who repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, pervading the entire body up to access concentration (upacāra). It also arises for one who repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha; for a monk who reflects on the fourfold purifying virtue (catupārisuddhi-sĩla) maintained unbroken for a long time; for laypeople who reflect on the five or ten precepts; for one who reflects on their generosity, thinking, 'We have given such fine food to fellow practitioners during times of famine and peril'; for laypeople when they reflect on the gifts given to virtuous ones during such times; and for one who reflects on the existence within themselves of those qualities by which deities attained their celestial status. For one who reflects on the defilements (nĩvaraṇa) suppressed by meditative attainments for sixty or seventy years...
199:
(The Factor of Enlightenment of Joy) arises for one who reflects that [defilements] have not arisen [for sixty or seventy years]; for one who avoids 'dry' persons who, like the dust on a donkey's back, are devoid of the moisture of faith and devotion toward the Triple Gem, as evidenced by their lack of respect when visiting shrines, Bodhi trees, or senior elders; for one who associates with 'moist' persons of gentle mind who have great faith in the Buddha and so forth; for one who reflects on inspiring Suttas that illustrate the virtues of the Triple Gem; and for one whose mind is inclined toward producing joy while standing, sitting, and so forth. For one in whom it has thus arisen, the Factor of Enlightenment of Joy reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga).

Seven things lead to the arising of the Factor of Enlightenment of Tranquillity (Passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga). They are: using superior food, using comfortable weather, using comfortable postures, middle application (majjhatta-payoga), avoiding persons with restless bodies, associating with persons of tranquil bodies, and having a mind inclined toward that Factor of Enlightenment of Tranquillity.

Tranquillity arises for one who partakes of superior, soft, and gentle food; for one who makes use of suitable weather among cold and hot climates; and for one who makes use of suitable postures such as standing and so forth. This is not said with reference to a person of the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) type who can endure all climates and postures. It arises only for a person who has suitability and unsuitability (sabhāga-visabhāga), when they avoid unsuitable weather and postures and use those that are suitable. Middle application (majjhatta-payoga) is said to be the reflection on the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā) of oneself and others. Through this middle application, (tranquillity) arises. It also arises for one who avoids persons with restless bodies who wander about harassing others with clods, sticks, and so forth; for one who associates with persons of tranquil bodies whose hands and feet are restrained; and for one whose mind is inclined toward producing tranquillity while standing, sitting, and so forth. For one in whom it has thus arisen, the Factor of Enlightenment of Tranquillity reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship.

Ten things lead to the arising of the Factor of Enlightenment of Concentration (Samādhi-sambojjhaṅga). They are: making the basis clean, balancing the faculties (indriya), skill in the sign (nimitta), uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time, gladdening the mind at the proper time, looking on with equanimity at the proper time, avoiding unconcentrated persons, associating with concentrated persons, and having a mind inclined toward that Factor of Enlightenment of Concentration. Among these ten, making the basis clean and balancing the faculties should be understood in the manner already described.

Uplifting the mind at the proper time means: when the mind is shrinking and sluggish due to excessively lax energy and so forth, one uplifts and raises that mind by causing the Factor of Enlightenment of Investigation of States (Dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga), the Factor of Enlightenment of Energy (Viriya-sambojjhaṅga), and the Factor of Enlightenment of Joy (Pīti-sambojjhaṅga) to arise. Restraining the mind at the proper time means: when the mind is distracted due to excessively exerted energy and so forth, one checks and suppresses that mind by causing the Factor of Enlightenment of Tranquillity, the Factor of Enlightenment of Concentration, and the Factor of Enlightenment of Equanimity to arise. Gladdening the mind at the proper time means: when the mind is joyless due to weak wisdom or due to not attaining the bliss of peace, one causes it to be stirred by reflecting on the eight grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu). The grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu) are: the four—birth, aging, sickness, and death; the fifth, the suffering of the woeful planes; the suffering rooted in the round (vaṭṭa) of the past; the suffering rooted in the round of the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present.
200:
Skill in the sign (nimitta-kusalatā) means skill in grasping the sign of the kasiṇa. Uplifting the mind at the proper time means that when the mind is sluggish due to excessively lax energy and so forth, one uplifts it by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), energy (vīriya), and rapture (pīti). Restraining the mind at the proper time means that when the mind is restless due to excessively exerted energy and so forth, one restrains it by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā). Gladdening the mind at the proper time means that when the mind is listless due to weak application of wisdom or the absence of the bliss of peace, one strikes it with a sense of urgency by reflecting on the eight grounds for urgency (saṃvega-vatthu). The eight grounds for urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these are four; the suffering of the woeful states is the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for food in the present. One also generates confidence by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem. This is called "gladdening the mind at the proper time."

Looking on with equanimity at the proper time means that when the mind, by virtue of right practice, is neither sluggish nor restless nor listless, but proceeds evenly on the object and has entered the path of serenity (samatha), one does not then exert effort in uplifting, restraining, or gladdening it. This is like a charioteer who does not interfere with horses that are running evenly. This is called "looking on with equanimity at the proper time." Avoiding persons who are not concentrated means keeping far away from persons whose minds are distracted and who have not attained either access concentration (upacāra) or absorption concentration (appanā). Associating with concentrated persons means associating with, frequenting, and attending to those whose minds are concentrated through either access or absorption. Inclination towards that concentration means having a mind that leans, slopes, and inclines only towards the arising of concentration while standing, sitting, and so forth. For one practicing in this way, this enlightenment factor of concentration arises. Once it has arisen, it reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship.

Five things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga): equanimity towards beings, equanimity towards formations, avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations, associating with persons who are equanimous towards beings and formations, and inclination towards that enlightenment factor of equanimity. Among these five, one arouses equanimity towards beings in two ways: by reflecting on ownership of kamma (kammassakatā), thinking, "You have come by your own kamma and will depart by your own kamma; this person too has come by their own kamma and will depart by their own kamma—whom are you attached to?" and by reflecting on the absence of a being (nissatta), thinking, "In the ultimate sense, there is no being at all—whom are you attached to?" One arouses equanimity towards formations also in two ways—
201:
—by reflecting on the ownerless nature (assāmika-bhāva), thinking, "This robe will gradually undergo change in color and reach a state of decay, becoming a foot-rag, and will eventually be discarded with the tip of a walking stick. If this robe had an owner, that owner would not allow it to perish in this way"; and by reflecting on its temporary nature (tāvakālika-bhāva), thinking, "This robe is not lasting; it is only temporary." (In these ways, one arouses equanimity towards formations). As with the robe, the same application should be made regarding the alms-bowl and so forth.

In the phrase "avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations," a person who is attached to beings (satta-kelāyana) is one, whether lay or ordained, who dotes on their own children or students, resident pupils, and so forth. Such a person performs tasks like shaving their hair, sewing, washing and dyeing their robes, and firing their alms-bowls with their own hands. If they do not see them for even a moment, they look here and there like a frightened deer, asking, "Where is such-and-such a novice? Where is such-and-such a young monk?" Even when requested by another to send someone for a moment for the purpose of hair-shaving and so forth, they do not give permission, saying, "We ourselves do not make him work; if you take him, you will only tire him out." A person who is attached to formations (saṅkhāra-kelāyana) is one who is possessive of robes, alms-bowls, cups, walking sticks, and so forth, not even allowing another to touch them with their hand. Even when asked to lend them for a moment, they say, "We ourselves, treasuring these things, do not use them; how can we give them to you?" A person who is neutral and indifferent toward both these types of objects is called a person equanimous towards beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-majjhatta). Thus, this enlightenment factor of equanimity arises for one who avoids from afar such persons attached to beings and formations, for one who associates with persons equanimous towards beings and formations, and for one who has a mind that leans, slopes, and inclines towards the arising of that equanimity while standing, sitting, and so forth. Once it has arisen, this enlightenment factor of equanimity reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship.

"The sign of foulness" (asubha-nimitta) refers to the ten foul objects of meditation, such as the bloated corpse (uddhūmātaka) and so forth. In the phrase "making much of wise attention" (yoniso-manasikāra-bahulīkāra), wise attention means attention to means, attention to the right path, and attention that produces the perception of foulness. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire (kāmacchanda): learning the sign of foulness, devotion to the meditation on foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, noble friendship, and suitable talk.

Sensual desire is abandoned in one who learns the ten signs of foulness, in one who develops them, in one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, and in one who [knows the measure] of four or five mouthfuls of food...
202:
Even for one who knows moderation in food, sensual desire is abandoned because of the habit of living moderately by drinking water when there is still room for four or five mouthfuls of food. Therefore, it is said: "One should not eat the last four or five mouthfuls, but drink water; this is enough for the comfortable living of a bhikkhu with a resolute mind" (Theragāthā 983). Sensual desire is also abandoned for one who associates with a good friend like the Elder Tissa, the practitioner of foulness meditation, who delights in the meditation on foulness, and by suitable talk concerning the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire." Sensual desire abandoned by these six things is completely eradicated by the Path of Arahantship so that it does not arise again in the future.

In the phrase "mettā cetovimutti" (loving-kindness, the liberation of mind), when "mettā" is mentioned, both absorption (appanā) and access (upacāra) are appropriate; but when "cetovimutti" is mentioned, only absorption is appropriate. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) has the characteristics already mentioned. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill-will: learning the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the meditation on loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of kamma, frequent reflection, good friendship, and suitable talk.

Ill-will is abandoned for one who learns loving-kindness by way of either specific or non-specific pervasion of the quarters, and likewise for one who develops loving-kindness by way of specific or non-specific pervasion of the quarters. "What can you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue and so on? Have you not come by your own kamma and will you not go by your own kamma? To be angry with another is like wanting to strike another after taking hold of glowing coals without flame, a hot iron rod, or excrement. What can this person do by being angry with you? Will he be able to destroy your virtue and so on? He has come by his own kamma and will go by his own kamma. Like an unaccepted gift or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger will fall back on his own head." Thus, ill-will is abandoned for one who reflects on the ownership of kamma of oneself and others, for one who stands in reflection after considering the ownership of kamma of both, for one who associates with a good friend like the Elder Assagutta who delights in the meditation on loving-kindness, and by suitable talk related to loving-kindness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of ill-will..."
203:
...lead to the abandoning of ill-will." Ill-will abandoned by these six things is completely eradicated by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga) so that it does not arise again in the future.

"Bhikkhus, there is boredom (arati)," etc., the meaning of this is just as already stated. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: attention to the sign of overeating, changing postures, attention to the perception of light, living in the open air, good friendship, and suitable talk.

For one who, after eating excessively such as "hand-filler" (āharahatthaka), "vomit-eater" (bhuttavimitaka), "rolling-there" (tatravaṭṭaka), "cloth-sufficient" (alaṃsāṭaka), or "crow-morsel" (kākamāsaka) meals, sits and practices the recluse's duties during the night or day, sloth and torpor come over him like a great elephant. But for a bhikkhu who has the habit of living moderately by leaving room for four or five mouthfuls and drinking water, this does not happen. Thus, sloth and torpor are abandoned for one who notes the sign of overeating. Sloth and torpor are also abandoned for one who changes to another posture when sloth and torpor descend in a certain posture; for one who attends to the light of the sun by day, and the light of the moon, lamps, or torches by night; for one who lives in the open air; for one who associates with good friends like the Elder Mahākassapa who has abandoned sloth and torpor; and by suitable talk related to the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor." Sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things are completely eradicated by the Path of Arahantship so that they do not arise again in the future.

"Bhikkhus, there is tranquility of mind," etc., these words have the meanings already stated. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse: great learning, questioning, proficiency in the Vinaya, serving the elders, good friendship, and suitable talk.

Restlessness and remorse are abandoned for one who, through great learning, studies one, two, three, four, or all five Nikāyas both in text and in meaning; for one who frequently questions what is allowable and what is not; for one who is proficient in the Vinaya through mastery of its rules; for one who approaches elder theras who are mature in years and virtue; for one who associates with good friends like the Elder Upāli who is a master of the Vinaya; and by suitable talk related to what is allowable and what is not while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse."
204:
Among restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) abandoned by these six things, restlessness is abandoned by the path of arahantship (arahattamagga), and remorse is abandoned by the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga), so that they do not arise again in the future. The terms such as "wholesome and unwholesome states" (kusalākusala dhammā) have the same meanings as already stated. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt (vicikicchā): great learning, frequent questioning, proficiency in the Vinaya, abundance of firm conviction (adhimokkha), noble friendship, and suitable conversation.

For a monk who studies one or all five Nikāyas by way of the Pali text and by way of the meaning through great learning, doubt is abandoned. Doubt is also abandoned for one who frequently asks questions concerning the Three Jewels, for one who has mastery through practice in the Vinaya, for one who has an abundance of firm conviction known as faith that is settled in the Three Jewels, and for one who associates with noble friends like the Elder Vakkali who was eminent in faith. Doubt is also abandoned through suitable conversation based on the virtues of the Three Jewels while standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt." Doubt abandoned by these six things reaches the state of non-arising in the future through the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). Thus, in this discourse, the Blessed One turned the teaching away from the three realms of existence and crowned it with arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks attained arahantship.

## 2. Pariyāyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second discourse, "many" (sambahulā) means, according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called "many," and more than that is called the "Saṅgha." According to the Suttanta method, three are called just "three," and only more than three are called "many." In this discourse, it should be understood as more than three monks according to the Suttanta method. "They entered for alms" means those who have already entered. In reality, although those monks had not yet entered the city of Sāvatthī, it was said "they entered" because they had set out with the intention, "We will enter." How is this? It is like a man who has set out saying, "I will go to the village," and although he has not yet reached the village, when asked, "Where is so-and-so?" it is said, "He has gone to the village." "The park of the wanderers" (paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo) refers to the park of the wanderers of other sects located not far from the Jetavana monastery. "Friends, the ascetic" means "Friends, your teacher, the ascetic Gotama."

Regarding the statement, "Friends, we also teach the Dhamma to our disciples in this way," although there is no such teaching as "the five hindrances should be abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment should be developed" in the doctrines of the other sects, those wanderers went to the monastery, stood at the edge of the assembly, and pretending to look elsewhere or as if they had other business, they listened to the Blessed One's teaching. Because of such listening, [they knew] "the ascetic Gotama [teaches] these hindrances and the path..."
205:
...do not exist.
