Indeed, those disciples of the wanderers went to the park, stood at the edge of the assembly, and acting as if they were looking at something else or as if they were occupied with other matters, they listened to the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One. After listening, they noted, "The Ascetic Gotama says, 'Abandon these things, develop these things,'" and returned to their own park. Having prepared seats in the middle of the park, surrounded by their male and female lay supporters, they would lift their heads and raise their bodies, acting as if they had realized it through their own self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), and say, "The five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are to be abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are to be developed."

In the phrase "Here, friends" (idha no āvuso), "here" means in this proclamation. "What is the distinction?" (ko viseso) means what is superior? "What is the difference in intention?" (ko adhippayāso) means what is the superior application? "What is the difference?" (kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ) means what is the diversity? "Between teaching and teaching" (dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesanaṃ) means if one were to speak of the specific difference between the Dhamma teaching of the Ascetic Gotama and our Dhamma teaching, or between our Dhamma teaching and that of the Ascetic Gotama, what would that be? The same method applies to the second phrase.

"They neither approved" (neva abhinandisu) means they did not accept it saying, "It is just so." "Nor rejected" (nappaṭikkosisu) means they did not deny it saying, "It is not so." If one asks whether those monks did this because they were capable or because they were incapable, the answer is that they did it while being capable. Indeed, it was not that those monks were unable to say even this much: "Friends, in your doctrine, there is no such thing as the five hindrances to be abandoned, nor the seven factors of enlightenment to be developed." However, this thought occurred to them: "We have this gift of words; we will report this to the Blessed One, and then the Teacher will give us a sweet Dhamma discourse."

"Method" (pariyāya) means the reason. "They will not be able to explain fully" (na ceva sampāyissanti) means they will not be able to speak in a complete manner. "And further distress" (uttariñca vighātaṃ) means they will encounter further suffering because of their inability to explain. For suffering arises in those who are unable to explain fully. In the phrase "As it is, monks, in what is not one's domain" (yathā taṃ bhikkhave avisayasmiṃ), "taṃ" is a mere particle, and "yathā" is a word showing the reason. The meaning is: because a question was asked in a matter that is not one's domain. "With the devas" (sadevaka) means together with the devas. The same method applies to the terms "with the Māras" (samāraka) and so on. Thus, by including the three realms of devas, Māras, and Brahmās in the world, and by encompassing the entire world of beings with the term "two generations/classes of beings" (dve pajāyā), in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās...
206:
He shows: "I do not see any god or human in the world [who can answer this question]." "Or having heard from here" means having heard from this Dispensation (Sāsana) of Mine. He shows that only by hearing from this Dispensation can the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata satisfy and please [the questioner]; there is no such thing as satisfying them by any other means.

Now, wishing to show the satisfaction of the mind by answering their questions, He said: "And what, monks, is the method (pariyāya)..." and so forth. Therein, "internal sensual desire" (ajjhattaṃ kāmacchanda) is the desire and lust arisen regarding one's own five aggregates. "External sensual desire" (bahiddhā kāmacchanda) is the desire and lust arisen regarding the five aggregates of others. "Reaches the count" (uddesaṃ gacchati) means it enters the enumeration. "Internal ill-will" (ajjhattaṃ byāpāda) is the aversion arisen regarding one's own hands, feet, and so forth. "External ill-will" (bahiddhā byāpāda) is the aversion arisen regarding those [limbs] of others. "Internal doubt regarding dhammas" (ajjhattaṃ dhammesu vicikicchā) is doubt regarding one's own aggregates. "External doubt regarding dhammas" (bahiddhā dhammesu vicikicchā) is the great doubt regarding the eight external points [the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, etc.]. "Internal mindfulness regarding dhammas" (ajjhattaṃ dhammesu sati) is the mindfulness arisen in one who grasps the formations (saṅkhāra) within one's own continuity. "External mindfulness regarding dhammas" (bahiddhā dhammesu sati) is the mindfulness arisen in one who grasps the formations in an external continuity. The same method applies to the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga).

"Physical" (kāyika) refers to the energy arisen in one undertaking walking meditation (caṅkama). "Mental" (cetasika) refers to the energy arisen without physical exertion (kāyapayoga), such as: "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging." "Physical tranquillity" (kāyappassaddhi) is the calming of the distress of the three [mental] aggregates. "Mental tranquillity" (cittappassaddhi) is the calming of the distress of the consciousness aggregate. In the case of the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga), the judgment should be understood just as stated for the mindfulness enlightenment factor.

In this Sutta, the enlightenment factors are taught as a mixture [of mundane and supramundane]. Among those enlightenment factors, mindfulness, investigation, and equanimity regarding internal dhammas are only mundane (lokiya) because they take one's own aggregates as their object. Likewise, physical energy that has not yet reached the Path is mundane. Rapture (pīti) and concentration (samādhi) that are without thought and examination (avitakka-avicāra), although they can be of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), are only supramundane (lokuttara) because enlightenment factors are not found in the fine-material sphere [according to this specific view]. However, according to the opinion of the elders who extract the enlightenment factors in the context of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), insight, and the jhānas that serve as a basis for insight, they can be both of the fine-material sphere and the formless sphere (arūpāvacara). Indeed, among the enlightenment factors, only rapture is definitely not found in the formless sphere; the remaining six are mixed. At the conclusion of the teaching, some monks became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), some Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and some Arahants.
207:
## ၃။ အဂ္ဂိသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the third Sutta, "Monks, I say that mindfulness is useful in all circumstances (sabbattheka)" means He says it is desired in every situation [whether restraining or uplifting the mind], like roasted salt in all dishes, or like a multi-skilled minister in all royal affairs. For just as roasted salt is included in all curries, and just as a multi-skilled minister can perform military duties, advisory duties, and administrative duties, thus accomplishing all tasks; in the same way, the restraining of a restless mind and the uplifting of a sluggish mind—all this is accomplished by mindfulness. It is not possible to achieve this without mindfulness. Therefore, He spoke thus. In this Sutta, only the enlightenment factors of the preliminary stage of insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) are discussed.

## ၄။ မေတ္တာသဟဂတသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the fourth Sutta, the entire meaning of "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness" and so forth has been explained in detail in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga. The statement, "We also, friends, teach the Dhamma to disciples in this way," was said by those [wanderers] because they had heard the Buddha's teaching of the Dhamma, following the previous method. In truth, in the doctrine of the wanderers (titthiyas), there is no abandoning of the five hindrances nor the development of the divine abidings (brahmavihāra-bhāvanā) such as loving-kindness. "What is its destination (gati)?" means what is its accomplishment? "What is its supreme (parama)?" means what is the highest? "What is its fruit (phala)?" means what is its benefit? "What is its culmination (pariyosāna)?" means what is its end? "Accompanied by loving-kindness" (mettāsahagata) means accompanied by, associated with, or conjoined with loving-kindness. This method applies everywhere. Terms such as "supported by seclusion" (vivekanissita) have meanings that have already been explained.

"Non-repulsive" (appaṭikūla) is of two kinds: non-repulsive beings and non-repulsive formations. It refers to a pleasant (iṭṭha) object. "Perceiving as repulsive" (paṭikūlasaññī) means having the perception of the unpleasant (aniṭṭha). How does one dwell in this state? By pervading a non-repulsive being with [the perception of] foulness (asubha) or by attending to non-repulsive formations as impermanent (anicca). For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "How does one dwell perceiving as repulsive in a non-repulsive object? One pervades a pleasant object with foulness or applies [the perception of] impermanence." In a repulsive, unpleasant object, however, one who pervades it with loving-kindness or attends to it as elements (dhātu) is said to dwell "perceiving as non-repulsive" (appaṭikūlasaññī). As it is said: "How does one dwell perceiving as non-repulsive in a repulsive object? One pervades an unpleasant object with loving-kindness or applies [the perception of] elements." The same method should be understood for the mixed terms. In both non-repulsive and repulsive objects, one who pervades with the perception of foulness or attends to them as impermanent...
208: By attending to [things] as impermanent, one is said to dwell with the perception of the repulsive. In the case of both repulsive and non-repulsive objects, one who practices the aforementioned pervasion of loving-kindness or the attention to the four elements is said to dwell with the perception of the non-repulsive. One who develops the six-factored equanimity, described in the manner beginning with 'Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad...', should be understood as 'Avoiding both the non-repulsive and the repulsive, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.' With this sequence of teaching, for this monk, having produced the third and fourth jhānas through loving-kindness, and using that as a basis to develop insight (vipassanā), the teaching should have concluded upon his reaching Arahantship, as it shows the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) associated with the path along with insight and noble psychic power. However, even when contemplating formations (saṅkhāra) based on this jhāna of loving-kindness, if a monk is unable to reach Arahantship, it is because loving-kindness does not have Arahantship as its culmination for him. Rather, whatever state is its culmination should be shown. Therefore, this teaching was begun to show that state. Later, in passages such as 'By the complete surmounting of perceptions of form...', the purpose of beginning the teaching again in this manner should be understood. 'Subhaparamam' means having the liberation of the beautiful (subha-vimokkha) as its end, its peak, its completion. 'Idhapaññassa' means one whose wisdom is only in this world, whose wisdom does not transcend this world; it means one who possesses mundane wisdom. 'Uttari-vimuttiṃ appaṭivijjhato' means for one who does not penetrate the supramundane Dhamma. For one who can penetrate it, his loving-kindness indeed has Arahantship as its culmination. This same method applies to compassion and the others. Why did the Blessed One state that loving-kindness and the others have 'the beautiful' and so on as their culmination? Because of their being a strong dependence (upanissaya) for those respective states through similarity. For one who dwells in loving-kindness, beings are not repulsive. Because of his familiarity with the non-repulsive, when he directs his mind toward pure colors such as the blue kasiṇa, his mind enters into it easily and without difficulty. Thus, loving-kindness is a strong dependence for the liberation of the beautiful, but not beyond that. Therefore, it is called 'culminating in the beautiful' (subha-parama). For one who dwells in compassion, seeing the suffering of beings caused by physical factors such as the impact of heat, compassion arises, and thus the disadvantage (ādīnava) in form is already well-known.
209:
Because the disadvantage in form is already well-known, when such a person removes one of the kasiṇas like the earth kasiṇa and directs the meditative mind toward the concept of space, which is the escape from form, the mind enters into that concept of space through the power of absorption (appanā) without difficulty. Thus, compassion is a strong dependence for the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), but not beyond that (i.e., not for the sphere of infinite consciousness, etc.). Therefore, it is said to 'culminate in the sphere of infinite space.'

Furthermore, for one who dwells in appreciative joy (muditā), as he repeatedly contemplates with wisdom the consciousness of beings who are joyful due to various causes of joy, the arising of appreciative joy is possible, and thus he becomes familiar with grasping consciousness. Consequently, for that person dwelling in appreciative joy, when he transcends the sphere of infinite space attained in due order and directs the meditative mind toward the consciousness that has the sign of space as its object, the meditative mind enters into that consciousness through the power of absorption without difficulty. Thus, appreciative joy is a strong dependence for the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), but not beyond that. Therefore, it is said to 'culminate in the sphere of infinite consciousness.'

Furthermore, for one who dwells in the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā), because there is no such attention as 'May beings be happy,' or 'May they be liberated from suffering,' or 'May they not be parted from their attained prosperity,' there is a turning away from grasping ultimate realities (paramattha) such as happiness and suffering. Thus, a mind skilled in grasping what is not present in an ultimate sense (i.e., the concept of a being) arises. Consequently, for that person dwelling in the divine abiding of equanimity, whose mind is familiar with turning away from grasping ultimate realities and is skilled in perceiving what is not present in an ultimate sense, when he transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness attained in due order, and directs the mind toward the concept of non-existence (natthibhāva-paññatti)—the absence of the consciousness that was an ultimate reality—the mind enters into that concept of non-existence through the power of absorption without difficulty. Thus, the divine abiding of equanimity is a strong dependence for the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), but not beyond that. Therefore, it is said to 'culminate in the sphere of nothingness.' At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks attained Arahantship.

## 5. Saṅgārava Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'pageva' means 'at the very first.' 'Kāmarāga-pariyuṭṭhitena' means one who is possessed by sensual lust. 'Kāmarāga-paretena' means one who is overcome by sensual lust. 'Nissaraṇaṃ' means the escape from sensual lust is threefold: escape by suppression (vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa), escape by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-nissaraṇa), [and so on].
210:
Samuccheda-nissaraṇa means escape by absolute eradication. Among those three, the first jhāna based on the object of foulness (asubha) is called vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa (escape by suppression). Insight (vipassanā) is called tadaṅga-nissaraṇa (escape by substitution of opposites). The Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) is called samuccheda-nissaraṇa (escape by absolute eradication). The meaning is that one does not know the escape from sensual lust (kāmarāga) which is of these three kinds. In the passage beginning with 'attatthampi', one's own benefit to be attained, known as the fruition of Arahantship, is called attattha (one's own welfare). The benefit to be attained by the donors who provide the requisites is called parattha (the welfare of others). Both of these together are called ubhayattha (the welfare of both). In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

This which follows is a distinction. In the passages beginning with 'the escape from ill-will (byāpāda)', there are only two kinds of escape: vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa and samuccheda-nissaraṇa. Between these two, first, the first jhāna of loving-kindness (mettā) for ill-will is called vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa, and the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) is called samuccheda-nissaraṇa. For sloth and torpor (thina-middha), the perception of light (āloka-saññā) is vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa, and the Path of Arahantship is samuccheda-nissaraṇa. For restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), any kind of calm (samatha) is vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa. Specifically here, for restlessness (uddhacca), the Path of Arahantship is samuccheda-nissaraṇa, and for remorse (kukkucca), the Path of Non-returning is samuccheda-nissaraṇa. For doubt (vicikicchā), the defining of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna) is vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa, and the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga, the first path) is samuccheda-nissaraṇa.

In this sutta, the Blessed One taught similes such as, 'Brahmin, just as a water bowl mixed with lac,' and so on. In those similes, 'udapatto' refers to a bowl filled with water. 'Saṃsaṭṭho' means mixed by way of causing a change in color. 'Pakkuthito' means boiling over. 'Usmudakajāto' means water that is steaming. 'Sevālapaṇakapariyonaddho' means overspread and entwined by moss such as sesame-seed-like plants or by water-weeds having the color of a green frog's back. 'Vāterito' means stirred or shaken by the wind. 'Āvilo' means turbid or not clear. 'Luḷito' means unsettled or not having the sediment subsided. 'Kalalībhūto' means becoming like mud. 'Andhakāre nikkhitto' means placed in a lightless place such as the interior of a granary. In this sutta, the Blessed One delivered the teaching by way of the three planes of existence and concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. The Brahmin Saṅgārava, however, established himself in the refuges.

## 6. Abhayasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'aññāṇāya adassanāya' means for the purpose of ignorance and for the purpose of non-seeing. 'Taggha bhagavā nīvaraṇā' means 'Certainly, O Blessed One, they are hindrances (nīvaraṇa)'.
211:
'Kāya-kilamatha' means physical fatigue (physical distress). 'Citta-kilamatha' means mental fatigue (mental distress). In the phrase 'that physical and mental distress has also subsided for me'—it is said that when the Teacher entered and sat in a place with a cool and suitable climate, his physical distress subsided, and following that physical subsidence, his mental distress also subsided. Alternatively, it should be understood that both of these subsided for him by means of the Path itself.

## 7. Ānāpānavagga
## 1. Aṭṭhikamahapphalasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta and others, 'aṭṭhika-saññā' (perception of a skeleton) is the perception that arises in a monk who meditates on 'skeleton, skeleton'. For one who develops this perception, as long as the sign (nimitta) does not arise, the outer skin and inner skin still appear. But when the sign arises, the outer and inner skins no longer appear; only the pure skeleton, white like the color of a conch shell, appears. This is like the novice who looked at King Dhammika Tissa riding on the back of an elephant, or like the Elder Tissa, a resident of Cetiya Mountain, who looked at a woman laughing on the road. These stories are detailed in the Visuddhimagga. 'Sati vā upādisese' means if there is a remainder of clinging (upādāna-sesa) left.

## 2-10. Puḷavakasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
239-247. 'Puḷavaka-saññā' (perception of a worm-infested corpse) is the perception that arises in a monk who meditates on 'a mass of worms, a mass of worms'. The same method applies to the perception of a discolored corpse (vinīlaka-saññā) and others. The analytical discussion here, along with the method of development, is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Loving-kindness (mettā) and the others should be understood by way of the threefold and fourfold systems of jhāna. Equanimity (upekkhā), however, is to be understood only by way of the fourth jhāna.

## 8. Nirodhavagga
## 1-10. Asubhasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
248-257. 'Asubha-saññā' (perception of foulness) is the perception of the first jhāna based on the object of foulness. 'Maraṇa-saññā' (perception of death) is the perception that arises in one who constantly reflects, 'I must certainly die; my life is bound to death'...
212:
...the perception that arises in the monk. 'Āhāre paṭikūla-saññā' (perception of repulsiveness in food) is the perception that sees the swallowed nutriment, such as boiled rice and cakes, as disgusting and loathsome. 'Sabba-loke anabhirati-saññā' (perception of non-delight in the whole world) is the perception that arises in a monk who produces non-delight in the entire world. 'Pahāna-saññā' (perception of abandoning) and 'virāga-saññā' (perception of dispassion)—these two occur in the preliminary stage of the Path. 'Nirodha-saññā' (perception of cessation) is a mixture of mundane and supramundane. Thus, these twenty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), beginning with the perception of a skeleton, are explained. Among those twenty meditation subjects, absorption (appanā) occurs in nine, and eleven have access concentration (upacāra-jhāna). The remaining analytical discussions in this regard have already appeared in the Visuddhimagga. The Gangā-peyyāla and others should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Magga Saṃyutta.

## The Commentary on the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta is finished.
213:
## 3. Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta
## 1. Ambapālivagga
## 1. Commentary on the Ambapālisutta
In the first sutta of the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta, the phrase "Ambapālivane" means in the mango grove planted by the courtesan named Ambapālī, who lived by her beauty. That mango grove had formerly been her garden. Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One and being inspired with faith, she had a monastery built in that mango grove and offered it to the Tathāgata. It is with reference to that Ambapālī monastery that this word "Ambapāli" was spoken.

The word "Ekāyanvāyaṃ" should be resolved as "Ekāyano ayaṃ". Among those words, "Ekāyano" means a single path (magga). Regarding the names of a path:
"Magga, pantha, patha, pajja, añjasa, vaṭuma, āyana,
nāvā, uttarasetu, kulla, bhisi, saṅkama"—thus there are many names.

In this sutta, that path is spoken of by the name "āyana". Therefore, in this passage, "Monks, this path is a one-way path," it should be understood to mean, "Monks, this path is a single path; it is not a forked path." For what reason is it called "magga"? It is called magga because it is the means of going to Nibbāna, and because it is to be sought (magganiya) by those who desire Nibbāna.

"Sattānaṃ visuddhiyā" means for the sake of the exceptional purification of beings whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust (rāga) and by upakkilesas such as covetousness (abhijjhā) and unrighteous greed (visamalobha). "Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya" means for the overcoming and abandoning of sorrow and lamentation. "Dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya" means for the disappearance and cessation of these two: physical pain (dukkha) and mental distress (domanassa).

In the passage "Ñāyassa adhigamāya", the Noble Eightfold Path is called "ñāya"; it means for the attainment and reaching of that path. This is because the mundane (lokiya) satipaṭṭhāna path, when developed in the preliminary stage, leads to the attainment of the supramundane (lokuttara) path. Therefore, it is said, "Ñāyassa adhigamāya". "Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya" means for the realization, for the personal witnessing, of the Deathless Nibbāna, which receives its name because it is free from the bond of craving (taṇhā-vāna). When this path is developed, it gradually achieves the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, "Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya".
214:
In this way, the Blessed One spoke the praise of the one-way path with seven phrases. Why did he speak thus? It was for the purpose of generating zeal in the monks. Indeed, upon hearing the words of praise, those monks will think: "This path removes these four afflictions: sorrow, which is the burning of the heart; lamentation, which is verbal wailing; pain, which is physical unpleasantness; and distress, which is mental unpleasantness. It brings these three special benefits: purification (visuddhi), the way (ñāya) which leads to Nibbāna, and Nibbāna itself, which is free from the bond of craving." Thus, with a mind full of effort, they will think that this teaching should be learned, studied, and remembered, and this path should be developed. Just as a blanket merchant praises the qualities of blankets and so on, the Buddha spoke of the qualities to generate zeal in those monks.

"Yadidaṃ" is a particle; its meaning is "which is this". "Cattāro" is a numerical delimitation. By that word, he shows the boundary of the satipaṭṭhānas as "not less than four, and not more than four". In the word "Satipaṭṭhāna", there are three kinds of satipaṭṭhāna. The object of mindfulness is called satipaṭṭhāna; the Teacher's state of being free from attraction and aversion towards disciples who practice in three ways is also called satipaṭṭhāna; and mindfulness itself is also called satipaṭṭhāna.

In such passages as: "Monks, I will teach the origin and the disappearance of the four satipaṭṭhānas; listen to that. And what, monks, is the origin of the body? From the origin of nutriment comes the origin of the body," the object of mindfulness is called satipaṭṭhāna. Likewise, in such passages as: "The body is the establishment (upaṭṭhāna), not mindfulness; mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness." The meaning of that word satipaṭṭhāna is: it stands (patiṭṭhāti) in this object, therefore it is "paṭṭhāna". What stands? Mindfulness stands. The object where mindfulness stands is satipaṭṭhāna. Alternatively, "paṭṭhāna" means a principal station. Just like an elephant station or a horse station, the principal station of mindfulness is satipaṭṭhāna.

In the passage: "There are three satipaṭṭhānas which the Noble One frequents, frequenting which the Teacher is worthy to instruct the group of disciples," the Teacher's state of being free from attraction and aversion towards disciples who practice in three ways is called satipaṭṭhāna. The meaning of that passage is: it is "paṭṭhāna" because it is to be set up; it means because it is to be exerted. By what is it set up? It is set up by mindfulness. The station set up by mindfulness is satipaṭṭhāna.

However, in such passages as: "The four satipaṭṭhānas, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment," mindfulness itself is called satipaṭṭhāna. The meaning of that word satipaṭṭhāna is: it is "paṭṭhāna" because it stands; it means it is "upaṭṭhāna" because it occurs by plunging into and leaping forward.
215: Mindfulness itself is the foundation; therefore, it is called Satipaṭṭhāna. Alternatively, it is mindfulness in the sense of remembering, and foundation in the sense of establishing; thus, because it is both mindfulness and foundation, it is called Satipaṭṭhāna. This is the meaning intended here. If that is so, why is the plural form 'Satipaṭṭhānā' used? It is because of the plurality of mindfulnesses. Indeed, mindfulnesses are many due to the diversity of objects. However, why is 'Maggo' (the path) used in the singular form? It is because it is one in the sense of seeking. For these four mindfulnesses become one in the sense of seeking Nibbāna. Indeed, it was said: 'In what sense is the path called Magga? It is called Magga in the sense of seeking Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna.' These four also, in the subsequent stage, while accomplishing their task regarding the objects such as the body, go to Nibbāna; and from the beginning, they are sought by those who desire Nibbāna. Therefore, these four are called the one path (Maggo). In this way, the teaching is consistent with the sequence of words. 'Which four?' is a question asked with the desire to explain. 'Kāye' means in the material body. 'Kāyānupassī' means one who is in the habit of contemplating the body, or one who is contemplating the body. This bhikkhu contemplates this body as impermanent through the power of the seven types of contemplation, such as the contemplation of impermanence; he does not contemplate it as permanent. He contemplates it as suffering, not as happiness. He contemplates it as non-self, not as self. He becomes disenchanted, not delighted. He becomes dispassionate, not passionate. He causes cessation, not origination. He relinquishes, not grasps. It should be understood that as he contemplates that body as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence. As he contemplates it as suffering, he abandons the perception of happiness. As he contemplates it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self. As he becomes disenchanted, he abandons delight. As he becomes dispassionate, he abandons lust. As he causes cessation, he abandons origination. As he relinquishes, he abandons grasping. 'Viharati' means he dwells in the postures. 'Ātāpī' means 'ardent' because it burns up the defilements in the three realms of existence; this is a name for energy (viriya). Because he possesses that ardency (effort), he is called 'ātāpī'. 'Sampajāno' means endowed with the wisdom known as clear comprehension. 'Satimā' means endowed with the mindfulness that grasps the body. This is because this bhikkhu, having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates it with wisdom. Indeed, for one devoid of mindfulness, there is no such thing as contemplation. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, I say that mindfulness is useful in all things.' Thus, in this context, by the mere words 'kāye kāyānupassī viharati', the Satipaṭṭhāna of the contemplation of the body is taught. Alternatively, because...
216: For one who is lazy and lacks effort, internal indolence becomes an obstacle to the meditation subject. A person devoid of clear comprehension becomes confused in grasping the right means and in avoiding the wrong means. A bhikkhu who is forgetful is unable to relinquish what is not a means and to grasp what is a means. Because of this, that meditation subject of that yogi bhikkhu cannot be perfected. Therefore, it should be understood that these three terms, 'ātāpī sampajāno satimā', are spoken to show those qualities—ardor, wisdom, and right mindfulness—by whose power that meditation subject is perfected. Having thus shown the contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness and its associated factors, the Blessed One now said 'vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ' (having removed covetousness and grief in the world) to show the factors to be abandoned. In that phrase, 'vineyya' means having removed by way of removal by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vinaya) or removal by suppression (vikkhambhana-vinaya). 'Loke' (in the world) means in that very material body. Indeed, here the material body is intended as the 'world' in the sense of breaking up and dissolving. However, the covetousness and grief of that yogi are not abandoned only in the material body; they are also abandoned in feelings and so forth. Therefore, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'The five aggregates of clinging are the world.' Alternatively, this is stated because those states such as feelings are called the world, or by the method of extracting the meaning. As for what was said, 'Therein, what is the world? That very body is the world,' this is the meaning intended here. It should be understood as connected thus: 'having removed covetousness and grief in that world which is the material body.' In the word 'vedanāsu', the three feelings—pleasant, painful, and neutral—are intended. Those three feelings are only mundane feelings. The mind is also only the mundane mind. Likewise, the mental objects (dhammā) are only mundane mental objects. One should be known as a contemplator of feelings (vedanānupassī) who contemplates feelings with insight-knowledge in such a manner as they should be contemplated. This same method applies to the mind and mental objects. And how should feelings be contemplated? First, pleasant feelings should be contemplated as suffering because they are subject to change. Painful feelings should be contemplated as a dart. Neutral feelings should be contemplated as impermanent. Therefore, the Buddha taught thus: 'The bhikkhu who has seen pleasure as pain, has seen pain as a dart, and has seen the peaceful neutral feeling as impermanent; such a bhikkhu, seeing rightly, will wander about fully at peace.' Furthermore, all those feelings should also be contemplated as suffering because they are the suffering of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha). Indeed, it has been taught: 'Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering, I say.' They should also be contemplated as pleasure and pain...
217:
As the Blessed One said: "Friend Visākha, a pleasant feeling is pleasant when it persists and painful when it changes" (M. i. 465). This should be understood in detail. Furthermore, it should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence (anicca), and so forth.

Among mental phenomena (citta-dhamma), first, the mind (citta) should be contemplated by way of its diversity such as object (ārammaṇa), predominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), plane (bhūmi), kamma, result (vipāka), and functional (kiriya); by way of the contemplations of impermanence, etc.; and by way of distinctions such as with lust (sarāga) and without lust (virāga). Mental objects (dhamma) should also be contemplated by way of their individual characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa); by way of the nature of emptiness (suññata) called non-self (anatta); by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence, etc.; and by way of distinctions such as knowing "when there is sensual desire within oneself, one knows there is sensual desire," and so forth. The rest is as previously explained. This is the summary here; the details should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāya commentaries.

## 2. Commentary on the Sati Sutta

In the second sutta, "mindful" (sato) means being endowed with the mindfulness that contemplates the body, etc. "Clearly comprehending" (sampajāno) means being endowed with the wisdom of the fourfold clear comprehension. In the phrase "in going forward and returning" (abhikkante paṭikkante), "going forward" means moving ahead, and "returning" means turning back. Both of these are found in the four postures. In walking, one who moves the body forward is said to "go forward" (abhikkamati); one who turns back from there is said to "return" (paṭikkamati). In standing, one who leans the body forward while standing is said to "go forward"; one who leans back is said to "return". In sitting, one who moves toward the front of the seat while sitting is said to "go forward"; one who moves back toward the rear of the seat is said to "return". The same method applies to lying down.

"He acts with clear comprehension" (sampajānākārī hoti) means he habitually performs all his duties with clear comprehension, or he habitually practices clear comprehension itself. For he indeed practices clear comprehension in going forward and so on; he is never devoid of clear comprehension in any posture.

In that context of acting with clear comprehension, there are four kinds of clear comprehension: clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of resort (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). Among these, when the thought of going forward arises, instead of going according to the mind's whim, one considers the benefit or lack thereof, asking: "Is there a purpose for me in going here or not?" Grasping what is purposeful is clear comprehension of purpose. In this context, "purpose" (attha) refers to growth in accordance with the Dhamma by way of seeing a shrine (cetiya), seeing the Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing an elder (thera), or contemplating foulness (asubha)...
218:
...growth. For having seen a shrine and aroused joy (pīti) with the Buddha as the object, or having seen the Saṅgha and aroused joy with the Saṅgha as the object, one who contemplates that very joy by way of its destruction (khaya) reaches Arahantship. Indeed, while standing at the south gate of the Mahāvihāra and looking at the Great Shrine (Mahācetiya), thirty thousand monks reached Arahantship. Likewise at the west gate, the north gate, and the east gate; likewise at the Pañhamaṇḍapa area, the Abhaya tank embankment, the gate of the Thūpārāma shrine, the south gate of the city, and the Anurādha tank embankment (they reached Arahantship).

The Elder Mahā-ariyavaṃsabhāṇaka, however, said: "What do you say? From the lower part of the circumferential railing (kucchi-vedikā) around the Great Shrine, in every place visible to the eye where two feet can be placed evenly, it can be said that thirty thousand monks reached Arahantship at every step (where the sole of the foot was placed)." Another Great Elder said: "More monks than the grains of sand spread on the courtyard of the Great Shrine have reached Arahantship." Having seen the elders and established oneself in their advice, or having seen a foul object (asubha) and produced the first absorption (jhāna) in that object, one who contemplates that very absorption by way of its destruction reaches Arahantship. Therefore, seeing these shrines, elders, and so forth is purposeful.

Some teachers, however, say: "Growth by way of material requisites (āmisa) is also a purpose, because one practices for the support of the holy life (brahmacariya) depending on those requisites."

In such going, considering what is suitable and unsuitable and choosing what is suitable is clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña). How? First, seeing a shrine is purposeful. However, if a great festival is held at the shrine and people from within ten or twelve leagues gather, women and men, decorated according to their wealth, wander about like painted figures. In the midst of such a crowd, greed for a pleasant object, aversion for an unpleasant object, and delusion in improper looking may arise for that monk. Due to physical contact, he may fall into an offense of physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggāpatti), or there may be danger to his life and holy life. In such a case, that place is unsuitable. If the aforementioned dangers are absent, it is suitable. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. However, if people build a great pavilion in the village and hold an all-night Dhamma talk, and a crowd and danger arise in the same manner as mentioned, then that place is unsuitable. If there is no danger, it is suitable. The same method applies to seeing elders who have large followings.
219:
Viewing a corpse (asubha) is also beneficial. To illustrate this benefit, there is this story: Once, a young monk took a novice (sāmaṇera) and went to find tooth-sticks. While the novice stepped off the path and went ahead, he saw a corpse and attained the first jhāna. Using that very jhāna as a basis, he contemplated conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), realized the three fruits (phala), and stood there developing his meditation for the sake of the higher path. The young monk, not seeing the novice, called out, 'Novice!' The novice thought, 'Since the day of my ordination, I have not spoken even two words with a monk; on another day, I will strive to attain the higher distinction,' and replied, 'What is it, Bhante?' When told, 'Come here,' he came with just that one word and said, 'Bhante, please go along this path and look toward the east for a moment at the place where I stood.' The young monk did as told and attained the same distinction as the novice. Thus, one corpse became beneficial for two people. However, although it is beneficial, a female corpse is unsuitable for a man, and a male corpse is unsuitable for a woman. Only a corpse of the same sex is suitable. Discerning what is suitable in this way is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña).

A monk who has thus discerned what is beneficial and suitable, having grasped an object known as his preferred meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, and going to the alms-resort without letting go of that meditation subject, is said to have clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña).

To clarify this clear comprehension of the domain, this fourfold group should be understood: In this Dispensation, a certain monk carries (the meditation subject) when going but not when returning. A certain one carries it when returning but not when going. A certain one carries it neither when going nor when returning. A certain one carries it both when going and when returning.

Among these four, a certain monk purifies his mind from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by walking and sitting during the day. Likewise, he purifies it during the first watch of the night, sleeps during the middle watch, and spends the last watch in sitting and walking. Early on, he performs duties at the stupa (cetiya) courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, waters the Bodhi tree, sets out drinking water and washing water, and undertakes the duties toward his teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya). Having performed his bodily ablutions, he enters his dwelling, sits cross-legged two or three times to generate bodily warmth, and applies himself to his meditation. When it is time for the alms-round, he rises, takes his bowl and robes while keeping the meditation subject foremost, and leaves the dwelling. While reflecting on the meditation subject, he goes to the stupa courtyard. If his meditation is the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), he enters the stupa courtyard without letting go of it. If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the stairs and, as if putting down an object held in his hand, he leaves that meditation subject there and ascends the stupa courtyard, taking the joy (pīti) that has the Buddha as its object. If it is a large stupa, he should circumambulate it three times to the right and pay homage at four places. If it is a small stupa, he should likewise circumambulate it three times and pay homage at eight places. Having paid homage to the stupa, [he goes] to the Bodhi tree courtyard...
220:
Taking the joy (pīti) that has the Buddha as its object, he ascends the stupa courtyard. If it is a large stupa, he should circumambulate it three times to the right and pay homage at four places. If it is a small stupa, he should likewise circumambulate it three times and pay homage at eight places. Having paid homage to the stupa, when he reaches the Bodhi tree courtyard, he should pay homage to the Bodhi tree, showing such reverence as if he were in the presence of the Blessed Buddha. Having thus paid homage to the stupa and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where he left [his meditation subject] and, as if taking up a stored item with his hand, he picks up the meditation subject he had set down. Keeping the meditation subject foremost, he dons his robes near the village and enters the village for alms.

Then, when people see him, they come out to meet him, saying, 'Our noble lord has arrived.' They take his bowl, seat him in a rest house or a house, and offer him gruel (yāgu). Until the meal is finished, they wash and massage his feet, sit before him, and ask questions or desire to hear the Dhamma. Even if they do not urge him to preach, the teachers of the Commentaries say that a Dhamma talk (dhamma-kathā) should indeed be given for the sake of favoring the people. Indeed, there is no Dhamma talk that is devoid of the meditation subject. Therefore, having preached the Dhamma with the meditation subject as the basis, and having consumed the food with the meditation subject as the basis, he gives the blessing (anumodanā). When returning, he is followed by the people; he leaves the village with them, sends them back, and then sets out on the path.

At that time, novices and young monks who have finished their meal outside the village come out first. Seeing the elder, they come to meet him and take his bowl and robes. It is said that monks of old did not perform duties by looking at the face, thinking, 'This is our preceptor (upajjhāya), this is our teacher (ācariya),' but performed them simply according to the occasion. They ask him, 'Bhante, how are these people related to you? Are they relatives from the mother's side or the father's side?' When asked, 'What did you see that makes you ask?' they reply, 'We ask because we see their love and great respect for you.' He goes along speaking of their virtues, saying, 'Friends, these people do for us what is difficult even for parents to do. Our bowl and robes belong to them. Because of their power, even when there is danger, we know no danger; even when there is famine, we know no hunger. There are no such benefactors to us as these.' This monk is called one who carries (the meditation subject) when going but not when returning.

However, for a certain monk, while he is performing the aforementioned duties, the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo) blazes up. It lets go of the unclung-to (anupādinnaka) and takes hold of the clung-to (upādinnaka). Sweat pours from his body. He is unable to enter the path of meditation. That monk takes his bowl and robes early and quickly pays homage to the stupa. Even at the time when bats are coming out, he goes to the village and enters for alms. When he drinks the gruel, his internal fire (vamma-mī-tejo) lets go of the clung-to stomach and takes hold of the unclung-to objects such as the rice. Like being doused with a hundred pots of water, he reaches a state where the distress caused by the fire element is calmed...
221:
Having paid homage to the Cetiya, at the very time when the cattle go out [from their pens], he enters the village for congee alms. Having obtained the congee, he goes to the alms-hall and drinks it. At that time, for that monk, with just two or three swallows, the digestive fire born of kamma (kammaja-tejo) releases the clung-to matter (upādiṇṇaka-rūpa, the stomach) and takes hold of the non-clung-to matter (anupādiṇṇaka-rūpa, the congee, etc.). Just as if he had bathed with a hundred jars of water, he reaches the cooling of the feverish heat of the fire element. Taking meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) as his primary focus, he partakes of the congee, washes his bowl and mouth, and in the interval before the main meal, he applies his mind to meditation. He then wanders for alms in the remaining places, partakes of the food with meditation as his primary focus, and from then on, he returns while maintaining the meditation that has appeared in succession. This monk is called 'one who brings back [the meditation], but does not carry it [out].' Monks such as these, who drank congee, initiated insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship in the Buddha’s Dispensation, are so numerous they are beyond counting. In the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka) alone, there is almost no place in the alms-halls of various villages where monks have not attained Arahantship after drinking congee.

However, a monk who lives negligently, who has laid down the burden of exertion, who has broken all duties, and who lives with a mind bound by the five mental shackles (cetovinibandha), enters the village for alms without even the perception that 'there is such a thing as meditation.' He wanders and eats while associating with laypeople in an unsuitable manner, and returns empty, devoid of meditation. This monk is called 'one who neither carries [out] nor brings back [the meditation].'

Who is the one called 'he who both carries [out] and brings back'? That monk should be understood by way of the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatikavatta). Sons of good family, desiring their own benefit, having gone forth in the Dispensation and living together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred, live having made a pact: 'Friends, you did not go forth because you were oppressed by debt, or by fear, or because you lacked a livelihood. You went forth here only because you desired to be liberated from suffering. Therefore, suppress the defilements that arise while walking, even while walking; suppress the defilements that arise while standing, sitting, or lying down, in those very postures.' Having made such a pact, when they go for alms, there are stones at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, and one gāvuta; they go while applying their minds to meditation, using those stones as landmarks. If defilement arises in any monk while walking, he suppresses it right there. If he is unable to suppress it, he stands still. Then, the monk coming behind him also stands still. At that, the monk with the defilement admonishes himself, 'This monk knows the thought that has arisen in you; this is not suitable for you.' He then develops insight and enters the Noble plane (the Path and Fruit) right there.
222:
If he is unable [to suppress it while standing], he sits down; this method is the same as that described for standing. Even if he cannot yet enter the Noble plane, he goes on only after removing that defilement and applying his mind to meditation; he does not lift his foot with a mind devoid of meditation. If he does lift it [without mindfulness], he turns back and returns to the previous spot where he was not devoid of meditation, like Elder Mahāphussadeva who resided in Ālindaka.

That Elder, it is said, lived for nineteen years fulfilling the duty of going and returning. Even people who were plowing, sowing, threshing, and doing other works along the way, seeing the Elder going in that manner, would say to one another, 'This Elder is turning back and going again and again; is he perhaps confused about the way, or has he forgotten something?' The Elder, not paying attention to their words, practiced the recluse's Dhamma with a mind joined with meditation and attained Arahantship within twenty years. On the day he attained Arahantship, a deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood lighting a lamp with her fingers. The Four Great Kings, Sakka the king of gods, and Brahmā Sahampati also came to attend on him. Seeing that radiance, Elder Vanavāsī Mahātissa asked him the next day, 'Venerable sir, there was a radiance in your presence during the night; what was that radiance?' The Elder, wishing to divert the conversation [to hide his attainment], said things like, 'Radiance can be the light of a lamp, or the light of a gem.' Then, being repeatedly urged with the words, 'Venerable sir, do not hide it,' he acknowledged it and informed him [of the truth].

It is also like Elder Mahānāga who resided in Kāḷavallimaṇ္ḍapa. That Elder also, fulfilling the duty of going and returning, first resolved on only standing and walking for seven years, thinking, 'I will honor the Great Effort (Mahāpadhāna) of the Blessed One.' Again, having fulfilled the duty of going and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahantship. That Elder lifted his foot only with a mind joined with meditation; if he lifted it with a mind devoid of meditation, he would return [to the original spot]. When he reached the vicinity of a village, he would stand at a place where there might be doubt as to whether it was 'a cow or a monk,' wrap his robe, wash his bowl with water from the pitcher carried in his armpit, and take a mouthful of water. For what reason? He thought, 'Let there not be a distraction of meditation even by the mere words "May you live long" to the people who come to offer me alms or to pay homage.' [He did this so that if asked] 'Venerable sir, what day of the month is today?' or about the number of monks, or a question...
223:
When asked, he swallows the water (in the Nissaya, it says 'spits it out') and speaks. If there is no one asking about the day and so forth, he spits out the water at the village gate when leaving and proceeds.

It is like the fifty monks who entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery. It is said that on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, they made a vow: "We will not speak to one another until we reach Arahantship." When entering the village for alms, they also held a mouthful of water. They acted according to the method already mentioned regarding asking about the day and so forth. At that time, people, seeing the water spat out at the village gate, knew: "Today one came, today two came."

Those people thought: "Do these monks not speak only with us, or also with each other? If they do not speak with each other, they must surely be in a state of dispute. Come, let us make them ask for forgiveness from each other." Saying this, they all went to the monastery, but among the fifty monks, they did not see even two together in one place. Then, a wise man among those people said: "Friends, the place of those who quarrel cannot be like this; the terrace of the shrine (cetiyangaṇa) and the terrace of the Bodhi tree (bodhiyaṅgaṇa) are well-swept and cleaned; the brooms are well-stored; the drinking water and used water are well-placed." Those people turned back from there. Those monks attained Arahantship within the three months of the rains and performed the Visuddhipavarāṇā on the day of Mahāpavarāṇā.

Thus, like the Elder Mahānāga who lived in Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, and like the monks who entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery, lifting the foot only with a mind joined with meditation, when reaching the vicinity of the village, holding a mouthful of water and observing the streets, he proceeds to a street where there are no drunkards and the like, no quarrellers, or wild elephants and horses. When wandering on that alms-route, he does not go very fast. There is no benefit to the dhutaṅga of alms-gathering by going fast. He goes steadily like a water-cart on uneven ground. When entering houses in order, he waits for a suitable time to know whether one wishes to give or not, receives the alms, and having come back to the village, outside the village, or to the monastery, sits in a comfortable and suitable place, reflecting on meditation, establishing the perception of repulsiveness in food, reflecting with the similes of oiling an axle, applying medicine to a wound, or eating the flesh of one's own son, he consumes food endowed with the eight factors: "not for play, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification..." and so forth. After eating, having performed the duties with water, he relieves the fatigue caused by the meal for a moment...
224:
As before the meal, so also after the meal, in the first watch and the last watch of the night, he reflects only on the meditation subject. This practice is called "carrying it [on the way out] and carrying it back."

A practitioner who fulfills this Gatapaccāgatikavatta (the duty of going and returning), if endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), reaches Arahantship in the first stage of life. If not in the first stage, then in the middle stage. If not in the middle stage, then in the last stage. If not in the last stage, then at the time of death. If not at the time of death, then after becoming a deva. If not after becoming a deva, he is born when no Buddha has appeared and realizes Paccekabodhi. If he does not realize Paccekabodhi, then in the presence of a Buddha, he becomes one of quick intuition (khippābhiññā) like the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya, or one of great wisdom like the Elder Sāriputta, or one of great psychic power like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, or a proponent of dhuta practices like the Elder Mahākassapa, or one with the divine eye like the Elder Anuruddha, or a bearer of the Vinaya like the Elder Upāli, or a Dhamma teacher like the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, or a forest dweller like the Elder Revata, or one of great learning like the Elder Ānanda, or one who desires training like the Buddha's son, the Elder Rāhula. Thus, for the monk who carries the meditation subject back and forth in this fourfold group, his clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña) reaches its peak.

Non-delusion in such acts as moving forward is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammohasampajañña). This clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood thus: In this Dispensation, when a monk moves forward or backward, he does not get deluded like blind worldlings who, in moving forward etc., are deluded thinking, "The self moves forward, the movement forward is produced by the self," or "I move forward, the movement forward is produced by me." Instead, when the thought "I will move forward" arises, the air element (vāyodhātu) born of mind arises together with that mind, producing bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). Thus, by the power of the diffusion of the air element produced by mental activity, this skeleton, which is conventionally called a body, moves forward.

In lifting each foot of that skeleton moving forward thus, the two elements of earth (pathavīdhātu) and water (āpodhātu) are weak; the other two elements [fire and air] are predominant and strong. So it is in carrying forward and moving across. In releasing the foot, the two elements of fire (tejodhātu) and air (vāyodhātu) are weak; the other two elements, earth and water, are strong. So it is in placing the foot on the ground and establishing it.

In those six modes, the mental and material phenomena (nāmarūpa) that arise at the moment of lifting the foot do not reach the moment of carrying the foot forward. The mental and material phenomena that arise at the moment of carrying the foot forward do not reach the moment of moving the foot across. The mental and material phenomena that arise at the moment of moving the foot across do not reach the moment of releasing the foot. The mental and material phenomena that arise at the moment of releasing the foot [do not reach] the moment of placing the foot on the ground...
225:
In this manner, when lifting each foot of that skeleton moving forward, the earth element and the water element are small in quantity and weak. The remaining two, the fire element and the wind element, are excessive in quantity and strong. It is the same in carrying the foot forward and moving it across to the left or right. When releasing the foot, the fire element and the wind element are small in quantity and weak. The remaining two, the earth element and the water element, are excessive in quantity and strong. It is the same in placing the foot on the ground and keeping it steady.

Among those (six modes), the mental and physical phenomena (rūpa-nāma-dhamma) occurring at the moment of lifting the foot do not reach the moment of carrying the foot forward. The mental and physical phenomena occurring at the moment of carrying the foot forward do not reach the moment of moving it across to the left or right. The mental and physical phenomena occurring at the moment of moving it across do not reach the moment of releasing the foot. The mental and physical phenomena occurring at the moment of releasing the foot do not reach the moment of placing the foot on the ground. The mental and physical phenomena occurring at the moment of placing or steadying the foot on the ground do not reach the moment of the cessation of action through treading after steadying the foot. In each of those moments of placing the foot, etc., they break up part by part, joint by joint, and limit by limit, like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan making a 'tata-tata' crackling sound. In such moving forward, if it is asked, 'Who is it that moves forward?' or 'Whose moving forward is it?', in the ultimate sense, it is only the movement of elements, the standing of elements, the sitting of elements, and the lying down of elements. Indeed, in each part, along with the form, one consciousness arises and another consciousness ceases. The continuity of consciousness or the continuity of form, connected without interval, proceeds like the flow of a river. Thus, non-delusion in such matters as moving forward is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña).

The explanation of the sentence "He acts with clear comprehension in going forward and returning" (abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānākārī hoti) is finished.

In the phrase "in looking ahead and looking aside" (ālokite vilokite), looking straight ahead is called ālokita, and looking towards the intermediate directions (sideways) is called vilokita. There are also looking down (olokita), looking up (ullokita), and looking back (apalokita) by way of looking below, above, and behind. These, such as olokita, are not taken here as they are unsuitable for monks. Only these two, ālokita and vilokita, are taken by way of suitability for monks. Or, it should be understood that all of them are included by this brief mention.

In this matter of ālokita and vilokita, the decision should be known. When the thought "I will look ahead" arises, the wisdom that reflects on whether it is beneficial or not, without following the whim of the mind, is called clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). This clear comprehension of purpose should be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda as a witness. For the Blessed One said: "Monks, if Nanda has to look towards the eastern direction, Nanda looks towards the eastern direction after having thoroughly reflected with his mind: 'As I look towards the eastern direction in this way, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief will not flow into me.' Thus, by looking with such investigation, Nanda is one endowed with clear comprehension of purpose. Monks, if Nanda has to look towards the western, northern, southern, upper, lower, or intermediate directions, he looks towards those directions after having thoroughly reflected with his mind: 'As I look towards such and such a direction in this way, evil unwholesome states will not flow into me.' Thus, he is one who has clear comprehension." In this matter of ālokita and vilokita, the state of being beneficial and the state of being suitable should be understood only by way of seeing a shrine (cetiya), etc., as mentioned before.
226:
"As I look towards the eastern direction in this way, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and grief (domanassa) will not flow into (arise in) me." Having thoroughly reflected with his mind, he is one who has clear comprehension in that matter. "Monks, if Nanda has to look towards the western, northern, southern, upper, lower, or intermediate directions, Nanda looks towards those directions after having thoroughly reflected with his mind: 'As I look towards such and such a direction in this way, evil unwholesome states of bad passion and corrupted grief will not flow into me.' ... He is one who has clear comprehension."

Furthermore, in this matter of ālokita and vilokita (looking ahead and looking aside), the state of clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) and the state of clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood only by way of seeing a shrine, etc., as mentioned before. Not abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is indeed clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña). Therefore, monks who take the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) as their meditation subject should look ahead or look aside only by way of their own meditation subject; or those who take meditation subjects such as kasiṇa should do so by making the meditation subject the primary focus.

"Inside the body, there is no such person called a 'self' (atta) that looks ahead or looks aside. When the thought 'I will look ahead' arises, the wind element (vāyo-dhātu) born of that mind arises, producing bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti). Thus, by the power of the diffusion of the wind element caused by the mental action, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper eyelid rises up. There is no one who is opening them with a machine. Furthermore, eye-consciousness arises, performing the function of seeing." Knowing in this way is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña).

Furthermore, in this ālokita and vilokita, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of the full understanding of the root (mūla-pariññā), the state of being a guest (āgantuka), and the state of being temporary (tāvakālika). First, I shall speak by way of the full understanding of the root:

"There are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting (āvajjana), the seeing (eye-consciousness), the receiving (sampaṭicchana), the investigating (santīraṇa), the determining (voṭṭhabbana), and the seventh is the impulsion (javana)."

Among those states of consciousness, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) proceeds, performing the function of a factor of the rebirth-process. Having adverted that life-continuum, the functional mind-element (pañcadvārāvajjana) occurs, performing the function of adverting. Due to the cessation of that adverting, eye-consciousness occurs, performing the function of seeing. Due to the cessation of that eye-consciousness, the resultant mind-element occurs, performing the function of receiving. Due to the cessation of that receiving, the resultant mind-consciousness-element occurs, performing the function of investigating. Due to the cessation of that investigating, the functional mind-consciousness-element occurs, performing the function of determining. Due to the cessation of that determining, the impulsion (javana) runs for seven times. Among those seven impulsions, even in the first impulsion...
227:
Looking forward and looking aside with the power of lust, hatred, and delusion, thinking, "This is a woman, this is a man," does not occur in the first javana, nor does it occur from the second javana up to the seventh. However, just as warriors on a battlefield fall and perish in order from bottom to top, when the five-door javanas have ceased, looking forward and looking aside with lust and so on, thinking, "This is a woman, this is a man," occurs in the mind-door. In this way, first, the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood by way of defining the root in this looking forward and looking aside.

When a visible object comes into the range of the eye-door, after the vibration of the bhavanga, the adverting (āvajjana) and other consciousnesses arise and cease, each performing its own function; at the end, the javana arises. That javana is like a visiting man in the eye-door, which is the home of the previously arisen adverting and other consciousnesses. Just as it is not proper for a visiting man who has entered another's house to ask for something to give orders while the householders remain silent, so too, while the adverting and other consciousnesses in the eye-door (their home) are themselves without lust, hatred, or delusion, it is not proper for the javana (the guest) to have lust, hatred, or delusion. Thus, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of the guest-status.

Furthermore, those consciousnesses that arise in the eye-door ending with determining (vottthabbana) perish right there along with their associated states; they do not see one another and are of a temporary nature, perishing shortly after arising. In this regard, for example, if all the people in a house have died and the one remaining person is also of the nature to die at that very moment, it is not proper for him to delight in dancing, singing, and so on. Similarly, when the adverting and other consciousnesses, along with their associated states, have perished right there in the single door, it is not proper for the remaining javana, which is also of the nature to perish at that very moment, to delight through lust, hatred, or delusion. Thus, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of its temporary nature.

Moreover, this should also be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditions (paccaya). Herein, the eye and the visible object are the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha); the consciousness of seeing is the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha); the feeling associated with that seeing-consciousness is the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha); the perception is the perception aggregate (saññākkhandha); and the volitional formations such as contact are the formations aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha). Thus, when these five aggregates combine, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. In that manifestation, what single thing looks forward? What looks aside? Likewise, the eye is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana); the visible object is the visible-object-base (rūpāyatana); the consciousness of seeing is the mind-base (manāyatana); and the associated states such as feeling are the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana). Thus, when these four bases combine, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. In that, what single thing looks forward?
228:
What looks aside? Likewise, the eye is the eye-element (cakkhudhātu); the visible object is the visible-object-element (rūpadhātu); the seeing is the eye-consciousness-element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu); and the associated states such as feeling are the mental-object-element (dhammadhātu). Thus, when these four elements combine, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. In that, who looks forward? Who looks aside?

Likewise, the eye is the support condition (nissaya-paccaya); the visible object is the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya); the adverting is the proximity, contiguity, decisive support, absence, and disappearance conditions (anantara, samanantara, upanissaya, natthi, vigata-paccaya); light is the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya); and feeling and so on are the co-nascence conditions (sahajāta-paccaya). Thus, when these conditions combine, looking forward and looking aside are manifested. In that, who looks forward? Who looks aside? In this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) in this looking forward and looking aside should also be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.

'In bending and stretching' (samiñjite pasārite) refers to the bending and stretching of the joints. In that bending and stretching of the joints, not doing so merely according to the mind's desire, but discerning the benefit and non-benefit of bending and stretching the limbs and choosing the beneficial is called clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). In that regard, for one who remains with limbs bent or stretched for too long, painful feelings arise at every moment, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) falls away, and one does not achieve distinction. However, for one who bends at the proper time and stretches at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise, the mind is one-pointed, the meditation subject increases, and one achieves distinction. Thus, the discernment of benefit and non-benefit should be understood.

Even when there is a purpose, discerning what is suitable and unsuitable and choosing the suitable is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña). In this regard, this is the method: It is said that at the courtyard of the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya), young monks were reciting their studies. Behind those monks, young nuns were listening to the Dhamma. Among those young monks, one monk stretched out his hand, came into bodily contact [with a nun], and for that reason, he became a layman. Another monk stretched out his foot and happened to stretch it into a fire, burning his foot to the bone. Another stretched into an anthill and was bitten by a cobra. Another stretched into a robe-rack and was bitten by a green pit viper. Therefore, one should not stretch in such unsuitable places but only in suitable places. This is the clear comprehension of suitability in this bending and stretching.

Clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña) should be illustrated by the story of the Great Elder. It is said that while a Great Elder was sitting in his daytime quarters talking with his disciples, he suddenly bent his arm. Then, he placed it back in its original position and bent it again slowly. When the disciples asked, "Venerable Sir, why did you bend your arm suddenly and then, after putting it back, bend it again slowly?" he replied, "Friends, since the time I began reflecting on the meditation on elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna), I have never bent my arm while letting go of the meditation subject."
229:
The Great Elder suddenly (unintentionally) bent his hand, then placed it back in its original position and bent it again slowly. His disciples asked, "Venerable sir, why did you suddenly bend your hand, then put it back and bend it again slowly?"

"Friends, from the time I began to apply my mind to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), I have never bent my hand while letting go of the meditation subject. But just now, while speaking with you, I bent it while letting go of the meditation subject. Therefore, I placed it back in its original position and bent it again (along with the meditation subject)," he replied. They said, "Venerable sir, it is excellent; a monk should indeed be like this." Thus, in this bending and stretching, not abandoning the meditation subject is to be understood as clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña).

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" (atta) that bends or stretches. In reality, due to the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind as previously described, bending and stretching occur like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden mechanical puppet by the pulling of strings. Discerning in this way is to be understood as clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammohasampajañña).

In the phrase "saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe," "bearing" (dhāraṇa) refers to the use of the double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) and the robes (cīvara) by way of wearing and dressing, and the use of the bowl (patta) by way of receiving alms-food, etc. In that bearing of robes, first, for a monk who wanders for alms after dressing and wearing the robes, the acquisition of material gifts (alms-food, etc.) and the benefit described by the Blessed One as "for the sake of warding off cold," etc., is called "purpose" (attha). By virtue of knowing that purpose, clear comprehension of purpose (sātthakasampajañña) is to be understood.

For one who is naturally hot-blooded or weak, a fine robe is suitable. For one who is sensitive to cold, a thick double-layered robe is suitable. A robe that is the opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is simply unsuitable. This is because it causes an impediment (palibodha) to that monk through patching, etc. Similarly, an attractive robe such as one made of silk or fine cloth is also unsuitable. Such a robe can cause danger to the religious life or even danger to the life of a monk living alone in the forest. Strictly speaking, a robe obtained through wrong livelihood (micchājīva) such as giving signs, or a robe that causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline for the monk using it, is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By virtue of knowing that suitable robe, clear comprehension of suitability (sappāyasampajañña) is to be understood here, and by virtue of not abandoning the meditation subject, clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña) is to be understood.

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" (atta) that wears the robe. In reality, the wearing of the robe occurs only by the power of the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind as previously described. In that wearing of the robe...
230:
The robe is insentient, and the body is also insentient. The robe does not know, "I am worn by the body." The body also does not know, "I am covered by the robe." Just as a wooden puppet is covered by a worn-out cloth, only elements cover a collection of elements. Therefore, one should not feel joy upon receiving a good robe, nor should one feel dejection upon receiving a poor robe. For instance, some people make offerings of flowers, scents, incense, and cloth to a termite mound where a nāga resides, a shrine, or a tree, while others show disrespect by smearing them with excrement, urine, or mud, or by striking them with sticks and weapons. Those termite mounds, shrines, and trees do not feel joy or dejection because of those people. In the same way, one should not feel joy upon receiving a good robe, nor should one feel dejection upon receiving a poor robe. Thus, by virtue of the reflection that proceeds in this manner, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammohasampajañña) is to be understood here.

In bearing the bowl as well, one should not grasp the bowl suddenly without reflection. By virtue of the benefit to be obtained through the cause of grasping the bowl, thinking, "By taking this and wandering for alms, I shall receive alms-food," clear comprehension of purpose (sātthakasampajañña) is to be understood. For one with a very thin and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. For any monk, a bowl that has four or five knots (repairs) and is difficult to clean is simply unsuitable. A bowl that is difficult to wash is not proper, as the very act of washing it becomes an impediment (palibodha) for that monk. A bowl with the color of a gem is attractive and is unsuitable in the same way as described for the robe. A bowl obtained by way of giving signs, etc., or a bowl that causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline for the monk using it, is absolutely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By virtue of that suitable bowl, clear comprehension of suitability (sappāyasampajañña) is to be understood here, and by virtue of not abandoning the meditation subject, clear comprehension of the resort (gocarasampajañña) is to be understood.

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" (atta) that grasps the bowl. Grasping the bowl occurs only by the power of the various movements (bodily intimation/kāyaviññatti) of the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the mind as previously described. In that grasping of the bowl, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are also insentient. The bowl does not know, "I am grasped by the hands." The hands also do not know, "The bowl is grasped by us." Just as a piece of glowing iron is grasped with tongs, only elements grasp a collection of elements. Thus, by virtue of the reflection that proceeds in this manner, clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammohasampajañña) is to be understood here.
