Furthermore, just as compassionate people, seeing destitute persons in a hospice whose hands and feet have been severed, with pus and blood oozing from their wounds, infested with maggots and surrounded by bluebottles, offer them rags for binding wounds and medicines in broken potsherds, etc. In that offering, some destitute persons receive fine rags, while others receive coarse ones. Among the broken potsherds for medicine, some receive well-shaped ones...
231:
Some beggars receive broken medicine pots of unsightly appearance. They are neither glad nor sad upon receiving them. This is because their purpose is fulfilled by a mere rag to cover a wound and a mere broken pot to receive medicine. In the same way, a monk reflects on the robe as a rag for covering a wound, the bowl as a broken pot for medicine, and the alms-food received in the bowl as medicine in a broken pot. This monk should be known as one who acts with supreme clear comprehension through the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) in carrying the outer robe, the bowl, and the robes.

Among the terms beginning with 'asita': 'asita' means eating alms-food; 'pīta' means drinking gruel and so forth; 'khāyita' means chewing hard food and so forth; 'sāyita' means tasting honey, molasses, and so forth. In these acts of eating and so forth, the eightfold benefit taught by the method beginning with 'not for fun' is called 'attha' (purpose). Through the power of that benefit, the clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.

Among coarse, fine, bitter, sweet, and other foods, whatever food causes discomfort to someone is unsuitable (asappāya) for that person. Whatever food is obtained through hinting (nimitta-kamma) and so forth, and whatever food, when consumed, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, that food is definitely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable (sappāya). Through the power of that suitability, the clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood here. Through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood.

Internally, there is no such thing as a 'self' (atta) who eats. Only through the diffusion of the mind-produced air element (cittakiriya-vāyodhātu) as described, do the receiving of the bowl, the lowering of the hand into the bowl, the making of the morsel, the lifting of the morsel, and the opening of the mouth occur. No one opens the jaws with a key or a machine. Only through the diffusion of the mind-produced air element do the placing of the morsel in the mouth, the grinding by the upper teeth acting like a pestle, the receiving by the lower teeth acting like a mortar, and the action of the tongue acting like a hand occur. Thus, thin saliva from the tip of the tongue and thick saliva from the root of the tongue coat the morsel. That food, turned by the tongue-hand in the lower-teeth-mortar, moistened by the saliva-water, and ground by the upper-teeth-pestle, is not pushed inside by anyone with a ladle or a spoon; it enters by the air element alone. No one spreads straw to support the food as it enters; it stays there by the power of the air element alone. No one makes a tripod, lights a fire, and cooks the food as it stays; it is digested by the fire element (tejodhātu) alone. No one pushes the digested food out with a stick or a staff; the air element alone brings it out. Thus, the air element carries forward, brings in, establishes, turns, grinds, dries, and brings out. The earth element (pathavīdhātu) establishes, turns, grinds, and dries. The water element (āpodhātu) provides cohesion and maintains moisture. The fire element digests the food that has entered. The space element (ākāsadhātu) is the path for the nutriment. The consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu) knows with effort in the seeking of that nutriment and so forth. Through the power of reflection occurring in this manner, [the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood] in this consumption of alms-food and so forth.
232:
(The air element) carries, brings in, establishes, turns, grinds, dries, and brings out. The earth element establishes, turns, grinds, and dries. The water element provides cohesion and maintains the state of moisture. The fire element digests the food that has entered within. The space element is the path of entry and exit (for the nutriment). The consciousness element knows with effort in the seeking of various nutriments and so forth. Through the power of reflection occurring in this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) should be understood in this (eating and so forth).

Furthermore, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood here by reflecting on the repulsiveness in ten ways: through going, seeking, consuming, the receptacle (āsaya), storage, the undigested, the digested, the fruit, the discharge, and the smearing. The detailed explanation of this should be taken from the 'Description of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Food' in the Visuddhimagga.

'Uccāra-passāva-kamma' means the act of defecating and urinating. In that regard, for one who does not defecate or urinate when the time comes, sweat is released from the whole body, the eyes roll, the mind is not concentrated, and other diseases arise. For one who does perform the act, all those troubles do not occur; this is the meaning here. Through the power of that benefit, the clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood. For one who defecates or urinates in an unsuitable place, there is an offense (āpatti), loss of reputation, and even danger to life. For one who does so in a suitable place, those dangers do not occur; this is what is called 'suitable' (sappāya) here. Through the power of that suitability, the clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña) should be understood, and through the power of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood.

Internally, there is no such thing as a 'self' (atta) who performs the act of defecating and urinating. In reality, the act of defecating and urinating occurs only through the movement and diffusion of the mind-produced air element (kāyaviññatti). Just as when a ripe abscess bursts, the pus and blood come out involuntarily, and just as water comes out involuntarily from an overfilled water pot, so too, the feces and urine accumulated in the rectum and bladder, being pressed by the force of the wind (air element), come out even involuntarily. These feces and urine thus exiting belong neither to that monk himself nor to others; they are merely bodily discharges. How? Just as for someone pouring out old water from a water-gourd, that water belongs neither to himself nor to others, but is merely an act of cleaning. Through the power of reflection occurring in this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood in this act of defecating and urinating.
233:
In "going" (*gate*) and so forth: "going" means in the act of walking; "standing" (*ṭhite*) means in the act of standing; "sitting" (*nisinne*) means in the act of sitting; "sleeping" (*sutte*) means in the act of lying down; "waking" (*jāgarite*) means in the act of being awake; "speaking" (*bhāsite*) means in the act of talking; "silence" (*tuṇhībhāve*) means in the act of not talking.

In this context, a monk who, after walking for a long time or practicing walking meditation, stands at the end and reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of walking meditation have ceased right here"—this monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension in going."

A monk who, while reciting, answering questions, or attending to a meditation subject, stands for a long time and then sits down and reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of standing have ceased right here"—this monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension in standing."

A monk who, by virtue of reciting and so forth, sits for a long time and then lies down and reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of sitting have ceased right here"—this monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension in sitting."

A monk who, while lying down, falls asleep while reciting or attending to a meditation subject, and upon waking up later reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of lying down have ceased right here"—this monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension in both sleeping and waking." Indeed, the non-occurrence of functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*) is called "sleeping," and its occurrence is called "waking."

A monk who, while speaking, speaks with mindfulness and clear comprehension, thinking: "This thing called 'sound' arises depending on the lips, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate, and depending on the corresponding effort (*payoga*) of the mind." Or, after reciting, preaching the Dhamma, reviewing a meditation subject, or answering questions for a long time, he remains silent and reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of speaking have ceased right here"—this monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking."

A monk who, while remaining silent, attends to the Dhamma or a meditation subject for a long time and later reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of silence have ceased right here." When there is the occurrence of derived matter (*upādārūpa*) (sound), it is called "speaking"; when it is absent, it is called "remaining silent." This monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension in silence."

Thus, herein, clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*) and the state of acting with clear comprehension by its power should be understood. In this sutta, the preliminary stage of clear comprehension mixed with the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) is taught.
234:
## 3. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta

In the third sutta, "In the same way, here, some" (*evameva panidhekacce*) means that, as heard, that monk, after having a meditation subject explained to him, wanders here and there and does not devote himself to physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). Therefore, the Blessed One, desiring to restrain that monk, spoke in this way. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means "because you requested a teaching in brief." "View" (*diṭṭhi*) refers to the view of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatādiṭṭhi*).

## 4. Commentary on the Sāla Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "Dhamma-Vinaya" means both Dhamma and Vinaya; both are names for the Teacher's Dispensation itself. "Should be encouraged" (*samādape-tabbā*) means they should be made to take it up. "Become unified" (*ekodibhūtā*) means having a mind concentrated through momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*). "Concentrated, with one-pointed mind" (*samāhitā ekaggacittā*) means having a mind well-established by the power of access concentration (*upacāra*) and attainment concentration (*appanā*), and having a one-pointed mind. In this sutta, the foundations of mindfulness developed by new monks and by those whose taints are destroyed (Arahants) are the preliminary (mundane) foundations of mindfulness, while those developed by the seven types of noble trainees (*sekha*) are mixed (mundane and supramundane).

## 6. Commentary on the Sakuṇagghi Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "falcon" (*sakuṇagghi*) is so called because it kills birds (*sakuṇa*); this is a name for the hawk. "Suddenly swooped down" (*sahasā ajjhapattā*) means it arrived with the violence of greed. "Unfortunate" (*alakkhikā*) means those without glory. "Of little merit" (*appapuññā*) means those with small merit. "If today we" (*sacejja mayaṃ*) means "if today we..." "The place of plowing with a plow" (*naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇa*) refers to the field area where plowing is done. "The place of clods" (*leḍḍuဋ္ဌာန*) means the place where clods of earth are located. "Boasting to one another" (*saṃvadamānā*) means speaking well of one's own strength. "Having climbed onto a large clod" (*mahantaṃ leḍḍuṃ abhiruhitvā*) means that among three clods of earth positioned like a tripod, he noted, "If the hawk comes from this side, I will exit this way; if it comes from that side, I will exit that way," and then stood on one of those clods, boasting with defiant words. "Preparing" (*sannayha*) means spreading the wings well and preparing, like preparing an arrow with a blade. "He has come a long way for me" (*bahuအာဂတော ခေါ မျာယံ*) means knowing, "This hawk has come from a far distance for my sake; only a little distance remains, now it will catch me," he turned quickly like a wooden ball and entered between those clods. "Entered" (*paccupādi*) means he went in. "Struck its own breast" (*uraṃ paccatāဠေသိ*) means "with a single blow, having cut off the head of the quail..."
235:
Thinking "I will catch it," he rushed in and, unable to check his speed, struck his breast violently against that clod of earth. At that very moment, the hawk's heart burst. Then the quail, joyful and delighted, thinking "Indeed, the enemy's ruin has been seen," walked to and fro upon the hawk's breast.

## 7. Makkaṭasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "duggā" refers to places that are difficult to traverse. "Cārī" means wandering. "Lepaṃ oḍḍenti" means they make a sticky trap (birdlime) by mixing the sap of the banyan tree and so on; having noted that place as a frequent haunt of monkeys, they place it on tree branches and such. "Pañcoḍḍito" means being caught in five places, like a carrying-pole's harness that is taken by inserting the pole. "Thunaṃ seti" means he lies moaning.

## 8. Sūdasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "sūdo" means a cook. "Nānaccayehī" means with various kinds of seasonings or ingredients. Alternatively, this reading "nānācayehī" is the text in the Pali. "Ambilaggehī" means with sour portions. This method should be understood in all places. "Abhiharati" means he stretches out his hand to take. "Bahuṃ gaṇhāti" means whether he takes much at once or takes repeatedly, it is called taking much. "Abhihaရာနံ" (Abhihārānaṃ) refers to royal rewards or gifts brought forth, amounting to a hundred or a thousand coins. "Upakkilesā" refers to the five hindrances. "Nimittaṃ na uggaṇhāti" means he does not know, "This meditation subject of mine has reached and stands at the stage of conformity (anuloma) or change-of-lineage (gotrabhū)"; he is unable to grasp the sign of his own mind. In this sutta, only the insight (vipassanā) and foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) occurring in the preliminary stage of the Path are taught.

## 9. Gilānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "Beḷuvagāmake" means in a small suburban village of this name located near the city of Vesālī. In the words beginning with "yathāmittaṃ", "mittā" means simply friends. "Sandiṭṭhā" means acquaintances met here and there, not very firm friends. "Sambhattā" means well-devoted, affectionate, and firm friends. The meaning is: "In whatever place such monk-friends exist for those monks, let them enter the rains retreat in those places." Why did He speak thus? It was for their comfortable living. It is heard that the lodgings in the small village of Beluva were not sufficient for those monks,
236: Alms were also scarce. However, around the city of Vesālī, there were many monasteries and alms were easy to obtain. Therefore, He spoke thus. If that is so, why did He not dismiss them, saying, "Go wherever you wish and live happily"? It was out of compassion for those monks that He did not dismiss them. It is heard that this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "I shall remain for about ten months and then attain Parinibbāna. If these monks go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my Parinibbāna. Then, those monks might feel remorse (vippaṭisāra) and dissatisfaction, thinking, 'The Blessed One, when about to attain Parinibbāna, did not even show us a sign of remembrance. Had we known, we would not have lived in such a distant place.' If they enter the rains retreat around Vesālī, they will be able to come eight times a month (on Uposatha days) to hear the Dhamma and receive the instruction of the Sugata." Thinking thus, He did not dismiss them. "Kharo" means harsh (pain). "Ābādho" means a discordant disease. "Bāဠှာ" (Bāḷhā) means very intense pains. "Māraṇantikā" means pains capable of leading to death. "Sato sampajāno adhivāsesi" means having established mindfulness well and having discerned with wisdom, He endured. "Avihaññamāno" means He endured without tossing to and fro following the pain, without being oppressed by the pain, and without suffering. "Anāmantetvā" means without informing. "Anapaloketvā" also means without informing, without giving advice and instruction. "Vīriyena" means with the preliminary energy and the energy of fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti). "Paṭipāṇāmetvā" means having dispelled. In this context of "jīvitasaṅkhāra", the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is called jīvitasaṅkhāra. That Dhamma of fruition attainment by which life is conditioned and by which life, which is about to be cut off, is connected and maintained, is also called jīvitasaṅkhāra. Here, that fruition attainment is intended. "Adhiṭṭhāya" means having determined, having brought it about; the summary meaning is: "I shall enter the fruition attainment capable of maintaining life." If one asks, "Did the Blessed One not enter fruition attainment before this time?", the answer is: He did. However, that attainment was a momentary attainment (khaṇikasamāpatti). A momentary attainment dispels pain only within the attainment. As soon as one emerges from the attainment, pain overwhelms the body again, just as water overwhelms severed moss when a piece of wood or a potsherd falls into it. Only the attainment entered by means of great insight (mahāvipassanā), having made the sevenfold groups of materiality (rūpasattaka) and the sevenfold groups of mentality (arūpasattaka) free from entanglement and knots, can well dispel the pain. For example, a man having descended into a lotus pond and with his hands and feet well...
237: Just as in a pond where the moss has been cleared, the moss covers the water again only after a long time, similarly, the painful feeling arose for the Blessed One only after a long time since he had emerged from that Great Fruition Attainment (Mahāphalasamāpatti). Thus, the Blessed One, as if initiating a new insight on the Great Bodhi Seat that day, made the sevenfold materiality (rūpasattaka) and sevenfold mentality (arūpasattaka) free from tangles and knots, and having saturated them with the sap of insight-joy through fourteen modes, he dispelled the feeling with great insight and entered the attainment with the resolution: "May it not arise for ten months." The feeling that was dispelled by the attainment did not arise for ten months. "Gilānā vuṭṭhito" means having recovered from a severe illness. "Madhurakajāto viya" means being heavy and sluggish as if due to pregnancy, or like a man who has been impaled. "Na pakkhāyanti" means not appearing clearly through various modes. "Dhammāpi maṃ nappaṭibhanti" means it is shown that the teachings of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna) previously cultivated did not appear clearly to me. As for the scriptural Dhamma (Pariyatti), it was already well-mastered by the Venerable Ānanda. "Na udāharati" refers to not giving the final exhortation. "Anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ" means not making a distinction between inner and outer, either by way of the Dhamma or by way of the person. If one thinks, "I will not preach this much of the Dhamma to others," one is said to make the Dhamma internal (keeping the teacher's fist). If one thinks, "I will preach this much of the Dhamma to others," one is said to make the Dhamma external. If one thinks, "I will preach to this person," one makes the person an insider. If one thinks, "I will not preach to this person," one makes the person an outsider. The meaning is that the Dhamma was preached without making such distinctions. "Ācariyamuṭṭhi" (teacher's fist) is like teachers outside the Dispensation who do not tell anyone anything in their youth, but only tell a beloved pupil while lying on their deathbed. It is shown that for the Tathāgata, there is nothing kept secret or hidden in a "fist," thinking, "I will preach this in old age at the final place." "Ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ" means thinking, "I alone shall lead the Saṅgha of monks." "Mamuddesiko" means thinking, "Let the Saṅgha of monks be one that points to me alone as the teacher to be relied upon, and let them depend only on me; let it not be so after my passing, or let it be in some other way." Such a thought might occur to someone. For the Blessed One, such a state does not exist. Since envy and avarice (issā-macchariya) were already abandoned by the Path of Arahantship at the very Seat of Enlightenment, the Blessed One does not have even the slightest of such thoughts. "Sakiṃ" means why is that so for the Blessed One? "Āsītiko" shows the state of having reached eighty years of age. "Veṭhamissakena" means by way of repairs such as binding the axle or the wheels of a cart... decay (aging)...
238:
Because envy and avarice have been removed and cleared by the Path of Arahantship at the very Seat of Enlightenment, such a state does not exist for the Blessed One even in the slightest. "Sa kiṃ" means why is that so for the Blessed One? "Āsītiko" means eighty years old; this was said to show the state of having reached the final stage of life. "Veṭhamissakena" means by way of repairs such as binding the axle and the wheels. "Maññe" means he keeps it going with repairs like an old cart; it shows that for the Tathāgata, the maintenance of the four postures is achieved through the maintenance of the physical body by the attainment of the Fruition of Arahantship.

Now, wishing to clarify that meaning, he spoke the words beginning with "Yasmiṃ Ānanda samaye." Therein, "sabbanimittānaṃ" means the signs of forms and so forth. "Ekaccānaṃ vedanānaṃ" means worldly feelings. "Tasmātihānanda" means because there is ease through this dwelling in the attainment of the Fruition of Arahantship, therefore you too should dwell in this way for the sake of that attainment. "Attadīpā" means dwell making the Supramundane Dhamma, called oneself, an island and a support, like an island in the great ocean. "Attasaraṇā" means be those who have the Supramundane Dhamma, called oneself, as a refuge; do not have anything other than the Supramundane Dhamma as a refuge. In the words "dhammadīpa" and "dhammasaraṇa," the method should be understood in the same way. Here, "Dhamma" should be understood as the ninefold Supramundane Dhamma. In the word "tamatagga," it should be joined as "tama-agge"; the letter 't' in the middle is spoken by way of euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). This is what is meant: these monks are the most excellent, therefore they are called "tamataggā." Ānanda, having thus cut off the entire stream of ignorance, these monks of mine will be in a state of extreme excellence among those who are not yet free from ignorance; they will be the foremost among them. Among all monks who desire the three trainings, only those who have the four foundations of mindfulness as their resort will be the foremost. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship.

## 10. Bhikkhunupassayasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "tenupasaṅkami" means there were bhikkhunīs practicing meditation in that nunnery; he approached them thinking, "I will encourage those bhikkhunīs and preach the meditation subject to them." "Uḷāraṃ pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ" means a lofty distinction that is later than the former distinction. Therein, the grasping of the great elements is the former distinction, and the grasping of derived materiality is the later distinction. Similarly, the grasping of all materiality is the former distinction, and the grasping of mentality is the later distinction. The grasping of both materiality and mentality is the former distinction,
239:
The comprehension of causes (paccaya-pariggaha) is called a subsequent distinction. Seeing mind-and-matter together with their causes is called a prior distinction. Applying the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) is called a subsequent distinction. In this way, it means that one knows the noble distinction of what is prior and what is subsequent.

'Kāyārammaṇa' means taking that very body which one is contemplating as an object, and the fever of defilements arises. 'Bahiddhā vā cittaṃ vikkhipati' means the arising of consciousness is scattered among various external objects. "The mind should be directed towards some inspiring sign (nimitta)"—thus, when defilement-fever, sluggishness, and external distraction arise, one should not proceed with a mind stained by defilements. Instead, one should place the meditation-mind on an inspiring object that brings clarity, such as the Buddha and so forth. 'Cittaṃ samādhiyati' means it is well-placed on the object; it is established firmly. 'Paṭisaṃharāmi' means I withdraw the mind from the inspiring place and direct it back towards the original meditation subject. That monk directs his mind towards the original meditation subject. He does not think thoughts associated with defilements, nor does he examine them. Being free from thoughts and examination associated with defilements, he is one without thought and without examination. With mindfulness occurring in his own field of meditation, he understands: "I am mindful and happy."

"Thus, Ānanda, there is development by directing (paṇidhāya)" means, Ānanda, there is development by placing [the mind elsewhere]. For instance, just as a man carrying a large load of sugarcane to a mill, when he is exhausted, places it on the ground, eats a piece of sugarcane, and then picks it up again to continue; even so, for this monk who has learned the meditation subject to attain Arahatship, when bodily fever and so forth arise, he pauses that meditation subject, clarifies his mind by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha and so forth, makes it fit for work, and then continues the development. Therefore, it is said: "paṇidhāya bhāvanā hoti."

Just as that man, having taken the load of sugarcane to the mill and pressed it, drinks the juice; so too, this monk, having brought the meditation subject to its peak and attained Arahatship, should be understood as experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).

'Bahiddhā' means leaving the original meditation subject and occurring in another external object. 'Appaṇidhāya' means occurring without placing [the mind elsewhere]. "Then, he understands the mind that is not scattered, liberated, and undirected, both after and before"—here, the meaning should be understood by way of the meditation subject, the body, or the teaching.
240:
Among those three, regarding the meditation subject: the initial application to the meditation subject is called 'before' (pure), and Arahatship is called 'after' (pacchā). In that meditation, a monk takes the original meditation subject and, without giving an opportunity for the fever of defilements, sluggishness, or external distraction to arise—like a man driving well-trained oxen to a pond, or like someone inserting a well-planed square peg into a square hole—he initiates insight (vipassanā) and reaches Arahatship without stopping or getting stuck. By way of the application to the meditation subject called 'before' and Arahatship called 'after', he is said to understand: "The mind is not scattered, liberated, and undirected, both after and before."

Regarding the body: the tips of the joints of the toes are called 'before', and the skull is called 'after'. In that body, a monk applies his mind to the bones of the tips of the toe-joints and, like untying a bundle of barley with a carrying pole, he comprehends the bones by way of color, shape, direction, and delimitation of space. Preventing the arising of defilement-fever and so forth in between, he brings the development as far as the skull. By way of the tips of the toe-joints called 'before' and the skull called 'after', he is said to understand: "The mind is not scattered, liberated, and undirected, both after and before."

Regarding the teaching: in the teaching on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), the hair of the head is called 'before', and the brain is called 'after'. In that teaching, a monk applies his mind to the hair of the head and, comprehending the hair and so forth by way of color, shape, direction, and space, he prevents the arising of defilement-fever and so forth in between, and brings the development as far as the brain. By way of the hair called 'before' and the brain called 'after', he is said to understand: "The mind is not scattered, liberated, and undirected, both after and before."

"Thus, Ānanda, there is development without directing (appaṇidhāya)" means, Ānanda, there is development without pausing. For instance, just as a man who has obtained a load of molasses and is carrying it to his own village, eats the pieces of molasses and sweets placed in his pocket while walking without stopping in between, and arrives at his own village; even so, for this monk who has started the development to attain Arahatship, preventing the arising of bodily fever and so forth, the development of the meditation subject proceeds. Therefore, it is called "appaṇidhāya bhāvanā." Just as that man, having taken the load of molasses to his village, enjoys it with his relatives; so too, this monk, having brought the meditation subject to the end and attained Arahatship, should be understood as experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition. In this Sutta, the Buddha taught insight (vipassanā) which is the preliminary stage of the Path. The remaining words are clear in all the Suttas. This is the end of the commentary on the tenth Sutta. The first chapter, the Ambapāli Vagga, is finished.
241:
It should be understood that this monk, having brought his meditation subject to its culmination and attained the fruit of Arahatship, experiences the bliss of the attainment of fruition. In this sutta, insight (vipassanā) which is the preliminary stage of the path is taught. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all suttas.

## The first Ambapāli Vagga is finished.

## 2. Nālanda Vagga

## 2. Nālanda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta of the second vagga, "Nālandāyaṃ" means in the city named Nālandā, having made that city a resort for alms. "Pāvārikambavane" means in the mango grove of the wealthy merchant Pāvārika. It is said that this was his park. Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One and being inspired with confidence in the Blessed One, that merchant Pāvārika built a monastery complex adorned with huts, caves, pavilions, etc., in that park and offered it to the Blessed One. That monastery became known as "Pāvārikambavana," just like Jīvakambavana. The meaning is that [the Buddha] was staying in that Pāvārika Mango Grove.

"Evaṃpasanno" means having such faith arisen, with the meaning "I believe thus." "Bhiyyobhiññataro" means more specially distinguished, or having a more specially excellent knowledge. "Sambodhiyaṃ" refers to omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) or the knowledge of the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa). Indeed, it is only through the path of Arahatship that the qualities of a Buddha are fully acquired. The two chief disciples also attain the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) only through the path of Arahatship. Paccekabuddhas attain the knowledge of solitary enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). Buddhas attain omniscience as well as all the qualities of a Buddha. All the benefits for these individuals are accomplished only through the path of Arahatship. Therefore, the knowledge of the path of Arahatship is called "Sambodhi." There is no one more excellent than the Blessed One in that knowledge of the path of Arahatship. Therefore, it was said: "There is no one more specially distinguished than the Blessed One in this knowledge of enlightenment."

"Uḷārā" means noble or excellent. This word "uḷāra" is used in the sense of "sweet" in such passages as "They eat sweet (uḷārāni) foods." It is used in the sense of "noble" in such passages as "The venerable Vacchāyana indeed praises the ascetic Gotama with noble (uḷārāya) praise." "Immeasurable..."
242:
...vast (uḷāro) radiance" and so forth, the word "uḷāra" is used in the sense of "vast." Here, however, it appears in the sense of "noble." Therefore, it is said: "Uḷārā means noble." "Āsabhī" refers to speech that is like the sound of a bull (usabha), fearless and unshakable. "Ekaṃso gahito" means that it was not spoken based on hearsay, or the tradition of teachers, or report, or the authority of scriptures, or logical reasoning, or reflection on reasons, or delight in a view, or mere logic, or a particular method; rather, it was taken as a certainty, as if having penetrated it with direct knowledge. The meaning is that a definitive statement was made. "Sīhanāda" means a noble roar; the meaning is that a supreme sound was uttered like a lion roaring in the forest.

Why did [the Buddha] start this teaching "Kiṃ nu te Sāriputta"? It was started for the purpose of inviting scrutiny (investigation). Indeed, some people, after uttering a lion's roar, cannot allow scrutiny of their roar, cannot endure being challenged, and become like a monkey stuck in tree sap. Just as impure lead becomes charcoal when smelted, they become like burnt charcoal. Some, however, can allow scrutiny of their lion's roar, can endure being challenged, and shine even more like pure gold when smelted. The Elder Sāriputta was such a type of Elder. Therefore, the Blessed One, knowing "This Sāriputta is capable of enduring scrutiny," started this teaching to invite scrutiny of the lion's roar.

In that text, "Sabbe te" means "all those [Buddhas] by you." "Evaṃsīlā" means having such virtue through the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, and mundane and supramundane virtue. In the phrase "Evaṃdhammā," the states associated with concentration (samādhi) are intended. The meaning is "having such concentration" through the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and mundane and supramundane concentration. "Evaṃpaññā" means having such wisdom by way of the wisdom of the path and so forth. In the phrase "Evaṃvihārino," since the states associated with concentration were already taken below, why is "dwelling" (vihāra) taken again? The Elder [Sāriputta] indeed took this term. This was said to indicate the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "Those Blessed Ones were such dwellers in the attainment of cessation."

In the phrase "Evaṃဝိမုတ္တာ," there are five kinds of liberation: liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquillization (paṭipassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti). Among those five, the eight attainments are called "liberation by suppression" because they are liberated from the hindrances and so forth, which are suppressed by themselves.
243:
The seven types of insight (anupassanā), such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), are called 'liberation by substitution of opposites' (tadaṅgavimutti) because they are liberated from the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) and so forth, which are abandoned by their respective opposites. The four noble paths are called 'liberation by uprooting' (samucchedavimutti) because they are liberated from the defilements (kilesas) which are completely cut off by them. The four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are called 'liberation by tranquilization' (paṭippassaddhivimutti) because they arise at the end of the tranquilization of defilements through the power of the path. Nirvana is called 'liberation by escape' (nissaraṇavimutti) because it is the escape from all defilements, being detached and standing far off. In this way, the meaning should be understood here as 'thus they are liberated' by means of these five types of liberation.

'Sāriputta, what about the Buddhas who will be in the future?' (the Buddha asked). As for the past Buddhas, they have first ceased and reached the state of being beyond designation; they are extinguished like the flame of a lamp. How can you know those Buddhas who have thus ceased and reached the state of being beyond designation? Do you know the virtues of the future Buddhas by delimiting them with your own mind? Wishing to ask this, He spoke thus.

'Sāriputta, what about me at present?' (the Buddha asked). The future Buddhas have not yet arisen, have not yet appeared, and have not yet been born; how can you know those Buddhas? Knowing them is like looking for footprints in the trackless sky. At present, you live in the same monastery with me, you wander for alms together, and you sit on the right side during the time of Dhamma teaching; even so, do you know my virtues by delimiting them with your own mind? Wishing to investigate and ask this, He spoke thus. To each and every question asked, the Elder replied, 'No, Bhante,' and denied it.

The Elder has things that are known and things that are unknown. Does the Elder deny in the area he knows, or in the area he does not know? He does not deny in the area he knows; he only denies in the area he does not know. It is said that when the investigation began, the Elder understood: 'This investigation is not about the Disciple's Perfection Knowledge (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), but it is about Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa).' Therefore, without denying his own Disciple's Perfection Knowledge, he only denied the Omniscience which he did not know. By denying in this way, it also serves to show: 'Bhante, I do not possess the Omniscience capable of knowing the virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.'

'Ettha' (herein) refers to those Buddhas categorized as past and so forth. 'If so, why do you speak thus (such bold words) when you do not have such knowledge?' He said. 'Dhammanvaya' refers to the inferential knowledge (anumānañāṇa) that arises by following the knowledge of direct perception of the Dhamma.
244:
The knowledge of grasping the method (nayaggāha) has been understood; he says, 'Bhante, standing only in the Disciple's Perfection Knowledge, I know in this manner.' Indeed, the Elder Sāriputta's knowledge of grasping the method is immeasurable and boundless. Just as there is no measure or limit to Omniscience, so too there is no measure or limit to the knowledge of grasping the method of the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta). Because it is thus boundless, the Elder knows: 'Because of this reason, the Teacher has such virtues; because of this reason, He is the Peerless One.' Indeed, the Elder Sāriputta's knowledge of grasping the method follows the course of Omniscience itself.

Now, wishing to show a simile to make that knowledge of grasping the method clear, He spoke the words beginning with 'Bhante, just as if.' In that simile, whether the high foundations and walls of a city in the Middle Country (majjhimadesa) are strong or weak, or even if they do not exist at all, there is no fear of thieves. Therefore, without taking such a city, He spoke of a 'border city.' 'Daḷhuddhāpa' means a city wall with a strong foundation. 'Daḷhapākāratoraṇa' means a city with strong walls and strong gate-pillars. Why did He say 'having a single gate'? In a city with many gates, there must be many wise gatekeepers, but in a city with only one gate, one is sufficient. There is no other equal to the wisdom of Sāriputta; therefore, to illustrate his own state of being wise, wishing to show only one gatekeeper, He said 'a single gate.'

'Paṇḍita' means being endowed with wisdom. 'Vyatta' means being endowed with proficient wisdom, having clear and sharp intellect. 'Medhāvī' means being endowed with sagacity, known as wisdom that arises instantly in various situations. 'Anupariyāyapatha' means the road that encircles the city wall. 'Pākārasandhi' means a gap between two bricks. 'Pākāravivara' means a breached part of the wall. 'Cetaso upakkilesa' means the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) which defile the mind, make it murky, cause distress, and oppress it; therefore, they are called 'defilements of the mind.' 'Paññāya dubbalīkaraṇa' means that when the hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen wisdom to arise; therefore, they are called 'things that weaken wisdom.' 'Supatiṭṭhitacittā' means having the mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). 'Satta bojjhaṅge yathābhūtaṃ' means having developed the seven factors of enlightenment according to their true nature. 'Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ' shows that they have penetrated and realized Arahatship and Omniscience.

It is also said: 'satipaṭṭhāna' is insight (vipassanā), 'bojjhaṅga' are the path (magga), and 'anuttara sammāsambodhi' is Arahatship. Or, 'satipaṭṭhāna' is insight, and 'bojjhaṅga' are mixed states (of serenity and insight)...
245:
Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) is indeed the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). However, the Elder Mahāsīva, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, said: "If one takes insight (vipassanā) in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and takes both the Path and Omniscient Knowledge in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), it would be a good answer; however, the former teachers did not take it this way." In this way, the Elder shows that there is no difference between the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇappahāna), the development of the foundations of mindfulness, and enlightenment (sambodhi) of all Buddhas, just like gold and silver that have been cut in the middle.

Standing at this point, the analogy should be compared. The Venerable Sāriputta showed the border city, the wall, the moat (or encircling road), the gate, the wise gatekeeper, the coarse beings entering and leaving the city, and how the gatekeeper knows the condition of those beings. In that analogy, what is similar to what? Nibbāna is like the city, virtue (sīla) is like the wall, shame (hiri) is like the encircling road, the Noble Path is like the gate, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) is like the wise gatekeeper, and the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are like the coarse beings entering and leaving the city. Just as the condition of those beings is clear to the gatekeeper, the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are clear to the Venerable Sāriputta through their virtue, concentration (samatha), and so on. With these words, the Elder gives the Blessed One the opportunity to scrutinize his lion's roar (sīhanāda), saying, "Thus, standing in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa), I know by way of the inference from the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) and by way of grasping the principle (nayaggāha)."

"Tasmā" (Therefore) is used because he says, "Venerable Sir, I do not have the knowledge of encompassing the minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) of the Arahants and Fully Enlightened Buddhas of the past, future, and present, but I do know the inference from the Dhamma."

"Abhikkhaṇaṃ bhāseyyāsi" means to preach repeatedly. It means: do not refrain from preaching in the afternoon or evening saying "I have already preached in the morning," and do not refrain from preaching on subsequent days saying "I have already preached today."

"Sā pahīyissati" means that the doubt or uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata held by those who think, "Even a disciple as endowed with swift wisdom as Sāriputta cannot know the mental conduct of the Buddhas; thus the Tathāgatas are indeed immeasurable in their qualities," will be abandoned.

## 3. Cunda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "among the Magadhans" (magadhesu) means in the province of that name. "In Nālaka village" (nālakagāmake) means in the village of that name, which belonged to his own family and was not far from Rājagaha. The Elder Cunda was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. He was called "Cunda the Novice" (Cunda Samaṇuddesa) during his time as a novice, and even when he became an Elder, people continued to call him that out of habit; thus he is referred to as "Cunda the Novice." He was the one who served [Sāriputta] by offering water for washing the face, tooth-sticks, sweeping the compound, massaging the back, and receiving the bowl and robes. "Parinibbāyī" means he attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).
246:
Samaṇuddesa means this Elder was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. Monks called him "Cunda the Novice" when he was not yet fully ordained, and they continued to call him the same even during his time as an Elder. Therefore, it is said "Cunda the Novice." "Upaṭṭhāko hoti" means he was an attendant who served by giving water for washing the face and tooth-sticks, as well as by sweeping the compound, performing back massages, and taking the bowl and robes. "Parinibbāyī" means he attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue. At what time did he attain Parinibbāna? It was in the very year of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna.

Regarding this matter, the sequential account is as follows: It is said that after the rainy season residence, the Blessed One left Veḷuva village and, returning by the same path he had come, saying "I will go to Sāvatthī," he eventually reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jetavana monastery. The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, after performing his duties toward the Blessed One, went to his place of day-rest. There, after his resident pupils had performed their duties and departed, he swept the place of day-rest, spread his leather sitting-mat, washed his feet, sat down cross-legged, and entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Then, having emerged from that attainment at the predetermined time, this thought arose in him: "Do the Buddhas attain Parinibbāna first, or the Chief Disciples?" Then, knowing that "the Chief Disciples attain Parinibbāna first," he looked at his own life-force (āyusaṅkhāra). He realized, "My life-force will continue for only seven more days," and then considered, "Where shall I attain Parinibbāna?"

Then he thought, "Venerable Rāhula attained Parinibbāna in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña at the Chaddanta Lake. Where shall I attain Parinibbāna?" As he thought repeatedly, he directed his mindfulness toward his mother: "My mother, though she is the mother of seven Arahants, has no confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Does she have the supporting condition (upanissaya) [for the Path], or not?" Seeing her supporting condition for the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), he looked further: "By whose Dhamma teaching will her realization (abhisamaya) occur?" He saw, "It will be by my Dhamma teaching alone, not by another's. If I were to remain indifferent, there will be those who say: 'The Elder Sāriputta is a refuge even for other people. Indeed, on the day he preached the Samacitta Suttanta, a hundred thousand crores of deities attained Arahantship, and the number of deities who penetrated the three lower Paths is beyond counting; and in other places, many realizations are found.'"

Furthermore, there are eighty thousand families who, having gained confidence in the Elder Sāriputta, were reborn in heaven. People would criticize, saying, "Venerable Sāriputta, who is the refuge for so many, is unable today to remove even his own mother's wrong view." Therefore, he decided, "I will free my mother from wrong view and attain Parinibbāna in the very room where I was born," and he thought, "I will ask the Blessed One for permission to depart this very day." He then called Venerable Cunda and said, "Friend Cunda, give the signal to our company of five hundred monks. Tell them, 'Friends, take your bowls and robes; our teacher, the General of the Dhamma, wishes to go to Nālaka village.'" Venerable Cunda did as Venerable Sāriputta had instructed. The monks put away their bedding and dwellings, took their bowls and robes, and came to Venerable Sāriputta. The Elder Sāriputta also put away his own bedding and dwelling, swept his place of day-rest, and...
247:
Assemblies who penetrated the Four Noble Truths are seen in other places as well. There were also eighty thousand families who were reborn in heaven after gaining confidence in the Elder Sāriputta. [People might say:] 'The Elder Sāriputta, the refuge of so many, is now unable to even remove the wrong view of his own mother.' Therefore, having made the resolution, 'I will attain Parinibbāna in my birth chamber only after liberating my mother from wrong view,' and thinking, 'I will take leave of the Blessed One and depart this very day,' he addressed the Elder Cunda: 'Friend Cunda, give the signal to our assembly of five hundred monks. Say, "Friends, take your bowls and robes; the General of the Dhamma (Dhamma-senāpati) Sāriputta wishes to go to Nālaka village."' The Elder Cunda did so. The monks tidied their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and came to the Elder. The Elder also tidied his lodging, swept the day-quarters, and standing at the doorway, looked at the place, reflecting: 'This is now the last sight; there will be no returning again.' Surrounded by five hundred monks, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said: 'May the Blessed One allow me, Bhante; may the Sugata allow me. It is time for my Parinibbāna; I have relinquished my life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra).'

Because if Buddhas say 'Attain Parinibbāna,' they would be praising death, and if they say 'Do not attain Parinibbāna,' they would be speaking of the virtues of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa); thus, those with wrong views would find fault. Therefore, the Buddhas say neither. Then the Blessed One asked the Elder Sāriputta: 'Sāriputta, where will you attain Parinibbāna?' When he replied, 'Bhante, there is the birth chamber in Nālaka village in Magadha; I will attain Parinibbāna there,' the Blessed One said: 'Sāriputta, you know the time for that. But now, for your elder and younger brothers, it will be difficult to see a monk such as you; preach the Dhamma to them.'

The Elder, knowing 'The Teacher desires a Dhamma teaching preceded by a display of psychic powers,' paid homage to the Blessed One, rose into the air to the height of one palm tree, descended, and paid homage to the feet of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala). Again, he rose to the height of two palm trees, descended, and paid homage to the feet. In this manner, rising up to the height of seven palm trees and performing hundreds of miracles, he began the Dhamma discourse. He preached with a visible body and an invisible body. He preached showing only the upper or lower body, or half the body. Sometimes he showed the form of the moon, sometimes the sun, sometimes a mountain, sometimes the ocean. Sometimes he appeared as a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), sometimes as the Great King Vessavaṇa, sometimes...
248:
...sometimes as Sakka, the king of gods, and sometimes as Mahābrahmā; thus showing hundreds of miracles, he preached the Dhamma. The people of the entire city gathered. The Elder descended from the sky, paid homage to the feet of the Ten-Powered One, and stood there. Then the Teacher asked the Elder Sāriputta: 'Sāriputta, what is the name of this Dhamma exposition?' 'Bhante, it is named Sīhavikīḷita (The Lion’s Play),' he replied. 'Indeed, Sāriputta, it is Sīhavikīḷita; indeed, Sāriputta, it is Sīhavikīḷita,' the Teacher said.

The Elder stretched out his hands, which were the color of lac, and holding the ankles and the tops of the feet of the Teacher—which were like golden tortoises—he said: 'Bhante, for the sake of paying homage to these feet, I have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons. My heart's desire has reached its pinnacle. From now on, there will be no more meeting or coming together in one place by way of rebirth. This intimacy is broken. I shall enter the city of Nibbāna—ageless, deathless, secure, happy, cool, and fearless—which has been entered by many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. If any of my bodily or verbal actions were not pleasing to you, may the Blessed One forgive them. It is time for my departure.' 'Sāriputta, I forgive you. Indeed, there is not even the slightest bodily or verbal action of yours that is unpleasing to me. Sāriputta, now you know the time you think is right to go,' the Teacher said.

Immediately after the Blessed One gave permission, as the Venerable Sāriputta rose after paying homage to the Teacher's feet, the great earth—though it supports Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāဠာ mountains, and the Himavantā range—trembled with a roar as if saying, 'Today I am unable to bear this mass of virtue,' shaking as far as the water's edge. Celestial drums sounded in the sky. A great cloud arose and poured down the Pokkharavassa rain.

The Teacher, thinking 'I will see off the General of the Dhamma,' rose from the Dhamma seat, went towards the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), and stood on a jeweled slab. The Elder circumambulated him three times to the right, paid homage at four points, and said: 'Blessed One, more than one incalculable period and a hundred thousand aeons ago, prostrating at the feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One Anomadassī, I aspired to see you. That aspiration has been fulfilled. I have seen you. That was the first sight; this is the last sight. There will be no more seeing you again.' Having said this, he raised his hands in añjali, shining with the radiance of his ten fingernails, and walked backward, facing the Buddha as long as he remained within the range of vision. At the point where he was out of sight, he paid homage once more and departed. Again, the great earth trembled as far as the water's edge, as if saying, 'I am unable to bear the great mass of the Venerable One's virtue.'
249:
(The Elder) withdrew, paid homage, and departed. Once again, the great earth shook as far as the water's edge, as if unable to bear the mass of the Elder's virtues. The Blessed One said to the monks standing around Him, "Monks, follow your elder brother." At that moment, the four assemblies also left the Blessed One alone in Jetavana and departed without exception. The residents of Sāvatthī, too, saying, "It is said that the Elder Sāriputta, having asked permission from the Blessed One, has departed wishing to attain Parinibbāna; let us go and see that Noble One," came out in such crowds that the city gates were blocked. Holding perfumes, flowers, and the like, with their hair disheveled, they lamented and wept, asking, "Where is the Great Wise One sitting now? Where is the General of the Dhamma sitting now?" and "To whom shall we go? In whose hands has the Elder left the Teacher and departed?" and so on, following the Elder.

Because the Elder was established in great wisdom, he exhorted the multitude, saying, "This path is one that cannot be avoided by any being." He then turned back the Saṅgha of monks, saying, "Friends, you too stay back; do not be negligent toward the Blessed One, the Ten-Powered One," and proceeded only with his own followers. Those people who followed him, lamenting, "In the past, the Noble One went on a journey from which he would return; but now this departure is not for the sake of returning again," he also turned back, exhorting them, "Friends, be diligent; conditioned things are of such a nature."

Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, staying only one night in each place and providing assistance to the people for seven days along the way, reached Nālaka village in the evening and stood at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate. Then, the nephew of the Elder named Uparevata, while going out of the village, saw the Elder, approached him, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked him, "Is your grandmother at home?" "Yes, Bhante," he replied. "Go and inform her of our arrival here." And if she asks, "Why has he come?" say, "He will stay inside the village for one whole day today; prepare the birth chamber, and also arrange a place for five hundred monks to stay." He went and said, "Grandmother, my maternal uncle has arrived." "Where is he now?" she asked. "At the village gate," he said. "Is he alone, or is there anyone else?" "There are five hundred monks," he said. "For what reason has he come?" she asked. He informed her of the matter. The Brahmin woman thought, "Why a place for so many?...
250:
The Brahmin woman, his mother, thinking, "My son went forth as a monk when he was young, and now in his old age, he likely wishes to become a layman," had the birth chamber prepared, arranged a place for the five hundred monks, lit torches, and sent word to the Elder.

The Elder, together with the monks, ascended the mansion, entered the birth chamber, and sat down. Having sat down, he dismissed the monks, saying, "Go to your own places of residence." As soon as they had gone, a severe illness arose in the Elder. Painful feelings of dysentery, which were terminal, occurred. (Waste) entered one vessel and left another. The Brahmin woman, thinking, "The condition of my son is not pleasing to me," stood leaning against the door of her own living quarters.

The Four Great Kings, looking to see "Where is the General of the Dhamma staying?" saw him lying on his deathbed in the birth chamber in Nālaka village and, saying, "We will go for a final sight," came, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked, "Who are you?" "Bhante, we are the Four Great Kings," they replied. "Why have you come?" "We have come to attend to the sick." "Let it be; I have an attendant. You may go," he dismissed them. After they had gone, in the same manner, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, arrived. After Sakka had gone, the Mahābrahmās also arrived. The Elder dismissed them in the same manner as well.

The Brahmin woman, seeing the coming and going of the deities, thought, "Who are these who pay homage to my son and then leave?" She went to the door of the Elder's chamber and asked, "Dear Cunda, what is the situation?" The Venerable Cunda explained the situation and said, "Bhante, the Great Lay-Devotee has come." The Elder asked, "Why have you come at an unusual time?" The mother said, "Dear son, I have come to see you," and then asked, "Dear son, who came first?" "Great Lay-Devotee, they were the Four Great Kings." "Dear son, are you greater than the Four Great Kings?" "Great Lay-Devotee, they are like the garden-guards of our Teacher. From the time our Buddha took conception, they have stood with swords in hand providing protection." "Dear son, after they left, who came?" "It was Sakka, the Lord of Devas." "Dear son, are you even greater than Sakka, the King of Devas?" "Great Lay-Devotee, this Sakka is like a novice who carries the bowl and robes. When our Teacher descended from Tāvatiṃsa, he followed, carrying the bowl and robes." "Dear son, after Sakka left, who was it that came shining with light?" "Great Lay-Devotee, this is Mahābrahmā, who is your refuge and teacher." "Dear son, are you even greater than my refuge, Mahābrahmā?" "Great Lay-Devotee, on the day our Buddha was born, these Mahābrahmās [received] the Great Man with a golden net..."
251:
“Dear son, are you greater and more eminent than the Blessed One and Mahābrahmā?” she asked. “Great lay devotee, it is so. Indeed, these Mahābrahmās received the Great Man with a golden net on the day our Teacher, the Blessed One, was born,” he replied.

Then the brahmin woman thought, “If even my son’s power is this great, how great indeed must be the power of the Blessed One, my son’s Teacher?” As she thought this, five-fold joy (pīti) suddenly arose and pervaded her entire body. The Elder thought, “Joy and gladness have arisen in my mother; now is the time to preach the Dhamma.” He asked, “Great lay devotee, what are you thinking?” She replied, “Dear son, I was thinking that if my son’s virtue is this great, how much greater must be the virtue of the Blessed One, my son’s Teacher?” “Great lay devotee, at the moment of my Teacher’s birth, at his Great Renunciation, at his Enlightenment, and at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. In virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no one equal to him. For such reasons, that Blessed One is worthy of praise as ‘Arahant’ and so forth.” Thus, he gave a detailed Dhamma discourse concerning the qualities of the Buddha.

At the end of the Dhamma discourse by her beloved son, the brahmin woman was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). She said to her son, “Dear son Upatissa, why did you do this? Why did you not give me this kind of Deathless Nibbāna for so long?” The Elder thought, “Now I have paid the debt of my upbringing to my mother, the brahmin woman Rūpasārī. With this wealth of the fruit of Stream-entry, she will be able to practice until reaching the path of Arahantship.” He then said, “Great lay devotee, you may go,” and sent her away. He then asked, “Cunda, what time is it?” “Venerable sir, it is the time of dawn,” he replied. “Assemble the community of monks,” the Elder said. “Venerable sir, the community of monks has assembled.” “Cunda, lift me up and help me sit.” He was lifted and seated.

The Elder addressed the monks: “Friends, if there is any action of mine, whether of body or speech, that you did not like while wandering with me for forty-four years, please forgive me, friends.” “Venerable sir, while we have been wandering with you without parting, like a shadow, for all this time, there has been nothing in your bodily or verbal actions that was unpleasant to us. Rather, venerable sir, please forgive us for our faults.” Then the Elder pulled his great robe over him, covered his face, and lying on his right side like the Teacher, he entered the nine successive attainments (samāpatti) in forward and reverse order. Starting again from the first jhāna up to the fourth jhāna...
252:
...he entered. Emerging from that, immediately after, making the great earth resound, he attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

The lay devotee mother thought, “Why does my son say nothing?” She stood up and felt the tops of his feet. Realizing he had attained Parinibbāna, she cried out loudly and fell at his feet, lamenting: “Dear son, before this, we did not know your virtues. Now, because of you, we have lost the chance to have hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of monks sit and eat in this house; we have lost the chance to offer robes; we have lost the chance to build hundreds and thousands of monasteries.” She lamented until dawn. Just as dawn broke, she summoned goldsmiths, opened the gold treasury, and had gold pots weighed on a large scale. She ordered, “Construct five hundred peaked buildings (kūṭāgāra) and five hundred pinnacles (agghika).”

Sakka, the king of devas, also called the young deva Vissakamma and said, “Friend Vissakamma, the General of the Dhamma has attained Parinibbāna. Create five hundred peaked buildings and five hundred pinnacles.” Thus, the total number of buildings, both those made by the lay devotee and those created by Vissakamma, was two thousand. Then, they had a great pavilion made of heartwood in the center of the city. Placing a large peaked building in the middle of the pavilion and surrounding it with the others, they began a righteous festival (sādhukīḷika). Humans were among the devas, and devas were among the humans, all mixed together.

A female attendant of Venerable Sāriputta named Revatī thought, “I will make an offering to the Elder,” and had three pots filled with golden flowers made. Sakka, the king of devas, descended surrounded by twenty-five million celestial dancers, thinking, “I will make an offering to the Elder.” Seeing Sakka descend, the great crowd turned back and moved away. There, that lay devotee Revatī, while moving back, was unable to move to a suitable place because of the heavy burden and fell among the people. The people, not seeing her, trampled her as they went. She died right there and was reborn in a golden mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At the moment of her rebirth, she possessed a body three gāvutas in height, like a mass of jewels, adorned with ornaments equivalent to sixty cartloads, and surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs. Then, a divine full-length mirror appeared before the goddess Revatī...
253:
(The devas) placed a full-length mirror before the goddess Revatī. Seeing the perfection of her own glory and splendor, she reflected, "This prosperity is indeed magnificent; what wholesome deed did I perform?" Upon reflection, she saw: "I made an offering with three pots of golden flowers at the place where the Elder Sāriputta attained parinibbana. The multitude of people, not seeing me, trampled over me as they went. I died right there and was reborn in this celestial realm. Now, I shall tell the people about the fruits of merit obtained by depending on the noble Elder." Thinking thus, she descended together with her celestial mansion (vimāna).

Seeing her from afar, the multitude of people looked and wondered, "Have two suns risen?" As the mansion approached, the shape of a celestial mansion with tiered roofs became clear, and they said, "This is not the sun; it is a celestial mansion." That mansion immediately arrived and stood in the air above the Elder's funeral pyre. The goddess left the mansion in the sky and descended to the ground. The people asked, "Noble lady, who are you?" The goddess replied, "Do you not know me? My name is Revatī. Having made an offering to the Elder with three pots of golden flowers, I was trampled by the people, died, and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Look at the perfection of my glory and splendor! You too should now give gifts and perform meritorious deeds." Having thus spoken in praise of performing wholesome acts, she circumambulated the Elder's pyre clockwise, paid her respects, and returned to her own celestial abode.

The multitude of people also celebrated the festival of honor (sādhukīḷita) for seven days and prepared the pyre with all kinds of perfumes. The pyre was ninety-nine cubits high. They placed the Elder's body upon the pyre and ignited it with bundles of usīra grass. Throughout the night at the cemetery, the preaching of the Dhamma continued. The Elder Anuruddha extinguished the Elder's pyre with all kinds of scented water. The Elder Cunda placed the relics in a water-strainer and thought, "It is not possible for me to remain here now. I shall inform the Fully Enlightened One about the parinibbana of my elder brother, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta." Taking the water-strainer with the relics, as well as the Elder's bowl and robes, he departed for Sāvatthī. Without staying for two nights in any single place, he reached Sāvatthī by staying only one night at each location. To show this matter, the words beginning with "Atha kho Cundo samaṇuddeso" were spoken.

In those words, "yenāyasmā Ānando" means he approached the place where his preceptor, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda, was staying. Why did this novice Cunda...
254:
Why did the novice Cunda go to the Elder Ānanda instead of going directly to the Teacher (the Buddha)? It was out of respect for both the Teacher and the Elder. It is said that after bathing in the pond at the Jetavana Monastery and coming out, while properly dressing in his robes, this thought occurred to him: "The Buddhas are to be revered like a great stone umbrella. They are difficult to approach, like a hooded serpent, a lion, a tiger, or a noble elephant in rut. I am not able to go directly to the Teacher to report this. To whom should I go?" Then he thought, "My preceptor, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda, is the best friend of my elder brother. I will go to him and, taking him along, I will report to the Teacher." Thus, out of respect for both the Teacher and the Elder, he approached him.

In the phrase "This is his bowl and robes," it means he pointed out each item, saying, "This is the bowl he used; this is the water-strainer containing the relics." In the Pali text, however, it is only mentioned as "This is his bowl and robes." The word "kathāpābhataṃ" refers to the basis of the conversation (a conversation-gift). The basis itself is called "pābhata." As it was said:

"With even a small capital, a wise and discerning man
Establishes himself, just as one blows
A small fire into a flame."

Regarding the phrase "to see the Blessed One," if one asks whether this Venerable Ānanda had not seen the Blessed One before, the answer is no, it is not that he had not seen Him. This Venerable one used to go to attend on Him eighteen times a day—nine times during the day and nine times at night. However, even if he wished to go a hundred or a thousand times a day, he would not go without a reason; he would only go by taking some question or matter as a reason. On that day, wishing to go by using that conversation-gift as a reason, he spoke thus. Regarding the phrase "This is his bowl and robes," the Elder Ānanda also pointed them out separately, saying, "This is his bowl and robes; this is the water-strainer with the relics."

The Teacher stretched out His hand, took the water-strainer with the relics, placed it in the palm of His hand, and addressed the monks: "Monks, that monk who, on a previous day, performed many hundreds of miracles and asked permission to attain parinibbana—now only these relics, resembling the color of a conch shell, remain of him. Monks, this monk is one who fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) for an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) plus a hundred thousand aeons. Monks, this monk [is the one who helped turn] the wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me..."
255:
“This monk is one who can roll the Wheel of Dhamma together with me, the Buddha. This monk is one who occupies the second seat. This monk is one who can fulfill the assembly of disciples. Excluding me, this monk is one who has no equal in wisdom throughout the ten thousand world systems. This monk possesses great wisdom. This monk possesses wide wisdom, joyous wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom. This monk has few desires, is contented, secluded, unentangled, and possesses exerted energy; he is an admonisher and a censurer of evil. This monk is one who renounced the great wealth obtained in five hundred births and went forth. In my Dispensation, this monk has patience like the great earth. This monk is like a bull with broken horns. This monk has a humble mind like a caṇḍāla boy. Monks, behold the relics of one with great wisdom. Monks, behold the relics of one who possesses wide wisdom, joyous wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom, few desires, contentment, seclusion, lack of entanglement, exerted energy, and the quality of an admonisher. Monks, behold the relics of one who censures evil.”

“He who went forth for five hundred births, renouncing delightful sensual pleasures; pay homage to that Sāriputta, who is free from lust, whose faculties are well-composed, and who has attained Parinibbāna.”

“Possessing the power of patience and being like the earth, he does not get angry, nor does he act under the influence of the mind; pay homage to that Sāriputta, who is sympathetic, compassionate, and peaceful, and who has attained Parinibbāna.”

“Just as a caṇḍāla boy, when entering a city, wanders with a humble mind, holding a basket in his hand; in the same way does this Sāriputta dwell. Pay homage to that Sāriputta who has attained Parinibbāna.”

“Just as a bull with broken horns wanders in the city or in the forest without harming others; in the same way does this Sāriputta dwell. Pay homage to that Sāriputta who has attained Parinibbāna.”
256:
Thus the Blessed One spoke the praise of the Elder Sāriputta with five hundred verses. In whatever manner the Blessed One spoke the praise of the Elder, in that same manner the Elder Ānanda was unable to steady his mind and trembled like a young chick in the mouth of a cat. Therefore, he said: “Venerable Sir, my body feels as if it were intoxicated,” and so on, which should be understood in detail. In that passage, the meaning of terms such as ‘madhurakajāto’ has already been explained. In this sutta, ‘Dhammā’ refers to the Dhamma of recitation (uddesa) and the Dhamma of inquiry (paripucchā). For that Ānanda, the mind could not incline toward learning the Dhamma of recitation and inquiry that had not yet been learned, nor toward reciting what had already been learned. Then the Teacher, opening his eyes which were beautiful with five kinds of clarity and looking at the Elder, thought, “I will console him,” and said: “Ānanda, did Sāriputta take away your virtue?” and so on.

In that context, ‘sīlakkhandha’ refers to mundane and supramundane virtue. The same principle applies to concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā). However, liberation (vimutti) is exclusively supramundane. Knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa), which is mundane only. ‘Ovādako’ means a giver of advice. ‘Otiṇṇo’ means one who has the nature of penetrating into various subjects. ‘Viññāpako’ means one who makes the meaning and the reason known during a Dhamma talk. ‘Sandassako’ means one who shows those various teachings by way of the aggregates, elements, and bases. ‘Samādapako’ means one who encourages others, saying, “Take up this and that.” ‘Samuttejako’ means one who inspires greatly. ‘Sampahaṃsako’ means one who gladdens and brightens others through the qualities they have attained.

‘Akilāsu dhammadesanāya’ means that while teaching the Dhamma, he is free from shrinking back or hesitation—such as saying, “My head aches, or my heart, stomach, or back hurts”—and without fatigue, he boldly enters into teaching even one or two people with the speed of a lion king. The meaning of the phrase ‘anuggāhako sabrahmacārīnaṃ’ (supporter of fellow celibates) has been explained in detail in the Khandhaka section. By the two terms ‘dhammaojaṃ dhammabhogaṃ’, only the enjoyment of the Dhamma is spoken of. ‘Dhammānuggaha’ means support through the Dhamma.

The Teacher, knowing that “this monk is greatly exhausted,” and wishing to console him again, said: “Ānanda, have I not told you before?” and so on. In that context, ‘piyehi manāpehi’ refers to the separation from loved and pleasing ones such as parents, brothers, and sisters, by way of different births, by way of death, and by way of change in existence. He said: “Ānanda, where can that (state of non-separation) be obtained here?”
257:
This is because of this reason. Since separation from all those who are dear and beloved is inevitable, even though [the Buddha] fulfilled the ten perfections, attained supreme enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dhamma, displayed the Twin Miracle, and performed the descent from the deva realm, there is no possibility that even the physical body of the Tathāgata—which is born, become, conditioned, and subject to disintegration—should not disintegrate. Even by weeping and wailing, that result cannot be obtained. "That branch should perish" means that the large branch breaks.

In this same way, the Saṅgha of monks should be understood as being like a great Jambu tree one hundred leagues in height. The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, should be understood as being like the great main branch fifty leagues long extending to the south of that great Jambu tree. Just as when that great branch breaks, there is no other branch capable of growing gradually from that place and filling it with flowers and fruits, so too, when the Elder Sāriputta attained Parinibbāna, there was no other monk like Sāriputta who had reached the summit of the sixteen kinds of wisdom and was capable of sitting in the seat to the right. Just as that tree becomes a tree with a broken branch when the main branch breaks, it should be understood that when Sāriputta attained Parinibbāna, the Saṅgha of monks also became like a tree with a broken branch. "Tasmā" means because all conditioned things are subject to disintegration, it is impossible to obtain the wish "may it not disintegrate."

## 4-5. Commentary on the Ukkacela Sutta, etc.

380-381. In the fourth sutta, "not long after Sāriputta and Moggallāna had attained Parinibbāna" refers to the time shortly after the two Chief Disciples passed away. Indeed, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, attained Parinibbāna on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika, and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained Parinibbāna half a month later on the Uposatha day of the new moon. After the two Chief Disciples had attained Parinibbāna, the Teacher, surrounded by a large Saṅgha of monks, wandered on tour and gradually reached the city of Ukkacela. Having wandered for alms in that city, he stayed on a sandbank by the Ganges, which was as white as a silver plate. Therefore, it is said: "not long after Sāriputta and Moggallāna had attained Parinibbāna." In this context as well, "the larger branches might perish" means the Saṅgha of monks is like a great Jambu tree one hundred leagues in height. The two Chief Disciples are like the two great branches, each fifty leagues long, extending to the south and north of that tree. The remaining meaning should be understood by applying the previous method. In the fifth sutta, "view" (diṭṭhi) refers to the view of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-diṭṭhi).
258:
## 6. Commentary on Uttiya Sutta

In the sixth sutta, 'maccudheyyassa pāraṃ' refers to Nibbāna, which is the further shore of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) occurring in the three realms.

## 8. Commentary on Brahma Sutta

In the eighth sutta, 'kāye vā bhikkhu' is spoken because at that time, as the Dhamma Wheel had not yet been turned, there were no monks as such. Nevertheless, the Buddha spoke thus to show that whoever meditates on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is indeed a monk because of their ability to destroy defilements. 'Ekāyana' means the one-way path (the Path). 'Jātikkhayantadassī' means one who sees Nibbāna, which is the end of birth and the end of the suffering of the cycle. 'Maggaṃ pajānāti' means that one understands the Path, which is the one-way journey known as 'ekāyana,' in its various aspects. The 'ekāyana' path refers to the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) of the path of mindfulness; the meaning is that one understands that path in its various aspects.

## 9. Commentary on Sedaka Sutta

In the ninth sutta, 'sumbhesu' refers to the district of that name. 'Medakathālikā' is a name obtained through the feminine gender. In the phrase 'Protect me, and I will protect you,' this was the teacher's view: if the teacher does not hold the raised bamboo pole well, does not follow the pupil as they move from side to side, and does not watch the tip of the bamboo at all times, he is said not to protect the pupil. A pupil who is not thus protected may fall and be crushed to pieces.
