282:
## 7. Iddhipāda Saṃyutta
## 1. Cāpāla Vagga
## 1. Apāra Sutta Commentary
In the first sutta of the Iddhipāda Saṃyutta, the concentration that occurs depending on desire (the desire to act) is called concentration due to desire (chanda-samādhi). The formations that perform the four functions of right effort are called exertion-formations (padhāna-saṅkhāra). 'Samannāgataṃ' means being endowed with those states (chanda-samādhi and padhāna-saṅkhāra). It is called 'iddhipāda' (basis of power) because it is the foot (basis) of the concentration and exertion-formations associated with wholesome consciousness, which leads to the supreme welfare and happiness of beings, or because it is the basis for the states that will arise above. In the remaining factors like energy-concentration, etc., it should be understood in the same way. This is a summary here; the details should be understood as they appear in the Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga. Its meaning is also explained in the Visuddhimagga. Similarly, in the Magga Saṃyutta, Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta, and Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta, as well as here in the Iddhipāda Saṃyutta, the meaning is explained with the same definition.

## 5. Iddhipadesa Sutta Commentary
In the fifth sutta, 'iddhipadesa' refers to the three paths and the three fruits.

## 6. Samatta Sutta Commentary
In the sixth sutta, 'samatta-iddhi' refers only to the fruit of Arahatship. From the beginning, in all nine suttas, only the bases of power (iddhipāda) that are the foundation for supramundane states (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 10. Cetiya Sutta Commentary
In the tenth sutta, 'nisīdana' refers to a piece of skin (for sitting). 'Udena Cetiya' refers to a monastery built for the Buddha at the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena. In the cases of Gotamaka Cetiya and others, it should be understood in the same way. 'Bhāvitā' means they have been developed. 'Bahulīkatā' means they have been practiced repeatedly. 'Yānīkatā' means they have been made so that they can be directed according to one's will, like a vehicle harnessed with thoroughbred horses. 'Vatthukatā' means they have been made like a foundation for special psychic powers, because of the sense of being a resting place. 'Anuṭṭhitā' means they have been firmly established. 'Paricitā' means they have been well-developed from all sides. 'Susamāraddhā' means they have been very well undertaken.

Having thus spoken without specific limitation (generally), the Buddha spoke the words "Tathāgatassa kho," etc., wishing to show it with specific limitation. Here, 'kappa' refers to the life-span (āyukappa), which at that particular time...
283:
He should remain for the full extent of a human's lifespan. 'Kappāvasesaṃ vā' means he could remain for a little more than the hundred years mentioned, perhaps from one to ten years extra. However, Mahāsīvatthera said: 'For the Buddhas, there is no such thing as speaking of what is impossible. Just as he suppressed the life-threatening pains that arose in Veḷuva village for ten months, so too, by repeatedly entering that attainment and suppressing them for ten months at a time, he could remain for this entire Bhaddakappa.'

As to why he did not remain: the so-called 'clung-to' body (upādinnaka-sarīra) is oppressed by broken teeth, grey hair, and so on. Buddhas, before reaching such states as broken teeth, pass away into parinibbāna in the fifth portion of their life, at a time when they are still beloved and pleasing to the majority of people. Furthermore, after the Great Disciples who followed the Buddha have attained parinibbāna, he would have to remain alone like a tree stump, or surrounded only by young novices. At that time, people might disparage them, saying, 'Oh, look at the Buddha's assembly!' Therefore, he did not remain. Although Mahāsīvatthera said this, it is not preferred; in the Commentary, it is specifically defined only as 'āyukappa' (a full human lifespan).

In the phrase 'yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto', the word 'taṃ' is merely a particle. Just as any other worldling (puthujjana) whose mind is overwhelmed and possessed by Mara would be unable to penetrate [the meaning], so too, it means that the Venerable Ānanda was unable to penetrate it. Mara overwhelms the mind of a worldling who has not yet abandoned all twelve perversions (vipallāsa). In the case of the Venerable Ānanda, because he had not yet abandoned the four perversions, Mara overwhelmed his mind. When Mara overwhelms the mind, what does he do? He either shows a terrifying visual object or causes a terrifying sound to be heard. Then, upon seeing or hearing that object, beings lose their mindfulness and their mouths gape open. Mara then acts as if he is putting his hand into their mouths and squeezing their hearts, causing them to fall into a swoon. Mara was not able to put his hand into the Venerable Ānanda's mouth. Rather, he showed a terrifying object, and upon seeing it, the Elder failed to penetrate the sign and hint (nimitta-obhāsa). Why did the Blessed One, though knowing this, speak up to three times? It was so that later, when [Ānanda] would beg, 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One remain,' the Buddha could say, 'This is your own wrongdoing, this is your own fault,' thereby reducing the Elder's grief through this censure.

In the phrase 'māro pāpimā', he is called 'Māra' because he kills beings by inciting them toward harm. 'Pāpimā' is another name for that same Mara. He is called 'Pāpimā' because he is possessed of evil states (pāpadhamma).
284:
He is called 'the Evil One'. Kaṇha, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu are also names for that same Mara. 'Venerable Sir, you have said this before' refers to the fact that this Mara came to the Bodhi seat in the eighth week after the Blessed One's attainment of Enlightenment and said: 'Venerable Sir, the purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has been attained; that goal is reached. Omniscience has been realized. What is the use of your wandering in the world?' and just as he does today, he begged: 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One now attain parinibbāna; may the Sugata attain parinibbāna.' The Blessed One rejected him, saying, 'Not yet,' and so on. It is in reference to that rejection that [Ānanda] said, 'Venerable Sir, you have said this before,' and so forth.

Among those terms, 'viyattā' means those who are accomplished through the Path. Likewise, 'vinītā' means those who are well-trained. 'Visāradā' means those who are confident. 'Bahussutā' means those who have much learning by way of the Tipiṭaka. 'Dhammadharā' means those who bear those teachings. Alternatively, it should be understood that they are 'dhammadharā' because they bear the teachings of both scriptural learning (pariyatti) and realization (paṭivedha). 'Dhammānudhammapatipannā' means those who practice the Dhamma of insight (vipassanā), which is the secondary Dhamma (anudhamma) of the Noble Dhamma. 'Sāmīcipatipannā' means those who practice the appropriate way. 'Anudhammacārino' means those whose habit is to live in accordance with the Dhamma. 'Sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ' means the doctrine of their own teacher, the Buddha. All terms such as 'ācikkhiyssanti' are merely synonyms of one another. 'Sahadhammena' means with speech that is accompanied by reason and cause. 'Sappāṭihāriyaṃ' means they will teach the Dhamma in a way that leads to liberation (niyyānika).

'Brahmacariyaṃ' means the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) as the holy life, which is comprised of the three trainings. 'Iddhaṃ' means prosperous through the power of the bliss of Jhana. 'Phītaṃ' means flourishing, having reached growth like a sal tree in full bloom, through the power of the attainment of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā). 'Vitthārikaṃ' means widespread, by virtue of being established in various regions. 'Bāhujuññaṃ' means known by many people through the power of their realization of the Four Noble Truths. 'Puthubhūtaṃ' means having reached a state of expansion in every aspect. How? It means it is well-proclaimed even unto devas and humans; as many wise devas and humans as there are, it is well-known by all of them.

'Appossukko' means being without concern or attachment. The Buddha is saying: 'O Evil One, from the eighth week you have been wandering around crying out, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One now attain parinibbāna; may the Sugata attain parinibbāna." From this day forward, be one who has lost his zeal; do not strive any further for my parinibbāna.'
285:
The Blessed One, being mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra). This means that while firmly establishing the fourfold mindfulness in the objects of his own body, feelings, mind, and mental qualities, he determined with his knowledge: 'I have completed my own welfare at the seat of awakening; the instruction of those to be tamed for the welfare of others will be completed within three months. Therefore, on the coming full moon day of Vesākha, I shall attain Nibbāna.' Thus, he relinquished the life-principle, which is the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) that sustains life. In this context, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-principle as if throwing a stone with his hand; rather, he gave rise to the thought: 'I will enter the attainment of fruition only for these three months; thereafter, I will not enter it again.' With reference to this mental determination, it is said 'ossaji' (relinquished). There is also a reading 'ussaji'.

'Mahābhūmicālo' refers to a great earthquake. At that time, it is said that the ten thousand world systems trembled. 'Bhiṃsanako' means causing terror. 'Devadundubhiyo ca phaliṃsu' means that the celestial drums resounded, thunder roared, unseasonable flashes of lightning appeared, and there was a sudden shower of rain.

Why did he make this inspired utterance (udāna)? Someone might say: 'The Blessed One relinquished the life-principle out of fear, being harassed by Māra who followed him and urged, "Venerable Sir, attain Parinibbāna; Venerable Sir, attain Parinibbāna."' To prevent such an opportunity for saying so, he made the inspired utterance. For one who is afraid, there is no such thing as an inspired utterance. Therefore, he made the inspired utterance due to the surge of joy (pīti) that arose from the thought: 'I shall soon lay down this great burden of suffering, this self-identity, which I have carried for a long time.'

The meaning of that verse is as follows: 'Tula' (measurable) refers to kāmāvacara-kamma (karma of the sensual sphere) because it is perceptible even to dogs, jackals, and the like. 'Atula' (immeasurable) refers to mahaggata-kamma (sublime karma) because there is no other mundane karma equal to it. Alternatively, kāmāvacara and rūpāvacara karma are called 'tula', while arūpāvacara karma is called 'atula'. Karma with small results is 'tula', and karma with great results is 'atula'. 'Sambhava' means the mass or heap that is the cause of arising. 'Bhavasaṅkhāra' is the karma that constructs a new existence. 'Avassaji' means he relinquished. 'Muni' refers to the Buddha-sage. 'Ajjhattarato' means constantly delighting in the internal states within his own continuity through the power of insight (vipassanā). 'Samāhito' means having a mind well-concentrated through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi). 'Abhindi kavacamiva' means he broke it as a great warrior breaks his armor. 'Attasambhavaṃ' refers to the defilements (kilesa) born within himself.

The intended meaning is: He relinquished the mundane karma known as 'tula' and 'atula', called 'sambhava' in the sense of yielding results and 'bhavasaṅkhāra' in the sense of constructing existence. Like a great warrior on the battlefield breaking his armor, he, delighting in internal states and being concentrated, broke the defilements born within himself.

Alternatively, 'tulaṃ' means weighing or investigating. 'Atulañca sambhavaṃ' refers to the incomparable Nibbāna and the three spheres of existence. 'Bhavasaṅkhāraṃ' refers to the karma that leads to existence. 'Avassaji muni' means that while weighing with wisdom, such as 'The five aggregates are impermanent, but Nibbāna, the cessation of the aggregates, is the permanent reality,' the Buddha-sage, seeing the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna, relinquished the life-formative karma which is the root of those aggregates, through the Noble Path (ariya magga) that brings about the destruction of karma. How did he relinquish it? Being delighted in internal states and concentrated, he broke the defilements born within himself as a warrior breaks his armor. Thus, the Blessed One, through the power of insight...
286:
"Nibbāna, the cessation of the five aggregates, is permanent." Weighing in this manner, the Great Sage (Mahāmuni), the All-Knowing Buddha, seeing the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna, relinquished the life-formative karma (bhavasaṅkhāra) which is the root of those aggregates, through the Noble Path (ariya magga) which is said to "lead to the destruction of karma." How did he relinquish it? Being constantly delighted in the internal states within his own continuity through the power of insight (vipassanā), and being concentrated, he broke the defilements born within himself as a warrior breaks his armor. That Blessed One, through the power of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) from the preliminary stage onwards—delighting in the internal through insight and being concentrated through tranquility—broke the entire mass of defilements known as 'attasambhava' because they arise within oneself, which stood like armor enveloping the self-identity (attabhāva). Because of the absence of defilements, karma no longer leads to rebirth and is thus said to be relinquished; in this way, he abandoned karma by abandoning the defilements. For one who has abandoned defilements, there is no such thing as fear. Therefore, he relinquished the life-principle without any fear. It should be understood that he made the inspired utterance to make known his state of fearlessness.

## End of the First Chapter, the Cāpāla Vagga.

## 2. Pāsādakampana Vagga

## 1-2. Commentary on the Pubba Sutta, etc.

823-824. In the first sutta of the second chapter, the terms such as "na ca atilīno" (not too slack) will become clear later. In this sutta, the bases of power (iddhipāda) which are the foundation for the six higher knowledges (abhiññā) are taught; likewise in the second sutta.

## 3. Commentary on the Chandasamādhi Sutta

In the third sutta, "chanda" refers to the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda). "Nissāya" means depending on, or making predominant. "Padhānasaṅkhāra" refers to the volitional formations of striving, which is a designation for the right exertion (sammappadhāna-vīriya) that accomplishes the four tasks. Thus, in the passages beginning with "this desire also," desire is endowed with the concentration of desire and the volitional formations of striving; the concentration of desire is endowed with desire and the volitional formations of striving; and the volitional formations of striving are also endowed with desire and the concentration of desire. Therefore, taking all those states together, it is said: "Monks, this is called the base of power endowed with the concentration of desire and the volitional formations of striving." In the Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga, however, the remaining mental states endowed with this concentration and energy are taught as the base of power in the manner beginning with: "Whatever aggregate of feeling there is for one who has become thus..."
287:
In this way, the remaining mental phenomena (nāma-dhamma) endowed with these states are called Iddhipādas (Bases of Power). Alternatively, these three states are both Iddhi and Iddhipāda. How? For one who develops desire (chanda), desire is called Iddhi, while concentration and striving-formations (padhāna-saṅkhāra) are called Chandiddhipāda. For one who develops concentration (samādhi), concentration is called Iddhi, while desire and striving-formations are called the base (pāda) of Samādhiddhi. For one who develops striving-formations, striving-formations are called Iddhi, while desire and concentration are called the base of Padhānasaṅkhāriddhi. This is because when one of the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) succeeds, the remaining states also succeed.

Alternatively, the nature of these states as Iddhipādas should also be understood by way of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) of those respective states. The first jhāna is called Iddhi; the states such as desire associated with the preliminary preparation (parikamma) of the first jhāna are called Iddhipāda. In this manner, the method should be applied up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), from the direct knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-abhiññā) up to the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), and from the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) up to the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga). The same method applies to the remaining Iddhipādas.

However, some teachers say, "Unrisen desire is called Iddhipāda." To refute their view, the section called Uttara-cūḷavāra appears in the Abhidhamma: "There are four Iddhipādas: Chandiddhipāda, Viriyiddhipāda, Cittiddhipāda, and Vīmaṃsiddhipāda. Therein, what is Chandiddhipāda? Here, a monk, at a time when he develops supramundane jhāna which is leading out (niyyānika), leading to the diminution of rebirth, for the abandoning of wrong views and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures... [pe]... enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is of painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge. At that time, whatever desire, state of desiring, will to act, or faultless desire for the Dhamma (dhamma-chanda) there is—this is called Chandiddhipāda. The remaining states are those associated with Chandiddhipāda" (Vibhaṅga 457-458). These states are mentioned only by way of the supramundane (lokuttara).

Among those four, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla brought about the supramundane state by making desire (chanda) the chief. The Elder Soṇa did so by making energy (viriya) the chief; the Elder Sambhuta by making the mind (citta) the chief; and the Venerable Mogharāja by making investigation (vīmaṃsā/wisdom) the chief. Among those four persons, for example, among four sons of ministers...
288:
...among the sons of ministers who lived depending on the king, desiring a position of rank, one son, having a strong desire for service and knowing the king's intent and preference, served day and night, pleased the king, and attained the rank. Thus should one be known who brings about supramundane states by making desire the chief.

Another son, however, thought, "I cannot serve every single day; I will please the king with effort only when a task arises." When a rebellion broke out in the border regions, he was sent by the king and, through great effort, suppressed the enemy and attained the rank. Like him, one who brings about supramundane states by making energy (viriya) the chief should be understood. Another son thought, "Serving every day or receiving spears and arrows with my chest is a great burden; I will please the king only through the power of counsel." Being well-versed in the science of statecraft (khatta-vijjā), he pleased the king through the arrangement of counsel and attained the rank. Like him, one who brings about supramundane states by making the mind (citta) the chief should be understood.

Another son thought, "What is the use of such service and so on? Kings usually give rank to those of noble birth; if he gives to such a person, he will give to me too." Relying only on his noble birth, he attained the rank. Like him, one who brings about supramundane states by making investigation (vīmaṃsā) the chief, relying on extremely pure wisdom, should be understood. In this sutta, Iddhi as the basis for the ending of the cycle (vivaṭṭa/Nirvana) is described.

## 4. Moggalāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "uddhata" means those of a restless nature, with a wavering mind. Due to restlessness (uddhacca), the mind wavers on a single object like a banner struck by the wind. "Unnaḷa" means those with raised reeds, meaning those with arisen empty pride. "Capala" means those endowed with the frivolity of decorating the bowl and robes, etc. "Mukhara" means harsh-mouthed, meaning those with harsh speech. "Vikiṇṇavācā" means those with unrestrained speech, who habitually speak useless and idle chatter all day long. "Muṭṭhassati" means those who have lost mindfulness. "Asampajāna" means those devoid of wisdom. "Asamāhita" means those devoid of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and fixed concentration (appanā-samādhi). "Bhantacitta" means those with a mind that has wavered and risen upward due to restlessness, which has found an opportunity because of the absence of concentration. "Pākatindriya" means those with unrestrained faculties. "Iddhābhisaṅkhāra" refers to entering the water-kasina attainment, and after emerging, resolving the portion of the ground where the palace stood to be "water," then flying up into the sky to the palace standing on the water and striking it with the big toe. "Gambhīranemo" means having a deep pit, or having a depth that has entered into the deep part of the ground.
289:
The meaning is: *Sunikhāta* means well-planted, well-established by pounding. In this fourth sutta, the psychic power (*iddhi*) that serves as the basis for higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) is discussed.

## 5. Uṇṇābhabrāhmaṇa Sutta Commentary
In the fifth sutta, *chandappahānattha* means for the purpose of abandoning the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*). In this sutta as well, the psychic power that serves as the basis for liberation (*vivaṭṭa*) is discussed.

## 9. Iddhādidesanā Sutta Commentary
In the ninth sutta, by the words "Monks, whatever path," the fourth jhana (*catutthajjhāna*) which is the basis for higher knowledge is intended.

## 10. Vibhaṅga Sutta Commentary
In the tenth sutta, *kosajjasahagata* means: in this Dispensation, a monk arouses desire and sits down, applying his mind to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). While doing so, a state of sluggishness (*līnākāra*) enters his mind. That monk, realizing "A state of sluggishness has entered me," threatens his mind with the fear of the lower realms (*apāyabhaya*), arouses desire again, and applies his mind to the meditation subject. While doing so, the state of sluggishness enters him again. He again threatens his mind with the fear of the lower realms, arouses desire, and applies his mind to the meditation subject. Thus, because it is mixed with laziness (*kosajja*), his desire is called *kosajjasahagata* (desire accompanied by laziness). *Kosajjasampayutta* is simply a synonym for that *kosajjasahagata*.

*Uddhaccasahagata* means: in this Dispensation, a monk arouses desire and sits down, applying his mind to the meditation subject. While doing so, his mind falls into restlessness (*uddhacca*). That monk, reflecting on the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, gladdens and satisfies his mind, making it fit for work, and then arouses desire again and applies his mind to the meditation subject. While doing so, his mind falls into restlessness again. He again reflects on the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, gladdens and satisfies his mind, making it fit for work, arouses desire, and applies his mind to the meditation subject. Thus, because it is mixed with restlessness, his desire is called *uddhaccasahagata* (desire accompanied by restlessness).

*Thinamiddhasahagata* means: in this Dispensation, a monk arouses desire and sits down, applying his mind to the meditation subject. While doing so, sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) arise in him. That monk, realizing "Sloth and torpor have arisen in me," wipes his face with water, pulls his ears, recites the Dhamma he has mastered, or applies his mind to the perception of light (*ālokasaññā*) acquired during the day, and [dispels] the sloth and torpor...
290:
...having dispelled (sloth and torpor), he arouses desire again and applies his mind to the meditation subject. While doing so, sloth and torpor arise in him again. In the same manner as mentioned, he dispels the sloth and torpor again, arouses desire, and applies his mind to the meditation subject. Thus, because it is mixed with sloth and torpor, the desire is called *thinamiddhasahagata* (accompanied by sloth and torpor).

*Anuvikkhitta* means: in this Dispensation, a monk arouses desire and sits down, applying his mind to the meditation subject. Then, his mind becomes distracted by the objects of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇārammaṇa*). That monk, realizing "My mind is distracted externally," reflects on the Anamatagga Sutta, Devadūta Sutta, Celopama Sutta, Anāgatabhaya Sutta, and so on. Threatening and disciplining his mind with the "staff of the Suttas" (*suttadaṇḍa*), he makes it fit for meditation, arouses desire again, and applies his mind to the meditation subject. Even when he applies his mind thus, the mind becomes distracted again. He again makes the mind fit for the work of meditation with the staff of the Suttas, arouses desire, and applies his mind to the meditation subject. Thus, because it is mixed with sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*), the desire is repeatedly distracted (*anuvikkhitta*) and repeatedly scattered (*anuvisaṭa*) regarding the five external objects of sensual pleasure.

In the phrase "*yathā pure tathā pacchā*" (as before, so after), the sequence of before and after should be understood both by way of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and by way of the teaching (*desanā*). How? In the meditation subject, the initial application to the meditation subject is called "before" (*pure*), and the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala*) is called "after" (*pacchā*). Between these two, a monk who applies himself to the primary meditation subject, preventing the mind from falling into the four states called overly sluggish (*atilīna*), overly exerted (*atipaggahita*), internally constricted (*ajjhattasaṃkhitta*), and externally distracted (*bahiddhāvikkhitta*), like a wagon-driver yoking and driving a wild ox, or like setting down a square cake-mold, without clinging to even one of the four states, contemplates the formations (*saṅkhāra*) and reaches the fruit of Arahantship. This monk is said to dwell "as before, so after." This is the sequence of before and after by way of the meditation subject.

By way of the teaching, the hair of the head is called "before," and the brain is called "after." There, a monk who applies himself to the hair of the head, grasping the hair and so on by way of color, shape, etc., without clinging to the four states, brings the meditation to the point of the brain. This monk is also said to dwell "as before, so after." Thus, the sequence of before and after by way of the teaching should be understood. The phrase "*yathā pacchā tathā pure*" is just a synonym for the previous statement.

In the phrase "*yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ*" (as below, so above), this should be understood by way of the body. Therefore, it is said: "From the soles of the feet upwards, from the hair of the head downwards." In that body, a monk, from the soles of the feet up to the hair of the head, by way of the thirty-two parts (*dvattiṃsākāra*), or from the tips of the toe-joints up to the skull, and from the skull down to the [toes]...
291:
Starting from the skull down to the joints of the toe bones, one achieves meditation through the power of the bones, without clinging to any of the four states such as being too withdrawn (*atilina*) or too over-exerted (*atipaggahita*). This monk is said to dwell contemplating above just as he does below, and below just as he does above.

"By whatever modes" means by whatever parts (*koṭṭhāsa*). "By whatever signs" means by whatever shapes (*saṇṭhāna*). "By whatever marks" means by whatever appearing signs (*nimitta*). "The perception of light is well-grasped" means that a monk, sitting in the open, directs his mind to the perception of light, sometimes closing his eyes and sometimes opening them. As he closes and opens them, when it appears to him exactly the same when his eyes are closed as when they are open and looking, then the perception of light (*āloka-saññā*) is said to have arisen. "Perception of day" (*divā-saññā*) is also a name for that same perception of light. If that perception of light arises during the night, it is said to be well-grasped. "Well-established" (*svādhiṭṭhita*) is also a synonym for it. Because it is well-established and well-placed, it is called "well-established." In essence, it is simply well-grasped. 

Alternatively, when a monk dispels sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*) through light, arouses desire (*chanda*), and directs his mind to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), for him, the perception of light is said to be well-grasped and well-established even during the day. Whether it be night or day, the perception that arises in that light which dispels sloth and torpor while directing the mind to the meditation subject is indeed called well-grasped. The same method applies to energy (*vīriya*) and so on. In this sutta, the psychic power (*iddhi*) which is the basis for the six supernormal knowledges (*abhiññā*) is taught.

## II. Pāsādakampana Vagga

## 3. Ayoguḷa Vagga

## 2. Ayoguḷasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta of the third chapter, "with this body consisting of the four great elements" means even though it is this heavy and burdensome body made of the four great elements. "Omāti" means he is able or capable; this is an uncompounded word in the Buddha's teachings of the Tipiṭaka. "He merges the body into the mind" means he takes the body and places it upon the mind, making it dependent on the mind, and directs it with a speed similar to the movement of the mind. "Mind" here refers to the exalted mind (*mahaggata-citta*); its movement is swift. "He merges the mind into the body" means he takes the mind and places it upon the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*), making it dependent on the physical body, and directs it with the movement of the body. "Body" here refers to the physical body (*karaja-kāya*); its movement is slow. In the passage "perception of bliss and perception of lightness," one should understand the perception associated with the mind of supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā-citta*). To explain this: that perception associated with the mind of supernormal knowledge is called "perception of bliss" (*sukha-saññā*) because it is endowed with peaceful bliss. It is called "perception of lightness" (*lahu-saññā*) because it lacks the sluggishness caused by defilements.
292:
He takes (the mind) and places it upon the physical body, making it dependent on the physical body, and directs it with the movement of the body. "Body" (*kāya*) refers to the physical body (*karaja-kāya*). Movement by the body's motion is very slow. "Perception of bliss" and "perception of lightness" refer to the perception co-arising with the mind of supernormal knowledge. That perception is called "perception of bliss" because it is endowed with peaceful happiness. It is called "perception of lightness" because it lacks the sluggishness caused by defilements.

An iron ball (*ayoguḷa*) heated all day long is very light. Even if that iron ball was lifted by two or three people and placed in a smithy's furnace, as it is heated all day, it becomes filled with the fire element (*tejo*) and air element (*vāyo*) entering through its pores, and thus becomes very light, accompanied by heat, air, and fire. Just as a blacksmith can grasp it with large tongs and turn it over, lift it, or take it outside, it also becomes soft and workable for whatever one wishes to do. The blacksmith can cut that iron ball into pieces, or by striking it with a hammer, make it into various shapes like long or rectangular forms. In this sutta, the power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) is taught.

## 3-10. Bhikkhusutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā

835-842. In the third sutta, the power based on openness (*viwaṭṭapādakiddhi*) is taught; likewise in the fourth. Furthermore, starting from the suttas such as "Dve phalāni," the mixed bases of power (*missakiddhipāda*) are taught below. In the seven Phala suttas, the preliminary bases of power (*pubbebhāga iddhipāda*) are taught. The four suttas starting from the seventh are just as taught below.

## 11-12. Moggallānasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā

843-844. In the eleventh and twelfth suttas, the six supernormal knowledges (*abhiññā*) are taught. The remaining words in all places have clear meanings.

## End of the Iddhipādasamyutta-vaṇṇanā.

## 8. Anuruddha Saṃyutta

## 1. Rahogata Vagga

## 1-2. Pathamarahogatasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā

899-900. In the first sutta of the Anuruddha Saṃyutta, "āraddhā" means completely fulfilled. Briefly, in this sutta, insight (*vipassanā*) leading to Arahantship in thirty-six instances is taught. In the second sutta, insight leading to Arahantship in twelve instances is taught.

## 3. Sutanusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "mahābhiññatā" means the state of possessing the six supernormal knowledges. In the passages starting with "hīnaṃ dhammaṃ," the meaning should be understood according to the following Pali text:

"Which states are inferior (*hīna*)? The twelve unwholesome thought-arisings (*akusala cittuppāda*); these states are inferior. Which states are middling (*majjhima*)? Wholesome states (*kusala*) in the three planes, resultant states (*vipāka*) in the three planes, functional indeterminate states (*kiriya-abyākata*) in the three planes, and all matter (*rūpa*); these states are middling. Which states are superior (*paṇīta*)? The four paths (*magga*) which are supramundane (*apariyāpanna*), the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*), and Nibbāna; these states are superior" (as found in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī).

## 4-7. Pathamakaṇḍakīsutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā

902-905. In the fourth sutta, "Kaṇḍakīvane" refers to the Mahākaramanda grove. In the sixth sutta, the phrase "a thousand worlds" (*sahassaṃ lokaṃ*) shows the Elder's constant dwelling (*vihāra*). For the Elder, after washing his face early in the morning, recollects a thousand aeons in the past and future with the knowledge of past lives. As for the present, ten thousand world-systems come into the range of his advertence in a single thought. The seventh sutta has a clear meaning.

## 8. Salaḷāgārasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "Salaḷāgāre" refers to a leaf-hut made of Salaḷa (pine/cedar) wood, or a dwelling named as such because it stood near a Salaḷa tree. In this sutta, the practitioner of insight (*vipassaka*) is taught along with insight (*vipassanā*).

## 9. Commentary on Ambapālivana Sutta
In the ninth sutta, "āsabhiṃ vācaṃ" refers to noble words that manifest one's own state of the fruit of Arahantship. The remaining words have clear meanings in all places.

## End of the first part of Rahogata Vagga.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Vagga
909-922. In the second vagga, through the Pali passages beginning with "ṭhānañca ṭhānato," the Elder Anuruddha claims the Ten Powers of Knowledge (Dasabalañāṇa). If it is asked, "Do these Ten Powers of Knowledge belong to the disciples (sāvakas)?", they do arise for the disciples partially, according to their respective aspirations. For the Omniscient Buddhas, however, those Ten Powers of Knowledge are without remainder and are complete in every aspect because they have an infinite range of objects.

## End of the Commentary on Anuruddha Saṃyutta.

The meaning of the Jhāna Saṃyutta is clear throughout.
