## 10. Ānāpāna Saṃyutta
## 1. Ekadhamma Vagga
## 1. Commentary on Ekadhamma Sutta

In the first sutta of the Ānāpāna Saṃyutta, "ekadhammo" means a single state. Everything that should be said in this sutta has already been stated in every aspect in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), in the section on the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (Ānāpānasati-kammaṭṭhāna-niddesa).

## 6. Commentary on Ariṭṭha Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "bhāvetha no" is a question meaning "do you develop?". "Kāmacchando" is the lust that arises in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā ca dhammesu" refers to the twelve internal and external sense bases (āyatanas). "Paṭighasaññā suppaṭivinītā" means that the perception associated with aversion is well-removed and completely cut off by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga). By this statement, he speaks of his own Path of Non-returning. Now, wishing to show the insight (vipassanā) of the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga), he spoke the words beginning with "he, being mindful, breathes out."

## 7. Commentary on Mahākappina Sutta

In the seventh sutta, by both terms "iñjitattaṃ vā phanditattaṃ vā," only movement (shaking) is spoken of.

## 8. Commentary on Padīpopama Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "the body is not fatigued, nor are the eyes distressed" means that for one who practices other meditation subjects, the body becomes fatigued and the eyes become distressed. For one who practices the meditation on the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna), the body becomes fatigued, as if it were put into a machine and squeezed. For one who practices kasiṇa meditation (kasiṇa-kammaṭṭhāna), the eyes throb and become fatigued, as if they were about to bulge out and fall. However, for one who practices this meditation of mindfulness of breathing, the body is not fatigued, nor are the eyes distressed. Therefore, he spoke in this way.
296:
Why was the passage beginning with "sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" (with the total transcending of perceptions of form) spoken? Is the removal of the kasiṇa sign (kasiṇuugghāṭana) obtainable in the meditation on mindfulness of breathing? The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: "Because the sign of mindfulness of breathing appears like a cluster of stars or a string of pearls, the removal of the kasiṇa sign is obtainable in that meditation." The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, however, said: "It is certainly not obtainable."

If it is not obtainable, why is this classification beginning with Noble psychic powers (Ariyan iddhi) mentioned? It is mentioned to show the benefits (ānisaṃsa). A monk who desires the Noble psychic power, or the four fine-material sphere jhanas, or the four immaterial attainments, or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), should carefully attend to this concentration of mindfulness of breathing. For example, when a city is captured, the revenues arising from the four directions enter the city only through the four gates; thus, the countryside is also captured. This is just a benefit of the city. Similarly, this classification beginning with Noble psychic power is a benefit of the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing. It was spoken to show the benefits, meaning that if the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is developed in every aspect, all these benefits will be accomplished for the yogi monk. In this passage "sukhañca," why is the word "so" (he) not spoken? Because the word "bhikkhū" (monks) does not appear in this particular section, the word "so" is not spoken.

## 9. Commentary on Vesālī Sutta
In the ninth sutta, the Vesālī Sutta, "Vesāliyaṃ" means in the city of that name, which is a term used in the feminine gender. That city is called "Vesālī" because it became wide and extensive (visālī-bhūta) by the expansion of its enclosure walls three times. It should be understood that this city of Vesālī reached its full prosperity in every aspect only when the Fully Enlightened One attained Omniscience. After showing the resort village for alms, he mentioned the dwelling place as "Mahāvane Kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ."

In that text, "Mahāvana" refers to a large, natural forest that was not planted by humans and has a defined boundary. However, the Mahāvana near Kapilavatthu is continuous with the Himalayas, without a boundary, and extends as far as the Great Ocean. This Mahāvana near Vesālī is not like that; it is called Mahāvana because it is a large forest with a defined boundary. The "Kūṭāgārasālā" (Gabled Hall) should be understood as the Fragrant Cell (Gandhakuṭī) of the Blessed Buddha, which was complete in every aspect, built with a roof shaped like a swan's curve, containing a gabled house within a monastery built depending on the Mahāvana forest.

"Anekapariyāyena asubhakathaṃ katheti" means he preaches a discourse that causes revulsion toward the body, which proceeds by showing the nature of foulness through many reasons. As follows:
297:
In this body, there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth... urine. What is meant by this? Monks, even if one searches throughout this fathom-long body in every way, one does not see even a tiny bit of purity like pearls, rubies, lapis lazuli, aloe wood, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, or scented powder. Instead, one sees only various kinds of impurity—foul-smelling, loathsome, and devoid of beauty—such as head hairs, body hairs, and so forth. Therefore, one should not develop desire or lust (chanda or rāga) for this body. Even the head hairs grown on the head, the highest part of the body, are unattractive, impure, and repulsive. Their unattractiveness, impurity, and repulsiveness should be understood in five ways: by color, shape, odor, origin (āsaya), and location (okāsa). The same applies to body hairs and the rest. This is a summary; the details should be understood as stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, the Blessed One teaches the discourse on impurity (asubha) in various ways, categorized into fivefold divisions for each part (koṭṭhāsa).

"He speaks in praise of impurity" means that, having set forth the matrix of impurity (asubha-mātikā) by way of the bloated corpse (uddhūmātaka) and so forth, he explains and praises it through the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya). "He speaks in praise of the meditation on impurity" means that he praises the virtues and shows the benefits of the meditation (bhāvanā)—the development and increase of the mind that takes up the aspect of impurity in the thirty-two parts such as head hairs, or in the ten types of impurity such as the bloated corpse, whether internally or externally. To illustrate: "Monks, a monk devoted to the meditation on impurity, whether in objects such as head hairs or in impurities such as the bloated corpse, attains the first jhāna, which is rid of five factors, possessed of five factors, beautiful in three ways, and endowed with ten characteristics. Relying on that casket of the mind (cittamañjūsā) known as the first jhāna, he develops insight (vipassanā) and reaches the supreme goal, Arahantship."

"Monks, I wish to go into retreat for half a month" means "Monks, I wish to live alone, in seclusion, for one half-month." "No one should approach me, except for the one who brings alms-food" means that, excluding the one monk who brings and offers the alms-food prepared by faithful families for the Buddha without engaging in speech himself, no other person—whether a monk or a layperson—should approach the Blessed One.
298:
Why did he speak thus? It is said that in the distant past, five hundred hunters surrounded a forest with large nets and so forth, and joyfully made their living by killing animals and birds throughout their lives, subsequently being reborn in hell. After suffering there, they were reborn among humans due to some past wholesome kamma. Because of their good supporting conditions (upanissaya), they all received the going-forth (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of the Blessed One. Due to that original unwholesome kamma, their unripened volitions (aparāparacetanā) provided the opportunity for the termination of their life-faculty within that half-month, either through their own effort or the effort of others. The Blessed One saw this. Indeed, the result of kamma (kamma-vipāka) cannot be averted by anyone. Among those monks, there were worldlings (puthujjana), as well as Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, and Arahants. Among them, the Arahants would not undergo rebirth; the other noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) had a certain destiny and were bound for a happy state; however, the destiny of the worldlings was not yet certain.

Then the Blessed One thought: "These worldling monks, being afraid of death due to desire and lust for their bodies, will not be able to purify their destiny. Let me teach them the discourse on impurity (asubha) to abandon their desire and lust. Having heard that, they will be free from desire and lust for the body, purify their destiny, and be reborn in the heavenly realm. In this way, their going-forth in my presence will be fruitful." Then, out of compassion for those monks, he taught the discourse on impurity as a meditation subject, not with the intention of praising death. After teaching the Dhamma, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "If the monks come to see me during this half-month, they will come and report, 'Today one monk has died, today two... today ten monks have died.' This result of kamma cannot be averted by me or by anyone else. Even if I hear those words, what can I do? What benefit is there for me in hearing news of such useless destruction? I shall go and stay where the monks cannot see me." Therefore, he said: "Monks, I wish to go into retreat for half a month. No one should approach me, except for the one who brings alms-food."

Other teachers, however, say that he spoke thus and went into retreat to avoid the blame of others. It is said that others might criticize the Blessed One, saying: "This person claims, 'I am the All-knowing One, the one who turns the wheel of the excellent True Dhamma,' yet he is unable to prevent even his own disciples from killing one another; how can he prevent others?" When such criticism arises, the wise will say: "The Blessed One is devoted to retreat and does not know of this occurrence; there is no one to report it to him."
299:
"There is none; if he knew, he would certainly prevent it," they say. However, this statement is merely a wish; the reason mentioned earlier is the only appropriate one. In the term "nāssudhā," "assudhā" is a particle used either for completing the verse or for emphasis; it means that no one approached the Blessed One.

It is called "anekākāravokāra" because it is mixed with many causes such as various colors and shapes. It means it is mixed with many aspects. What is that? It is the practice of the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā); they dwell engaged in that meditation on foulness which is mixed with many aspects. "Yuttappayuttā viharanti" means they dwell being intensely devoted. "Aṭṭīyamānā" means they are oppressed and suffering because of that body. "Harāyamānā" means they are ashamed. "Jigucchamānā" means they are disgusted. "Satthahārakaṃ pariyesanti" means they seek one who brings a weapon to take their lives. Not only do those monks seek a weapon and take their own lives themselves, but they also approach Migalaṇḍika, a sham ascetic, and say, "Good sir, please deprive us of life." In this matter, the Noble Ones (ariyas) did not commit the act of taking life themselves, nor did they incite others, nor did they approve of it. Worldlings (puthujjanas), however, did all of those things.

"Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" means that knowing those five hundred monks had reached the end of their lives, He arose from that solitary seclusion. Even though He knew, He addressed the Venerable Ānanda as if He did not know, in order to start a conversation: "Ānanda, why does the community of monks (bhikkhu-saṅgha) appear so diminished?" "Ānanda, before this time, many monks used to come together to attend [on Me], to learn the Pali and the Commentaries, and to recite them; the monastery appeared bright as if a single lamp were lit. But now, after the lapse of half a month, the community of monks has become diminished, sparse, and thin. What is the reason? Have the monks departed to various directions?"

Then, the Venerable Ānanda, not realizing that those monks had reached the end of their lives due to the result of their past kamma (kamma-vipāka), but noting only that it was because of their devotion to the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna), said, "It is so, Bhante, Blessed One," and so forth. Wishing to request another meditation subject for the monks to attain Arahantship, he said, "It is well, Bhante, Blessed One," and so forth. The meaning is: "Bhante, may the Blessed One teach another means by which the community of monks may [be established] in Arahantship..."
300:
...may be established in Arahantship. Just as there are many landing places for descending into the Great Ocean, there are many meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) for descending into Nibbāna, such as the ten recollections (anussati), the ten kasiṇas, the analysis of the four elements (dhātu-vavatthāna), the four sublime abodes (brahmavihāra), and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). Among those meditation subjects, may the Blessed One teach one that will bring relief to the monks," this is the intended meaning. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to do as the Venerable Ānanda requested and to encourage the Elder, said, "In that case, Ānanda," and so forth. In those words, "depending on Vesālī" means to assemble all the monks who dwell in the vicinity of Vesālī, within a distance of a gāvuta or half a league (yojana). "Having assembled them all in the assembly hall (upaṭṭhāna-sālā)" means He Himself went to the places where it was appropriate for Him to go, and sent young monks to other places, thus gathering all the monks without exception in the assembly hall in a single moment. In the words, "Bhante, the Blessed One now knows it is the time," the meaning is: "Bhante, the community of monks has assembled. This is the time to give a Dhamma talk and instruction to the monks. Now, whatever time the Blessed One deems appropriate, please give that Dhamma talk and instruction."

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-samādhi) also..." After addressing them, wishing to teach another method besides the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) previously taught for the monks to attain Arahantship, He said, "ānāpānasati-samādhi," and so forth. In those words, "ānāpānasati-samādhi" means concentration associated with mindfulness that grasps the out-breaths and in-breaths, or concentration occurring in the mindfulness of breathing. "Developed" (bhāvito) means produced or increased. "Cultivated" (bahulīkato) means done repeatedly. "It is both peaceful and sublime" means it is indeed peaceful and indeed sublime. In both terms, the word "eva" (indeed/only) should be understood as emphasizing the certainty. What is the meaning intended? This concentration through mindfulness of breathing is not like the meditation on foulness. The meditation on foulness is peaceful and sublime only by way of penetration (paṭivedha); however, because its object is gross and repulsive, it is neither peaceful nor sublime by way of the object. But this concentration through mindfulness of breathing is not unpeaceful or non-sublime by any means. Rather, it is peaceful, tranquil, and cooled because the object is peaceful; it is also peaceful because of the peacefulness of the factors known as penetration. It is sublime because the object is sublime, being something that one can never have enough of (extremely sublime), and it is also sublime because of the sublimity of the factors. Therefore, it is said, "It is both peaceful and sublime."
301:
In the phrase "asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro" (an unadulterated and pleasant dwelling), it is called "asecanaka" (pure by nature without being mixed with other things) because there is no other cause to be poured or added to bring about the peaceful and sublime state of this concentration on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati samādhi). It is a type of pleasant dwelling that is distinct and unassociated with other preliminary works (parikamma) or access concentration (upacāra). This means that in this mindfulness of breathing, there is no tranquility achieved through preliminary work or access concentration; rather, it is peaceful and sublime by its own nature from the very first moment of attention. Some teachers say that "asecanaka" means a state that is naturally nutritious and sweet without needing anything else to be poured into it. Thus, this concentration on mindfulness of breathing is unadulterated and pure, and it should be understood as a pleasant dwelling (sukhavihāra) because it brings about physical and mental happiness at every moment of attainment.

"Uppannuppanna" means those that have arisen and are not yet suppressed. "Pāpaka" means evil. "Akusala dhamma" refers to states born of a lack of wisdom. "Ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti" means to make them disappear or be removed instantly. "Vūpasameti" means to calm them well. It means that because it has the quality of leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), it gradually reaches the development of the Noble Path, cutting them off entirely and calming them (paṭippassambheti).

"Gimhānaṃ pacchime māse" refers to the month of Āsāḷha. "Ūhataṃ rajojallaṃ" refers to the dust and particles rising into the sky from the earth, which has been dried by the sun and wind for eight months and broken up by the trampling of cattle and buffaloes. "Mahā akālamegho" refers to a great rain that covers the entire sky and falls for a month and a half during the bright fortnight of Āsāḷha. Since this rain falls before the arrival of the rainy season, it is intended here as an "out-of-season cloud" (akālamegha). Just as that rain makes the dust settle peacefully on the ground so that it disappears instantly, this concentration on mindfulness of breathing removes and calms unwholesome states; this is shown by way of a simile. The words mentioned thereafter are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

## 10. Kimilasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, the Kimila Sutta, "Kimilāyaṃ" means in the town of that name. Regarding "etadavoca", it is said that the Elder Kimila thought, "This teaching is not yet connected to its sequence; I will make it reach its sequence." Desiring to join the sequence of the teaching, he spoke these words. "Kāyaññataraṃ" refers to the wind-body (vāyokāya), which is one among the bodies such as the earth-body. Alternatively, among the twenty-five groups of matter (rūpakāya) starting from the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and ending with nutriment (kabaḷīkāra āhāra), mindfulness of breathing...
302:
...is one of the bodies (kāyaññataraṃ) because it is included in the tangible-base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana); therefore, it was said thus. "Tasmātiha" means that because one repeatedly contemplates the wind-body, which is one among the four groups, or repeatedly contemplates mindfulness of breathing, which is one among the twenty-five groups of matter (rūpakāya), one is therefore called "a contemplator of the body in the body" (kāye kāyānupassī). In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places. "Vedanāññataraṃ" is said with reference to pleasant feeling (sukha vedanā), which is one among the three feelings.

"Sādhukaṃ manasikāraṃ" refers to the excellent attention that arises by way of experiencing rapture and so on. If it is asked, "Is attention a pleasant feeling?", the answer is no. However, this is the "head" (chief) of the teaching. Just as in the passage "aniccasaññābhāvanānuyogamanuyutta" (engaged in the development of the perception of impermanence), wisdom (paññā) is spoken of by the name of perception (saññā), so too here, the feeling associated with jhāna is spoken of by the name of attention (manasikāra). In the first phrase of this tetrad, feeling is spoken of with rapture (pīti) as the head; in the second phrase, feeling is spoken of by its own form as "sukhaṃ" (pleasure). In the two phrases regarding mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra), feeling is spoken of by the name of mental formation because of the statement: "These mental states, perception and feeling, are mental formations connected to the mind," and because of the statement: "Excluding initial and sustained thought, all mental states associated with the mind are included in mental formations." All that feeling is gathered under the name of attention and is called here "thorough attention" (sādhukaṃ manasikāraṃ).

Even so, since this feeling is not the object, would it be said that the contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā) is inappropriate? It is not inappropriate. Even in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and others, feeling experiences by making the respective bases of pleasure and so on the object. However, based on the occurrence of that feeling, it is merely a conventional expression to say "I feel." With reference to that convention, it is said: "Feeling a pleasant feeling, one knows: I feel a pleasant feeling," and so on. Furthermore, this answer has already been given in the explanation of the meaning of phrases such as "pītippaṭisaṃvedī" (experiencing rapture). It is also stated in the Visuddhimagga:

"Rapture is clearly known in two ways: through the object and through non-delusion."

How is rapture clearly known through the object? One attains the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. At the moment of attainment, because of the acquisition of the jhāna, rapture is clearly known through the object because the object is clearly known. How is rapture clearly known through non-delusion? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and having emerged from them, one contemplates the rapture associated with the jhāna by way of its rise and fall. For that monk, at the moment of insight, by the penetration of the characteristics...
303: Rapture is clearly known through non-delusion. This statement is taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "For one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of a long inhalation, mindfulness is established; through that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is clearly known." In this same way, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning. Just as rapture, pleasure, and mental formations are clearly known through the attainment of jhāna by way of the object, so too is feeling clearly known through the attainment of attention called feeling associated with this jhāna by way of the object. Therefore, it is well said: "At that time, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating feeling in feelings." "Ānanda, I do not say (the development of mindfulness of breathing is) for one who is forgetful and lacking clear comprehension." In this statement, the meaning is as follows: Because a bhikkhu who proceeds in the manner such as "I shall breathe in clearly knowing the mind," even if he takes the sign of inhalation and exhalation as the object, he proceeds by establishing mindfulness and clear comprehension towards the object of that mind; thus, he is truly one who contemplates the mind in the mind. Indeed, for one who is forgetful and lacking clear comprehension, there is no development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. Therefore, by way of clearly knowing the mind through the object, it is said: "At that time, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind in the mind." "The abandoning of that covetousness and distress is as it is; having seen that abandoning with wisdom, he is one who looks on with equanimity." In this statement, covetousness is indeed the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa); by way of distress, the hindrance of ill-will (byāpāda-nīvaraṇa) is shown. This tetrad is taught only by way of insight (vipassanā). Mindfulness of mental objects (dhammānupassanā) is also of five kinds by way of the section on hindrances (nīvaraṇapabba), etc. In that dhammānupassanā, the section on hindrances is the beginning; even in that, these two hindrances are the beginning. Thus, to show the beginning of dhammānupassanā, it is said: "of covetousness and distress" (abhijjhādomanassānaṃ). "Abandoning" (pahānaṃ) means the knowledge that effects abandoning in the manner: "through the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence." "Having seen that with wisdom" (taṃ paññāya disvā) means having seen that knowledge of abandoning, called the knowledge of impermanence, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment, with another insight wisdom; and seeing that other insight wisdom with yet another insight wisdom; thus, the successive stages of insight...
304: ...is shown. "He is one who looks on with equanimity" (ajjhupekkkhitā hoti) means he looks on with equanimity in two ways: looking on with equanimity by way of neither encouraging nor restraining the meditative mind that has reached the right path, and looking on with equanimity towards what has appeared directly. In such looking on with equanimity, there is equanimity towards conascent (sahajāta) states and equanimity towards the object. Here, equanimity towards the object is intended. "Therefore, Ānanda" (tasmātiha Ānanda) means because a bhikkhu who proceeds in the manner such as "I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence," etc., not only looks on with equanimity towards states such as the hindrances, but also, having seen with wisdom, looks on with equanimity towards the knowledge that effects the abandoning of those states mentioned at the head of covetousness and distress. Therefore, it should be understood: "At that time, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects." "Just so" (evameva kho): In this simile, the six sense bases (āyatana) should be understood like a junction of four main roads. The defilements (kilesa) occurring in the six sense bases should be understood like the heap of dust at that junction. The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) occurring in the four objects should be understood like carts and chariots coming from the four directions. The destruction of evil unwholesome states through the contemplation of the body, etc., should be understood like the crushing and destruction of the heap of dust by a single cart or chariot. ## First Chapter: Ekadhamma Vagga. ## 2. Second Chapter ## 1-2. Commentary on the Icchānaṅgala Sutta, etc. 987-988. In the first sutta of the second chapter, why does the Buddha declare his own meditative dwelling (vihāra-samāpatti) by saying, "You should answer thus"? It is to free the monks from the criticism of outsiders (titthiyas). For if those monks were to say, "We do not know," then the outsiders would criticize them, saying, "You do not even know that your teacher dwelt for the three months of the rains in such-and-such an attainment; why then do you dwell serving that teacher?" He spoke thus to free them from that criticism. In other suttas, the words "eva" (only/just) and "vā" (or) are used, such as "Mindful he breathes in... or breathing in long," but why are they not used here? It is because (this attainment) is an absolutely tranquil attention (manasikāra).
305:
For others, either the exhalation or the inhalation is evident. For the Blessed One, however, because he possesses constantly established mindfulness, both are always evident; thus, because his attention is absolutely peaceful, the word "vā" (or) is not spoken. If the word "vā" is not spoken, why did he say only this much: "I shall breathe out" (assasāmi), without saying "I shall train" (sikkhāmi)? It is because there is no training (sikkhā) left to be practiced. Indeed, the seven types of trainees are called "sekha" because they still have training to practice. The Arahants are called "asekha" because they no longer have training to practice. Likewise, for the Buddhas, all training is completed and there is no further task of training to be done; therefore, "I shall train" was not spoken. The second sutta is quite clear in its meaning.

## 3-10. Commentary on the First Ānanda Sutta, etc.

989-996. In the third sutta, "pavicinati" (investigates) means investigating by way of such aspects as impermanence. The other two terms are merely synonyms for this "pavicinati." "Nirāmisā" (unworldly) means that due to the subsiding of the distress of body and mind, which is free from defilements, both the body and the mind become tranquil. "Samādhiyati" (becomes concentrated) means being well-established, becoming like a mind that has reached absorption (appanā). "Ajjhupekkhitā hoti" (becomes equanimous) means being equanimous through conascent (sahajāta) tatramajjhattūpekkha.

In this way, for a bhikkhu who discerns the body in fourteen ways, the mindfulness that occurs regarding that body is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (sati-sambojjhaṅga). The wisdom associated with that mindfulness is the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga). The bodily and mental energy associated with that same mindfulness is the enlightenment factor of energy (viriya-sambojjhaṅga). Rapture, tranquility, and one-pointedness of mind (cittēkaggatā) are the enlightenment factors of rapture (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), and concentration (samādhi). The middle mode of these six enlightenment factors, characterized by neither receding nor overreaching, is the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga). Just as a charioteer, when the horses are running evenly, does not need to prick them saying "this one is lagging" or pull them saying "this one is running too fast," but merely looks on with a steady posture; even so, the middle mode of these six enlightenment factors, characterized by neither receding nor overreaching, is called the enlightenment factor of equanimity. By this much, the insight enlightenment factors (vipassanā-bojjhaṅga), which occur in a single mind-moment and have distinct individual functions and characteristics, are described.

Terms such as "vivekanissitaṃ" (dependent on seclusion) have the meanings already explained previously. In this sutta, mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) mixed with the enlightenment factors is taught by way of sixteen rounds. The foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) rooted in mindfulness of breathing are...
306:
[Those foundations of mindfulness] are states belonging to the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). Mindfulness of breathing, which is the root of those foundations of mindfulness, also belongs to the preliminary stage. The foundations of mindfulness rooted in the enlightenment factors also belong to the preliminary stage, and those enlightenment factors themselves also belong to the preliminary stage.

However, the enlightenment factors that fulfill true knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti) are the produced supramundane states. True knowledge and liberation are associated with the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala). Alternatively, true knowledge is associated with the fourth path (arahatta-magga), and liberation is associated with the fruit. The fourth, fifth, and sixth suttas also have the same scope as this sutta. The remaining meanings are clear in all the suttas.

## The Commentary on the Ānāpānasamyutta is finished.
307:
## 11. Sotāpattisamyutta
## 1. Veḷudvāra Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Cakkavattirāja Sutta

In the first sutta of the Sotāpattisamyutta, the word "kiñcāpi" is a particle used in the sense of both commendation and reproach. The Teacher spoke the words beginning with, "Bhikkhus, although a wheel-turning monarch [rules the four great islands]..." wishing to commend the state of a wheel-turning monarch who exercises sovereignty and lordship over the four great islands, while also reproaching the fact that he is not yet freed from the four lower realms (apāya). In that passage, "four great islands" refers to the four great islands together with their two thousand surrounding small islands. "Issariyādhipacca": sovereignty is called "issariya," and lordship is called "adhipacca." In the kingship of that wheel-turning monarch, although there is sovereignty and lordship, there is no cutting [of limbs] or destroying, etc.; thus it is called "issariyādhipacca." "Kāretvā" means having exercised (reigned over) such a kingship.

In the phrase, "Bhikkhus, although a noble disciple..." the word "kiñcāpi" is a particle used in the sense of commendation and praise. The Teacher spoke the words beginning with, "Bhikkhus, although a noble disciple..." wishing to commend the fact that he subsists on alms-food scraps, while also praising the fact that he is freed from the four lower realms. In that passage, "nantakāni" refers to clothes without borders or fringes. Even a robe thirteen cubits long is designated as "nantaka" (borderless cloth) from the moment its borders are cut off.

"Aveccappasāda" refers to unshakable confidence. If one asks whether that confidence is one or many, it is only one; it is the confidence attained through the Noble Path. However, because it is directed towards objects [Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha] without priority or posteriority, it is spoken of in three ways by way of those objects, such as "unshakable confidence in the Buddha." And because it is one, it is without differentiation. For a noble disciple, it is not the case that confidence, love, and reverence are great only toward the Buddha and not toward the Dhamma or the Saṅgha; or great only toward the Dhamma and not toward the Buddha or the Saṅgha; or great only toward the Saṅgha and not toward the Buddha or the Dhamma. Terms such as "Itipi so bhagavā" have already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Ariyakanta" refers to the virtues (sīla) that are desired, loved, and pleasing to the Noble Ones. Even when they have passed into another life, the Noble Ones do not violate the five precepts; thus these virtues are dear to them. This is said with reference to those virtues. The terms beginning with "akhaṇḍa" (unbroken) are spoken by way of analogies. A bowl with a piece broken off at the rim is called "broken" (khaṇḍa). One that is cracked in the middle is called "holed" (chidda). A cow with a different color in one spot is called "spotted" (sabala). One that is variegated with many spots is called "mottled" (kammāsa). In the same way...
308:
Virtue that is broken at the beginning or at the end in sequence is called 'broken' (khaṇḍa). Virtue broken in the middle is called 'holed' (chidda). Virtue broken in two or three places in sequence is called 'spotted' (sabala). Virtue broken at intervals is called 'mottled' (kammāsa). Due to the absence of these defects—being broken, holed, spotted, or mottled—the state of being unbroken and so forth should be understood. 'Bhujissehi' means by virtues that make one free (from the slavery of craving). 'Viññuppasatthehi' means by virtues praised by the wise, such as the Buddha and others. 'Aparāmaṭṭhehi' means by virtues that cannot be criticized or grasped with such words as, 'You have done this deed' or 'You have transgressed this virtue.' 'Samādhisavaṭṭanikehi' means by virtues capable of bringing about either absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).

## 2. Brahmacariyogadha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, by the words 'yesaṃ saddhā', devotion to the Buddha is taken. By the word 'sīlaṃ', the virtues dear to the noble ones (ariyakānta-sīla) are taken. By the word 'pasādo', devotion to the Saṅgha is taken. By the words 'dhamma-dassanaṃ', devotion to the Dhamma is taken. Thus, the four factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅga) are taught. 'Kālena paccenti' means they arrive at the appropriate time. 'Brahmacariyogadhaṃ sukhaṃ' means the happiness associated with the three higher paths, which stands having plunged into the noble life (brahmacariya) of the Path. What kind of devotion (pasāda) is this that appears in the verse? The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said, 'It is devotion associated with the Path (magga-pasāda).' The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said, 'It is the devotion associated with the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) of one who has attained the Path.' Both Elders are wise and learned; the words of both are well-spoken. This devotion should be understood as 'mixed devotion' (missaka-pasāda), combining both.

## 3. Dīghāvu Upāsaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'tasmā' means because it is evident in the four factors of stream-entry. 'Vijjā-bhāgiye' means those belonging to the side of knowledge. 'Sabba-saṅkhāresu' means in all conditioned things belonging to the three planes of existence. Thus, for this Dīghāvu Upāsaka, insight (vipassanā) for the three higher paths was taught. 'Vighātaṃ' means suffering.

## 4-5. Paṭhama Sāriputta Suttaādi Vaṇṇanā

1000-1001. The fourth sutta is clear in meaning. In the fifth sutta, 'sotāpattiyaṅga' refers to the factors for the preliminary attainment of the path of stream-entry. The four qualities such as unwavering devotion (aveccappasāda) to the Buddha are also called the factors of a stream-enterer who has already attained those qualities. However, those qualities also appear as 'sotāpattiyaṅga' in the third sutta and others. That is true. In this sutta, the Pali text where 'sotāpattiyaṅga' appears, and the Pali text where it says 'Sāriputta, what are the factors of stream-entry?', thus the term 'sotāpattiyaṅga' has two meanings.
309:
They are called the factors of a stream-enterer who has attained those qualities; these (such as unwavering devotion to the Buddha) also appear in the texts as 'sotāpattiyaṅga'. The word-definition (vacanattha) for both types is: because one attains the path of stream-entry by associating with superior persons, listening to the Dhamma, wise reflection, and practicing the practice that is in accordance with the Dhamma (the preliminary practice such as abhisamācārika), the factors such as association with superior persons (sappurisa-saṃseva) are called 'sotāpattiyaṅga' because they are factors for the sake of stream-entry. The other qualities (such as devotion to the Triple Gem) are also called 'sotāpattiyaṅga' because they are factors of stream-entry, which is known as the first path. They are also called 'sotāpattiyaṅga' because the path of stream-entry is the cause for the realized path of stream-entry.

## 6. Thapati Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'sādhuke paṭivasanti' means they live in their own small revenue-yielding villages named Sādhuka. Among them, Isidatta was a once-returner (sakadāgāmī), and Purāṇa was a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) who was content with his own wife. 'Magge purisaṃ ṭhapesuṃ' means the road at their village gate was the path the Blessed One would travel. Therefore, thinking, 'The Blessed One might pass by at a proper or improper time, while we are asleep or negligent, and then we would not get the chance to see him,' they stationed a man in the middle of the road to keep watch.

'Anubandhiṃsu' means they followed closely behind from a short distance. While the Blessed One traveled by the foot-path in the middle of the cart-road, the other two followed, flanking him on both sides. 'Maggā okkamma' means it is appropriate for Buddhas to perform the duties of hospitality (paṭisanthāra) while walking with someone, while standing, or while sitting during the day. Therefore, the Blessed One thought: 'It is not suitable to perform hospitality while walking with these people, nor while standing. These people are masters in my teaching, having attained the fruits of the noble ones. I will perform hospitality by sitting with them during the day.' Thinking thus, he stepped off the road and approached the foot of a certain tree.

'Paññatte āsane nisīdi' means they had brought an umbrella, sandals, a staff, foot-anointing oil, etc., as well as the eight kinds of drinks and a couch with legs like those of a sarabha deer (sarabha-pāda-pallaṅka). They prepared and offered the couch they had brought, and the Teacher sat upon it. 'Ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu' means after saying, 'Give the remaining items like the umbrella and sandals to the Saṅgha of monks,' they themselves paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at a respectful distance.
310:
The entire statement starting with "He will set out on a walking tour from Sāvatthī among the Kosalans" is spoken only in terms of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). Why? Because it is fixed. For the Buddha's walking tour and the rising of the dawn are fixed; he wanders only in the Middle Country and causes the dawn to rise only in the Middle Country. Therefore, it is spoken in terms of the Middle Country. In the phrase "Our Blessed One will be near us," their joy (somanassa) is not merely because of his proximity, but rather because they think, "Now we will have the opportunity to give gifts, make offerings with scents and garlands, hear the Dhamma, and ask questions," and thus joy arises in those devotees.

Therefore, carpenters, since you feel great displeasure (domanassa) when I am far away and great joy (somanassa) when I am near, for that reason also it should be known that "household life is crowded" (sambādho gharāvāso). This happens to you because of the faults of household life. If you were to leave the household life and go forth, then as you go and come with me, that [displeasure] would not occur. To show this meaning, he said this. In that context, "crowdedness" should be understood in the sense of being with defilements (kileasā) and obstacles. Even for one living in a large house, household life is crowded due to defilements and obstacles. "Rajāpatho" (the path of dust) means the path or place of arrival for the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Abbhokāso pabbajjā" (going forth is like the open air) means that renunciation is like the open air because it is free from defilements and obstacles. Even if two monks sit cross-legged with their knees touching in a small room of only four cubits, renunciation is called "open air" because of the absence of defilements and obstacles. Carpenters, it is fitting for you who live in such a crowded household life to practice only diligence (appamāda).

Those two people were said to have placed those women on two elephants adorned with all ornaments, and placing the King's elephant in the middle, they went on both sides. Therefore, they said, "We make one sit in front and one behind." The elephant must be guarded so that it does not behave erratically. Those sisters must also be guarded so that they do not fall into negligence. Oneself must also be guarded by not smiling, laughing, talking, or looking around, etc.
311:
By those who do not do so, even themselves must be guarded. (For those who do so, there is no need to guard themselves). One who acts in such a way [improperly] must be restrained, thinking, "This person is betraying the master." Therefore, carpenters, because the King always entrusts you with the royal property, living in the world is crowded and is a path for the dust of defilements. But for a monk who wears rag-robes (paṃsukūlika), there is no one who entrusts him so; therefore, renunciation is like the open air. Thus, in all these sentences, he shows, "Carpenters, it is fitting for you to be diligent; practice only diligence (appamāda)."

"Muttacāgo" means one who is liberal in giving. "Payatapāṇī" means one whose hands are washed for the purpose of giving to whoever comes. "Vossaggarato" means one who delights in relinquishment, which is called giving. "Yācayogo" means one who is fit to be asked. "Dānasaṃvibhāgarato" means one who delights in giving and in sharing even a small thing that has been obtained. "Appaṭivibhattaṃ" means not making a division such as "This will be for us, this will be for the monks," but rather everything is intended for giving.

## 7. Commentary on the Veḷudvāreyya Sutta
In the seventh sutta, Veḷudvāra is a village so named because of a large bamboo grove that has existed at the village gate for generations. "Attūpanāyikaṃ" means that which should be applied to oneself (compared to oneself). "Samphabhāsena" means speaking with thoughtless words. "Samphappalāpabhāsena" means speaking with frivolous talk that is useless and devoid of wisdom.

## 8-9. Commentary on the First Giñjakāvasatha Sutta, etc.
1004-5. In the eighth sutta, Ñātika refers to one of two small villages belonging to two cousins (sons of an elder uncle and a younger uncle) situated near a pond. "Giñjakāvasathe" means in a hall made of bricks. "Orambhāgiyānaṃ" means the lower fetters, which cause rebirth only in the sense sphere (kāmabhava). Alternatively, they are called "lower" (ora) because they are to be abandoned by the three lower paths. Among those five, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill will (byāpāda), if not suppressed by attainment (samāpatti) or eradicated by the path (magga), do not allow one to go to the higher realms of the fine-material sphere (rūpabhava) or the immaterial sphere (arūpabhava) by way of rebirth.
312:
The three fetters, beginning with personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), are all called lower fetters (orambhāgiya) because they pull even a person born in higher planes back to be reborn in this sense-sphere (kāma-bhūmi). 'Not subject to returning' (anāvattidhamma) means having the nature of not returning to this sense-sphere by way of rebirth.

Regarding the phrase 'thinning of greed, hatred, and delusion,' it should be understood as thinning in two ways: by occurring only occasionally and by the weakness of their obsessive arising (pariyuṭṭhāna). For a Once-returner (sakadāgāmi), greed and so on do not arise constantly as they do for worldlings (puthujjana); they arise only once in a while. Even when they do arise, they do not arise as thick or as strong as they do for worldlings, but arise thinly like a mosquito's wing. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya and master of the Tipiṭaka, said: 'Because a Once-returner has sons, daughters, and a harem, the defilements are thick; this statement is made in terms of the thinning of [future] existences (bhava-tanuka).' But that statement is rejected in the Commentary because it is said: 'Excluding the seven existences for a Stream-enterer, there is no thinning of existence in the eighth existence; excluding two existences for a Once-returner, there is no thinning of existence in the [remaining] five existences; excluding the fine-material and immaterial existences for a Non-returner, there is no thinning of existence in the sense-sphere existence; for an Arahant, there is no thinning of existence in any existence whatsoever.'

'This world' refers to this sense-sphere world (kāmāvacara-loka). The meaning here is: if one who has attained the fruit of Once-returning in the human realm is reborn in the deva realm and realizes the fruit of Arahantship, that is good. If they cannot, they will certainly return to the human realm and realize it. Likewise, one who attains the fruit of Once-returning in the deva realm, if they are reborn in the human realm and realize the fruit of Arahantship, that is good. If they cannot, they will certainly return to the deva realm and realize it.

Falling into states of woe is called 'vinipāta'; because there is no nature of falling into states of woe, it is called 'avini-pātadhamma.' This means having the nature of not falling into the four lower realms (apāya). 'Fixed' (niyata) means fixed by the law of Dhamma (dhamma-niyāma). 'Destined for enlightenment' (sambodhiparāyaṇa) means that enlightenment, consisting of the three higher paths, is one's destination, refuge, and shelter, which must certainly be reached. 'Vexation' (vihesāvesā) indicates: 'Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who looks at the destination of knowledge, the arising of knowledge, and the future state of knowledge of various individuals, there is only physical weariness.' For the Buddhas, there is no mental weariness.
313:
'Mirror of Dhamma' (dhammādāsa) means a mirror made of Dhamma. 'By which' (yena) refers to the person endowed with that Mirror of Dhamma. The phrase 'destruction of states of woe, bad destinations, and ruin' is spoken by way of synonyms for hell and so on. Indeed, hell and so on are called 'apāya' because they are devoid of the benefit called growth (aya). They are called 'duggati' because they are the destination and refuge of suffering. They are called 'vinipāta' because those who do evil fall into them helplessly. The ninth sutta is clear in meaning.

## 10. Tatiya Giñjakāvasatha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'more than fifty' (paropaññāsā) means those exceeding fifty. 'More than ninety' (sādhikanavutī) means those exceeding ninety. 'More than six' (chātirekāni) means six more than (five hundred). Although that village was not very large, there were many noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) there. In various places, 2,400,000 beings died at once from the plague (ahivāta-roga); among them, there were this many noble disciples (more than 50 Non-returners, more than 90 Once-returners, and more than 500 Stream-enterers). In all the remaining suttas, the meaning is clear.

## The First Chapter: Veḷudvāra Vagga.
## 2. Rājakārāma Vagga
## 1. Sahassa Bhikkhunī Saṅgha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'Rājakārāma' is the name of the monastery (ārāma) so called because it was built and offered by the King (King Pasenadi of Kosala). That monastery was built by King Pasenadi of Kosala. It is said that during the period of the first enlightenment (early Buddhahood), seeing the Teacher (the Buddha) had reached the pinnacle of gain, retinue, and fame, the ascetics (titthiyas) thought: 'The ascetic Gotama has reached the pinnacle of gain, retinue, and fame. However, this ascetic Gotama has not reached this pinnacle by depending on any other virtue (sīla) or concentration (samādhi). He has taken the 'head of the earth' (a superior location). If we too could have a monastery built near Jetavana, we would also reach the pinnacle of gain, retinue, and fame.' They urged their own supporters and, having obtained about a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas, took them and went to the King. The King asked, 'What is this?' They gave a bribe, saying, 'We will build an ascetic monastery near Jetavana. If the ascetic Gotama or the disciples of the ascetic Gotama come and forbid it, do not allow them to forbid it.' The King took the bribe and said, 'Go and build it.'
314:
Those heretics went and, having their attendants bring building materials such as timber, began erecting pillars and so on, making a great noise and a loud uproar. The Blessed One came out from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) and, standing at the porch, asked, "Ānanda, whose are these loud and great noises, like fishermen scrambling for fish in a net?" Venerable Ānanda replied, "Venerable Sir, the heretics (tirthikas) are building a monastery for themselves near the Jetavana Monastery." The Buddha said, "Ānanda, these people are thorns to the Dispensation (Sāsana); they will cause discomfort to the Saṅgha of monks. Therefore, inform the King and have them stopped."

Venerable Ānanda went to the palace gate with the Saṅgha of monks. Although the ministers informed the King, "Great King, the elders have arrived," the King did not come out because he had accepted a bribe. The elders returned and informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One then sent Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna. The King did not grant an audience to these two Chief Disciples either. They returned and reported, "Venerable Sir, the King did not come out." At that very moment, the Blessed One made a prediction: "This King will not be able to pass away while remaining in his own kingdom."

On the second day, the Blessed One himself, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, went and stood at the palace gate. Hearing that the Blessed One had arrived, the King came out, invited Him into the palace, seated Him on a noble throne, and offered rice gruel and hard food. After the Blessed One had finished the meal, the King came and sat near Him, intending to stay until the meal proceedings were fully concluded. The Blessed One, instead of saying directly, "Great King, you have done such a thing," thought, "I will make him understand through a reason," and brought forth this story of the past: "Great King, it is not proper to cause conflict among those who have gone forth. In the past, a King caused conflict among hermits and was submerged in the ocean along with his kingdom." The King asked, "Venerable Sir, when did that happen?"

"Great King, in the past, in the kingdom of Bharu, a king named Bharu reigned. Two groups of five hundred hermits each came from the foot of the mountains to the city of Bharu to seek salt and acidic foods. Near the city, there were two trees. The group of hermits that arrived first sat at the foot of one tree, and the group that arrived later sat at the other tree. Having stayed as long as they pleased, they returned to the foot of the mountains. When they came again, they sat at the foot of their respective trees. As time passed, one tree withered. The hermits who came to that withered tree thought, 'This tree is large; for us too...'"
315:
"...it will be sufficient for them too," and the remaining hermits sat in one part of the foot of the other tree. When the original occupants arrived later, they did not enter the foot of the tree but stood outside and asked, "Why are you sitting here?" The others replied, "Teachers, our tree has withered. This tree is very large; you also enter. It will be sufficient for both you and us." The hermits who arrived later said, "We do not wish to enter; you must leave." After an argument, they said, "Will you not leave of your own accord?" and, grabbing them by their hands and so on, they drove them out. Those who were driven out thought, "Wait, we will give those hermits a lesson they will remember." By psychic power, they created two golden wheels and a silver axle, and rolling them along, they went to the palace gate. The King was informed, "Great King, hermits are standing here with such a gift." The King was delighted and said, "Invite them in." After inviting them, he said, "You have performed a great deed. Is there anything I can do for you?" They replied, "Yes, Great King. There is a tree-foot where we used to stay. Other hermits have taken it. We would like you to have that place returned to us." The King sent his men and drove out the original hermits.

Those who were driven out stood outside and watched, "What did they give to get it?" Seeing the gift, they thought, "We too will give a bribe and take the place back." By psychic power, they created a golden chariot frame and took it to the King. Seeing it, the King was delighted and asked, "Venerable sirs, what should I do?" They replied, "Great King, another group of hermits is staying at the foot of our tree. We would like you to have that tree-foot returned to us." The King sent his men and drove those hermits out again. After the hermits had quarreled with each other, they felt remorse, thinking, "We have done an improper thing," and being troubled at heart, they returned to the foot of the mountains. Then the deities, angry that "This King took bribes from both groups of hermits and caused them to quarrel with each other," overturned the great ocean and turned the King's territory, about a thousand yojanas in extent, into the ocean.

"I have heard that King Bharu, having caused a rift among the sages, was destroyed along with his kingdom and came to ruin."

When the Blessed One had thus shown this story of the past, because the words of the Buddhas are trustworthy, the King reflected on his own actions and was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "I have done an improper thing." He gave the order, "Friends, drive out the heretics!" and had them expelled. Then he thought, "I have not yet built a monastery that should be built. I will build a monastery right here." He then took the timber and bamboo structures of those heretics...
316:
(The King) thinking, "I have done what should not be done without careful consideration," ordered, "Friends, expel the heretics," and after having them expelled, he thought, "There is no monastery built and offered by me yet; I will build a monastery in that very place." He then had the monastery built without even giving them the timber and materials. With reference to this, these words (regarding the Rājakārāma) were spoken.

## 2-3. Commentary on the Brāhmaṇasutta and Others

1008-9. In the second sutta, "udayagāminiṃ" means the practice that leads to growth in one's own doctrine. "Maraṇaṃ āgameyyāsi" means one should desire or long for death. The third sutta is quite clear in meaning.

## 4. Commentary on the Duggatibhayasutta

In the fourth sutta, by the words "sabbaduggatibhayaṃ samatikkanto," the lack of merit and deficiency in the human realm is excluded.

## 5. Commentary on the Duggativinipātabhayasutta

In the fifth sutta, by the words "sabbaduggativinipātabhayaṃ samatikkanto," the four woeful states along with the lack of merit in the human realm are excluded.

## 6. Commentary on the First Mittāmacchasutta

In the sixth sutta, "mittā" (friends) refers to companions who associate by consuming material gifts (giving and receiving) at each other's houses. "Amaccā" (associates) refers to those who perform tasks together in conversation, movement, posture, and so on. "Ñātī" (relatives) refers to relatives from the side of the parents-in-law. "Sālohitā" (blood relatives) refers to siblings, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and so on, who share the same blood.

## 7. Commentary on the Second Mittāmacchasutta

In the seventh sutta, "aññathattaṃ" (alteration/change) is of many kinds: change in devotion, change in state (bhāva), change in destination (gati), change in characteristic (lakkhaṇa), and change in transformation. Among these, "bhāvaññathattaṃ" (change in state) regarding the great elements is intended. Indeed, when the earth element, which exists in a solid state as gold and so on, melts and reaches the state of water, the previous solid state disappears and the liquid state (bhāvaññathatta) becomes apparent. However, the characteristic does not disappear; it remains as the characteristic of hardness (kakkhaḷa). In the state of liquid such as sugarcane juice...
317:
...when the water element dries up and reaches the state of solid earth, the previous (liquid) state disappears and another kind of state becomes apparent. However, the characteristic does not disappear; it remains only as the characteristic of cohesion (ābandhana). In this context, "aññathattaṃ" (alteration) refers to "gatiaññathattaṃ" (change in destination to a woeful state); such change in destination does not exist for a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka). Change in devotion (pasādaññathattaṃ) also does not exist; however, in this sutta, "gatiaññathattaṃ" is shown to illustrate the fruit of devotion. The remaining meanings are clear in all places.

## The Second Vagga, Rājakārāma Vagga, is finished.

## 3. Saraṇāni Vagga

## 1-2. Commentary on the First Mahānāmasutta and Others

1017-18. In the first sutta of the third vagga, "iddhaṃ" means being prosperous with oil, honey, molasses, and so on. "Phītaṃ" means being in a state of flourishing, as if well-bloomed with ornaments such as hand-ornaments, head-ornaments, and neck-ornaments. "Ākiṇṇamanussaṃ" means being crowded with people without any gaps. "Sambhādabyūhaṃ" refers to a city with many "byūhas," which are blind alleys or narrow lanes where one must exit by the same way one entered. By this word, the density of houses in the city is shown. "Bhantena" refers to one who moves with an agitated gait, wandering here and there. The second sutta is clear in meaning.

## 3. Commentary on the Godhasakkasutta

In the third sutta, the words "Only the Blessed One would know whether one is endowed with these qualities or not" were spoken by Godha the Sakyan with the meaning that only the Blessed One can know the state of stream-entry (sotāpanna) of a person endowed with three or four qualities.

"If some cause (dispute) should arise" means if, for some reason, the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks have different views and the Blessed One is on one side, and the Saṅgha of monks is on the other side, the Blessed One would be on one side speaking one doctrine, and this Saṅgha of monks would also be on one side speaking one doctrine.
318:
It means "on one side." Therefore, it is said, "Whatever doctrine you, venerable sirs, speak, that doctrine alone I shall accept." Indeed, is there not no difference in the devotion of a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) towards the Triple Gem? Yet, why is this said? It is because of the Buddha's omniscience (sabbaññutā). For to him, the thought occurs: "The Saṅgha of monks, not being omniscient, might speak without knowing; but for the Teacher, there is no such thing as not knowing." Therefore, he spoke thus. "Aññatra kalyāṇā aññatra kusalā" means I speak only of what is good, only of what is wholesome; I do not speak of anything apart from the good and wholesome. Alternatively, this should be noted as a fault of his lack of reflection.

## 4. Paṭhamasaraṇānisakkasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, the phrase "Mahānāma, here some person" is intended to show that not only are those who go for refuge liberated from the states of deprivation, but these persons are also liberated. "Mattaso nijjhanaṃ khamanti" means they accept (delight in) through measure and through reflection. By this, the person who is a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) on the path is shown. "One who does not go to hell" means it is not appropriate to say that a person on the path (maggattha) has already been liberated from the states of deprivation, nor that he will be liberated; rather, it is appropriate to say he is being liberated. Because he is being liberated, he is not one who goes; thus he is called "agantā," meaning he does not go. By the phrase "saddhāmattaṃ pemamattaṃ," the person who is a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) on the path is shown. "Mahāsālā" is said to point out the four great sal trees standing nearby. "He undertakes the training at the time of death" shows that at the time of death, he became one who fulfills the three trainings.

## 5. Dutiyasaraṇānisakkasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "dukkhettaṃ" means an uneven field. "Dubbhūmi" refers to poor soil, such as salty or alkaline soil that is ruined. "Khaṇḍāni" means broken seeds. "Pūtīni" means seeds that have become rotten due to being wet with water. "Vātātapahatāni" means seeds that have lost their essence due to the effects of wind and sun. "Asārādāni" means seeds that have no core (not worth taking). "Asukhasayitāni" means seeds that are not well-stored in granaries and the like. "Sukhasayitāni" means seeds that are well-kept without being moved for four months in their storage place.
319:
## 6. Paṭhamaanāthapiṇḍikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "ṭhānaso vedanā paṭippassambheyya" means the feeling should be calmed instantly. "Micchā-ñāṇena" means by wrong repeated reflection. "Micchā-vimuttiyā" means by a liberation that does not lead out (from the states of deprivation). Therefore, the verses beginning with "Tasmā saddhañca sīlañca" have the meanings already explained. "Yatra hi nāma" means having such a nature.

## 7. Dutiyanāthapiṇḍikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, "samparāyikaṃ maraṇabhayaṃ" means the fear of death rooted in the future life. "Gihisāmīcikāni" means practices appropriate for laypeople. The remaining words are clear in all the suttas.

## Saraṇānivaggo tatiyo.
The third chapter, the Saraṇāni Chapter, is finished.

## 4. Puññābhisandavaggo
4. The Puññābhisanda Chapter.

## 1. Paṭhamapuññābhisandasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, "puññābhisandā kusalābhisandā" means torrents of merit and torrents of wholesomeness, which are like great rivers. "Sukhasāhārā" means causes of happiness.

## 4. Paṭhamadevapadasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "devapadāni" means the paths (footprints) trodden by the knowledge of the devas, or by the knowledge of the Buddha, who is a deva. "Visuddhiyā" means for the sake of purification from defilements. "Pariyodapanāya" means for the sake of all-around cleansing and for the sake of illumination. In this sutta, the four persons established in the fruits (phalattha) are also called 'devas' because of their purity.

## 8. Vassasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, "pāraṃ gantvā": 'pāra' refers to Nibbāna; it means having reached that Nibbāna. "Āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattanti" means it is not that they first reach Nibbāna and then later lead to the destruction of the taints (āsavas); rather, while going towards Nibbāna, they lead to the destruction of the taints. The teaching, however, is presented in this way.
320:
## 10. Nandiyasakkasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "divā pavivekāya rattiṃ paṭisallānāya" means for the sake of seclusion during the day and for the sake of peaceful dwelling in the object of meditation at night. "Dhammā na pātubhavanti" means the states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) do not arise. The remaining words are clear in all the suttas.

## Puññābhisandavaggo catuttho.
The fourth chapter, the Puññābhisanda Chapter, is finished.

## 5. Sagāthakapuññābhisandavaggo
5. The Sagāthakapuññābhisanda Chapter.

## 1. Paṭhamaabhiasandasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, "asaṅkheyyo" means incalculable by the measure of an āḷhaka; however, in terms of leagues (yojana), there is a calculation for that ocean. "Bahu-bheravaṃ" means having many terrifying objects by way of both sentient and non-sentient terrifying objects. "Puthū" means many. "Savanti" means flowing. "Upayanti" means they approach.

## 2. Dutiyaabhisandasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "yatthimā mahānadiyo saṃsandanti samenti" means at the confluence where these great rivers like the Gaṅgā and Yamunā become one, joining without interval.

## 3. Tatiyaabhisandasutta-vaṇṇanā

## 3. Dhammadinnasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, Dhammadinna is one of seven persons. Indeed, during the time of the Buddha, there were seven persons: Dhammadinna the lay follower, Visākha the lay follower, Ugga the householder, Citta the householder, Hatthaka of Āḷavī, Cūḷaanāthapiṇḍika, and Mahaanāthapiṇḍika, each of whom had a retinue of five hundred lay followers. Among them, this Dhammadinna was one.

"Gambhīrā" (deep) refers to suttas such as the Salla Sutta, which are deep in Dhamma. "Gambhīratthā" (deep in meaning) refers to suttas such as the Cetanā Sutta, which are deep in meaning. "Lokuttarā" (supramundane) refers to suttas such as the Asaṅkhata Saṃyutta, which explain supramundane meanings. "Suññata-ppaṭisaṃyuttā" (connected with emptiness) refers to suttas such as the Khajjanika Sutta, which explain the emptiness of beings. "Upasampajja viharissāmā" means we shall dwell having attained it. "Dhammadinna, in this way you should train" means you should train while fulfilling the practice like the moon (candopama-paṭipadā), the practice of the relay chariots (rathavinīta-paṭipadā), the practice of the sage (moneyya-paṭipadā), and the practice of the great noble lineage (mahā-ariyavaṃsa-paṭipadā). Thus, the Teacher placed an unbearable burden upon these lay followers.
322:
Why? It is said that these people, not standing within their own level, requested an exhortation; instead, they requested, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One exhort us," as if they were capable of carrying the entire burden without distinction. Therefore, the Teacher, wishing to place an unbearable burden upon them, spoke thus. "Na kho netaṃ" is simply "Na kho etaṃ." Here, the letter "n" should be understood as a mere consonant junction (vyañjanasandhi). "Tasmā" (therefore) is because they now requested an exhortation while standing within their own level.

"Yadidaṃ vimuttiyā vimuttaṃ" means if one were to speak of the distinction of liberation based on this liberation, I do not speak of that distinction. Indeed, for the Saṅgha of monks, there is no measure in the duties of the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, nor in the eighty duties of the Khandhakas, and such incoming qualities; however, when the Path or Fruit is penetrated, there is no distinction between lay followers and monks.

In the first sutta of the Saccasaṃyutta, regarding "samādhiṃ, bhikkhave," it is said that those monks were declining from one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). In the passage "Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘idaṃ dukkhan’ti yogo karaṇīyo," the definition of the cause should be understood by way of knowing things as they really are.

To clarify this statement: Monks, because a concentrated monk knows the Four Noble Truths as they really are, therefore you too, being concentrated, should make an effort to know the Four Noble Truths as they really are, thinking, "This is suffering." Likewise, because the Four Noble Truths become manifest only upon the appearance of a Tathāgata, and because they are well-analyzed by the Tathāgata, and because in those Four Noble Truths there are immeasurable syllables and immeasurable words and phrases, and because the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) increases due to not penetrating those Truths, and does not increase from the time those Truths are penetrated, therefore you should make an effort, thinking, "This is suffering," so that "In this way, our round of rebirth will not increase."

## 10. Commentary on the Tiracchānakathā Sutta
In the tenth sutta, "anekavihitaṃ" means of various kinds. "Tiracchānakathā" (lowly talk) refers to talk that stands crosswise to the paths to heaven and Nibbāna, as it does not lead out of the lower realms or the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). In the case of "rājakathā" (talk about kings) and so forth, talk that proceeds by way of mentioning kings, such as "King Mahāsammata, King Mandhātu, and King Dhammāsoka possessed such great power," is called talk about kings. This same principle applies to "corakathā" (talk about thieves) and others.

Among these, talk that is based on sensual pleasure, such as "Such a king is handsome and beautiful to look at," is indeed lowly talk (tiracchānakathā). However, talk that proceeds in this way: "Even such a powerful king has come to destruction and passed away," stands as a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Regarding thieves, talk based on sensual pleasure, such as "Mūladeva was so powerful; Meghamāla was so powerful," and saying "Oh, how brave they were!" in reference to their deeds, is lowly talk. Regarding war, in the Bhārata war and others, talk that is motivated by the desire for sensual excitement, such as "This person was killed by that person in this way; he was stabbed in that way," is lowly talk. However, talk that proceeds as "Even they have come to destruction and passed away," becomes a subject of meditation in all instances. Furthermore, regarding talk about food and so forth, it is not proper to speak for the sake of sensual pleasure, saying, "We have chewed, eaten, drunk, and enjoyed such food that was endowed with color, aroma, taste, and texture." But it is proper to speak in a fruitful way, saying, "In the past, we offered food, drink, clothing, bedding, flowers, scents, and ointments endowed with color and so forth to virtuous ones, and we performed offerings at the stupa."

Regarding talk about relatives and so forth, it is not proper to speak for the sake of pleasure, saying, "Our relatives are brave and capable," or "In the past, we traveled and enjoyed ourselves with such exquisite vehicles." But it is proper to speak fruitfully, saying, "Those relatives of ours have also come to destruction," or "In the past, we offered such sandals to the Saṅgha." Regarding talk about villages and so forth, it is not proper to speak for the sake of pleasure regarding whether the village is well-situated or poorly-situated, whether food is abundant or scarce, or saying, "The inhabitants of this village are brave and capable." But it is proper to speak fruitfully, saying, "They have faith and devotion," or "They have come to destruction." The same principle applies to talk about market towns, cities, and districts.
326:
Talk about women should not be engaged in with a desire for enjoyment based on their appearance, figure, and so on. It is only appropriate to speak in this way: "They have faith, they are devoted, they have passed away (reached destruction)." Talk about heroes should not be engaged in with a desire for enjoyment, such as "The soldier named Nandimitta was a brave hero." It is only appropriate to speak in this way: "He had faith, he was devoted, he has passed away." There is also a variant reading "surākathā" (talk about liquor). That talk about liquor also should not be engaged in with a desire for enjoyment, such as "Drinking liquor of such a nature produces delight." However, it is appropriate to speak by way of seeing the faults, in such a manner as "It leads to madness," and so on. Talk about streets should not be engaged in with a desire for enjoyment, such as "Such a street is well-laid, or poorly-laid," or "Those living in this street are brave and capable." It is only appropriate to speak in this way: "They have faith, they are devoted, they have passed away." 

Kumbhaṭṭhānakathā refers to talk about watering places, or talk about water-carrying slave girls. That talk also should not be engaged in with a desire for enjoyment, such as "She is lovely, she is skilled in dancing and singing." It is only appropriate to speak in the manner of "They have faith, they are devoted," and so on. Pubbapetakathā is talk about departed relatives. In that talk, the decision is the same as talk about living relatives. Nānattakathā is pointless talk of various natures, which is free from preceding or succeeding talk. Lokakkhāyikā is the kind of Lokāyata and sophistical talk such as "Who created this world? Such a person created it. The crow is white because its bones are white; the crane is red because its blood is red," and so on. Samuddakkhāyikā is pointless talk about the ocean such as "Why is the ocean called Sāgara? It is called Sāgara because it was dug by King Sāgara. It is called Samudra because he indicated with a hand gesture (mudrā) saying 'It was dug by me (me khatā)'," and so on. 

Talk that proceeds by stating any pointless reason such as "It is thus, it is not thus" is called itibhavābhavakathā. Here, "bhava" means eternalism (sassata), and "abhava" means annihilationism (uccheda). "Bhava" means prosperity, and "abhava" means decline. "Bhava" means sensual pleasure, and "abhava" means self-mortification. These thirty-two kinds of talk, together with the six kinds of itibhavābhavakathā, are called tiracchānakathā (lowly talk). The remaining meanings are clear in all places.
