## 2. Dhammacakkappavattana Vagga
## 1. Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the second vagga, "Bārāṇasiyaṃ" means in the city named Bārāṇasī. "Isipatane Migadāye" means in the park known as Migadāya because it was given as a sanctuary for deer, and called Isipatana because it is the place where sages (isīs), such as the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas who possess virtues like the morality group (sīlakkhandha), descend and ascend. To explain further, in this Migadāya, all the Omniscient Buddhas who have appeared descend and reside there to turn the Wheel of Dhamma. After seven days, having arisen from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) from the Nandamūlaka cave, and having performed duties such as washing their faces at Lake Anotatta, the Paccekabuddha sages also descend here by traveling through the air. They assemble there for the purpose of the Uposatha or for other matters. When returning to Mount Gandhamādana, they also ascend from that very place. Thus, because it is the place of descent and ascent for sages, it is called "Isipatana."

"Āmantesi" (He addressed) refers to the Buddha who, since making the aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) and eventually renounced the world in his final birth. Having reached the Bodhi-maṇḍa and sat upon the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka), he defeated the hosts of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; and at the end of the last watch, causing the ten thousand world systems to echo, he attained omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). After spending seven weeks (49 days) at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, being requested by Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. Out of compassion for the world, he went to the city of Bārāṇasī, informed the group of five (Pañcavaggiya) that he had become a Buddha, and addressed them with the desire to turn the Wheel of Dhamma.

"Dveme bhikkhave antā" means "Monks, these two extremes (or portions)." As soon as these words were uttered, the sound of the utterance reached down to the Avīci hell and up to the highest point of existence (Bhavagga), spreading throughout the ten thousand world systems. At that very moment, eighteen crores of Brahmas, who had fulfilled their perfections to realize the Four Noble Truths and possessed mature roots of merit, assembled. In the west, the sun was about to set, and in the east, the full moon appeared in conjunction with the Āsāḷha constellation. At that time, the Blessed One, undertaking to teach this Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, spoke the words beginning with "Dveme bhikkhave antā."
328:
In that sentence, 'by one gone forth' (pabbajitena) refers to a person who has cut the bonds of a householder and attained the state of a monk. 'Should not be followed' (na sevitabbā) means should not be indulged in. 'Devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure in the sense-objects' (yo cāyaṃ kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogo) refers to the repeated pursuit of pleasure associated with the defilement of sensuality in the objects of desire. 'Lowly' (hīno) has the meaning of base or inferior. 'Vulgar' (gammo) refers to that which belongs to the village-dwellers. 'Of the worldlings' (pothujjaniko) refers to that which is constantly practiced by foolish worldlings who are blind to the eye of wisdom. 'Ignoble' (anariyo) means not noble, not pure, not superior, or not belonging to the Noble Ones (ariyas). 'Unprofitable' (anatthasaṃhito) means not connected with benefit, not relying on the cause that brings welfare and happiness. 'Devotion to self-mortification' (attakilamathānuyogo) means the repeated pursuit of one's own exhaustion, the act of making oneself suffer. 'Painful' (dukkho) refers to that which brings suffering through self-torture, such as sleeping on a bed of thorns.

Because it gives rise to the eye of wisdom, it is called 'vision-producing' (cakkhukaraṇī). The second term (ñāṇakaraṇī) is a synonym for that very vision-producing. 'For peace' (upasamāya) means for the purpose of stilling the defilements. 'For higher knowledge' (abhiññāya) means for the purpose of knowing the Four Noble Truths with special knowledge. 'For enlightenment' (sambodhāya) means for the purpose of fully penetrating those same Four Noble Truths. 'For Nibbāna' (nibbānāya) means for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna. Whatever else remains to be said in this sutta has already been mentioned in various places below. The entire discourse on the Truths (Saccakathā) has also been explained in detail in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga.

'Three rounds' (tiparivaṭṭaṃ) means having three rounds by way of the knowledge of the truth (sacca-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the task (kicca-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of what has been done (kata-ñāṇa). Herein, the knowledge that knows the Four Noble Truths as they really are, such as 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering,' is called sacca-ñāṇa. Within those same Four Noble Truths, the knowledge that knows the task to be performed, such as 'It should be fully understood, it should be abandoned,' is called kicca-ñāṇa. The knowledge that knows the completed state of each task, such as 'It has been fully understood, it has been abandoned,' is called kata-ñāṇa. 'Twelve modes' (dvādasākāraṃ) means having twelve modes by way of the three modes in each of the four truths. 'Knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassanaṃ) is the vision known as knowledge that arises by way of these three rounds and twelve modes. 'Dhamma-eye' (dhammacakkhu) refers to the three paths and three fruits in other contexts, but here it refers only to the first path (Sotāpatti-magga).

'Dhammacakka' refers to both penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and teaching knowledge (desanā-ñāṇa). For the penetrative knowledge of twelve modes that arose regarding the Four Noble Truths for the Buddha seated at the Bodhi-maṇḍa is called Dhammacakka; and the teaching knowledge set in motion by the discourse on the Truths of twelve modes by the Buddha seated at Isipatana is also called Dhammacakka. Both of these are indeed the knowledge that occurred within the heart of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala).

"Yatra hi nāma" means "those who". "More difficult than the difficult" means extremely difficult. "One should pierce tip with tip of a hair split sevenfold" means having split a single hair into seven parts, taking one part and tying it in the middle of an eggplant, and tying another part to the tip of an arrow, standing at a distance of about an usabha, one should pierce that tip tied to the eggplant with the tip tied to the arrow—this is the meaning. "Therefore" means because the Four Noble Truths are thus difficult to penetrate; therefore [it is said].
333:
## 7. Commentary on the First Chiggala Sutta

In the seventh sutta, "eating one another" (aññamaññakhādikā) means mutual devouring. "The strong eating the weak" (dubbalakhādikā) means strong fish, etc., eating weak fish, etc.

## 8. Commentary on the Second Chiggala Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "the great earth" (mahāpathavī) refers to the great earth within the interior of the universe (cakkavāḷa). "Venerable sir, this is a spontaneous occurrence" means it happens by chance. If that yoke did not rot, if the water in the ocean did not dry up, and if that blind turtle did not die, it might happen by a chance coincidence.

"Monks, this is very rare to happen by chance": In this context, the Elder Mahāsīva shows four yokes. Just as the neck of that blind turtle entering the hole of a yoke thrown by a man standing at the edge of the eastern universe is a chance acquisition, so is the attainment of human birth. The yoke thrown by a man standing at the edge of the southern universe, while wandering, reaches the first yoke and, being placed hole upon hole, the turtle's neck enters; this is rarer than the rare, like the arising of a Tathāgata. The yoke thrown by a man standing at the edge of the western universe, while wandering, reaches the previous two yokes and, being placed hole upon hole, the turtle's neck enters; this is even rarer than the previous two, like the illumination of the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. The yoke thrown by a man standing at the edge of the northern universe, while wandering, reaches the previous three yokes and, being placed hole upon hole, the turtle's neck enters; this should be known as extremely rare, like the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

The ninth sutta and others are in the same manner as stated in the Abhisamaya Saṃyutta.

## The Fifth Chapter: Papāta Vagga.

## 6. Commentary on Abhisamaya Vagga

The Abhisamaya Vagga has been explained in detail in the Abhisamaya Saṃyutta of the Nidāna Vagga.

## 7. The First Āmakadhaññapeyyāla Vagga

## 3. Commentary on Paññā Sutta

In the Āmakadhaññapeyyāla, "with the noble eye of wisdom" (ariyena paññācakkhunā) means with the eye of knowledge, both mundane and supramundane, beginning with insight (vipassanā).

## 4. Commentary on Surāmeraya Sutta

In the phrase "abstaining from the occasion of negligence of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants" (surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā paṭiviratā): Surā is of five kinds: liquor made from flour, from rice, from cakes, with yeast added, and mixed with ingredients. Meraya is any kind of intoxicant (āsava) such as flower-sap or fruit-sap. Majja refers to both of those, or any other intoxicating substance apart from surā and āsava. The volition (cetanā) with which they drink it is called "the occasion of negligence" (pamādaṭṭhāna) because it is the cause of negligence in wholesome deeds. The meaning is that they abstain from drinking intoxicants which are the cause of that negligence.

## 6-7. Commentary on Matteyya Sutta, etc.

1136-37. "Matteyyā" means those who seek the welfare of their mother, those who practice rightly towards their mother. In "Petteyya" and so on, one who seeks the welfare of their father is "Petteyya."

## 8-9. Commentary on Sāmañña Sutta, etc.

1138-39. Seeking the welfare of recluses (samaṇas) is "Sāmañña." Seeking the welfare of brahmins is "Brahmañña." These are designations for those who practice rightly towards those respective persons.

## 10. Commentary on Pacāyika Sutta

"Respectful to the elders in the family" (kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino) means those who respect the elders in their family, those who have a humble conduct.
335:
## 8. Dutiya-āmakadhaññapeyyālavagga

## 8. Commentary on Bījagāmasutta
"Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā" means abstaining from destroying—by means of cutting, cooking, crushing, and so forth—the five kinds of seeds (bījagāma), namely: root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, bud-seeds, and grain-seeds; and also the group of living plants (bhūtagāma) such as various green grasses, trees, and the like.

## 9. Commentary on Vikālabhojanasutta
"Vikālabhojanā" means eating at a time that exceeds the proper time for the Noble Ones. It means consuming food that is to be eaten within a limited time (yāvakālika) during the period starting from after noon until the following dawn.

## 10. Commentary on Gandhavilepanasutta
Among the words such as "mālā," "mālā" refers to any kind of flower. "Gandha" refers to any kind of scent. "Vilepana" refers to ointments applied to beautify the complexion. Among those flowers and scents, those who wear them are said to "dhārenti" (wear). Those who fill in deficient areas are said to "maṇḍenti" (adorn). Those who enjoy them for the sake of the scent or for beautifying the complexion are said to "vibhūsenti" (beautify). The word "ṭhāna" refers to the cause. Therefore, it means abstaining from those acts of wearing flowers and so forth, which the general public performs with the intention of violating virtue.

## 9. Tatiya-āmakadhaññapeyyālavagga

## 1. Commentary on Naccagītasutta
Viewing that which is like a thorn because it is inconsistent with the Dispensation (Sāsana) is called "visūkadassana." "Naccagītavāditavisūkadassana" refers to viewing dancing, singing, and music—whether performed by oneself or by causing others to perform, and even including such things as peacock dances—which are like thorns to the Dispensation. It is not allowable for monks or nuns to perform these acts of dancing and so forth themselves, to cause others to perform them, or to watch them when they are performed.
336:
## 2. Commentary on Uccāsayanasutta
A place that exceeds the proper measurements is called "uccāsayana" (high bed). Unallowable types of rugs or coverings are called "mahāsayana" (luxurious bed). It means abstaining from such high and luxurious beds.

## 3. Commentary on Jātarūpasutta
"Jātarūpa" refers to gold. "Rajata" refers to coins—such as copper coins, lac coins, or wooden coins—that are used in commerce. It means abstaining from accepting both gold and silver. They do not take it themselves, nor do they cause others to take it, nor do they consent to it being kept nearby.

## 4. Commentary on Āmakadhaññasutta
"Āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇā" means the acceptance of the seven kinds of raw grains, namely: hill rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and rye (kudrūsaka). Not only is the acceptance of these raw grains unallowable, but even touching them is unallowable for monks.

## 5. Commentary on Āmakamaṃsasutta
In this term "āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇā," except for meat and fish allowed through the proper procedure, the acceptance of raw meat and raw fish is unallowable for monks; however, touching them is not unallowable (it is allowable).

## 6. Commentary on Kumārikasutta
In this term "itthikumārikapaṭiggahaṇā," a woman who has gone to another man (is married) is called "itthī," and any other young woman is called "kumārikā." Both the acceptance and the touching of such women and young girls are unallowable.

## 7. Commentary on Dāsidāsasutta
In this term "dāsidāsapaṭiggahaṇā," the acceptance of those persons in the capacity of female or male slaves is unallowable. However, if they are offered using allowable terminology such as "I offer this attendant (kappiyakāraka)" or "I offer this monastery worker (ārāmika)," then it is allowable.

## 1. Commentary on Khettavatthusutta
## 10. Catuttha-āmakadhaññapeyyālavagga
The manner of what is allowable and unallowable regarding objects starting from goats and sheep up to fields and lands should be investigated according to the Vinaya. In this context, "khetta" (field) refers to the ground where grains are grown. "Vatthu" (land) refers to the ground where various beans and pulses are grown. Alternatively, the place where both are grown is called "khetta," and the portion of land not yet prepared for such cultivation is called "vatthu." By the primary terms "khetta" and "vatthu," things such as lakes, ponds, and dams are also included.

## 2-3. Commentary on Kayavikkayasutta, etc.
1162-63. "Kayavikkaya" refers to buying and selling. Carrying a written message or a verbal message of laypeople and going to various places is called the work of a messenger (dūteyya). Going on a short journey when sent from house to house is called running errands (pahiṇagamana). Engaging in both of these is called "anuyoga." Therefore, the meaning in the term "dūteyyapahiṇagamanānuyoga" should be understood in this way.

## 4. Commentary on Tulākူဋsutta
In "tulākūṭa" and so forth, "kūṭa" means deception. Among them, deception by scales (tulākūṭa) is of four kinds: rūpakūṭa, aṅgakūṭa, gahaṇakūṭa, and paṭicchannakūṭa. Among these four, "rūpakūṭa" is making two scales of similar appearance and, when taking from others, using the large scale, and when giving from oneself, using the small scale. "Aṅgakūṭa" is pressing the back part of the scale with the hand when taking, and pressing the front part when giving. "Gahaṇakūṭa" is holding the rope at the base when taking, and holding it at the tip when giving. "Paṭicchannakūṭa" is making the scale hollow and putting iron powder inside; when taking, one makes that powder move to the back, and when giving, one makes it move to the front.

A gold bowl is called "kaṃsa"; deception with that gold bowl is "kaṃsakūṭa." How? They make one genuine gold bowl and make two or three other copper bowls look like gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering a wealthy family, they say, "Buy these gold bowls." When asked the price, they intend to give them at a very cheap rate. Then, those people ask, "How can the genuine gold nature of these..."
338:
When it is asked, "How shall the genuineness of the gold be known?" they say, "Take it after testing," and having rubbed the gold plate on a stone, they give all the (other) copper plates and depart.

Fraudulent measurement (mānakūṭa) is of three kinds: piercing the heart (hadayabheda), breaking the crest (sikhabheda), and breaking the rope (rajjubheda). Among these, piercing the heart is found when measuring ghee, oil, and so on. For, one who takes those goods, using a measure with a hole at the bottom, says, "Pour it slowly," and having caused much to leak into his own vessel, he takes it; when giving, he closes the hole, fills it quickly, and gives. Breaking the crest is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so on. For, one who takes those goods raises the crest slowly and takes it; when giving, he quickly breaks down the crest and gives. Breaking the rope is found when measuring fields and lands. For, those who do not receive a bribe measure a small field by making it large.

## 5. Ukkoṭanasutta-vaṇṇanā
Among the terms such as ukkoṭana, ukkoṭana means taking a bribe to make an owner a non-owner. Vañcana means deceiving others by various means. In this regard, there is this story: A hunter comes bringing a large deer and a young deer. A trickster asks, "Friend, how much is the large deer, and how much is the young deer?" When told, "The large deer is two kahāpaṇas, the young deer is one," he gives one kahāpaṇa, takes the young deer, goes a little way, and returns. He says, "Friend, I have no need for the young deer; give me the large deer." The hunter says, "Then give two kahāpaṇas." The trickster says, "Friend, did I not give one kahāpaṇa at first?" "Yes, you did," the hunter replies. "Then take this young deer as well; thus, that one kahāpaṇa and this young deer worth one kahāpaṇa will make two kahāpaṇas." The hunter, thinking "He speaks with reason," took the young deer and gave the large deer.

Nikati (fraud) is deception by means of a counterfeit, whether through an act or through illusion, making what is not an ornament appear as an ornament, what is not a gem as a gem, and what is not gold as gold. Sāciyoga means crooked practice. It is indeed another name for these very things like ukkoṭana. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as ukkoṭana-sāciyoga, vañcana-sāciyoga, and nikati-sāciyoga. Some say that sāciyoga is the exchanging of one thing after showing another, but that is included within vañcana itself.

## 6-11. Chedanasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
1166-71. Among the terms such as chedana, chedana means the cutting off of hands, feet, and so on. Vadha means killing. Bandha means binding with ropes and the like. Viparāmosa (plundering under cover) is of two kinds: plundering under the cover of snow (himaviparāmosa) and plundering under the cover of thickets (gumbaviparāmosa). When, at the time of snowfall, being concealed by snow, one robs a person traveling on the road, this is called himaviparāmosa. When one robs while concealed by thickets and the like, this is called gumbaviparāmosa.

Ālopa refers to the plundering and destruction of villages, market towns, and so on. Sahasākāra means an act of violence; having entered a house and placed a weapon against the chests of people, it is the taking of desired goods. In this way, they abstain from these aforementioned acts of cutting, killing, binding, plundering under cover, looting, and acts of violence. The remaining words in all places have meanings that are quite clear.
